file: 2011/2011-10-26_big business_business ethics_ceo needs underling_drink industrial sludge_risk of brain worms_drink himself.gif
title: CEO's Sludge-Drinking Volunteer Wanted

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO needs an underling to drink our industrial sludge at a press conference to prove it's safe.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Um... Is there some reason he doesn't do it himself?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, but I forget the details. It was something about the risk of brain worms.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells Asok that the CEO needs a subordinate to drink the company's industrial sludge at a press conference to prove it is safe. Asok asks why the CEO won't drink it himself. The Boss casually says he forgets the details but it involved a risk of brain worms.
punchline: The CEO refuses to drink the sludge because of the danger of brain worms, which reveals the sludge is clearly unsafe and that an expendable underling is being asked to take the risk.
summary: A manager casually recruits a junior employee to publicly gulp toxic waste, brushing off the CEO's own refusal as a vague worm-related concern.

file: 2011/2011-04-01_therapy session_cloud_having meeting_tech talk_couch_shrink_avatar_engineer_engineering.gif
title: Therapist Misreads Virtual Cloud Meeting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was holding a virtual meeting using the cloud and...

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: You're already dead and you don't know it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... no, I'm an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: And yet your soul had a meeting in a cloud. Interesting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My people call it an avatar.

setting: A therapist's office, with Dilbert lying on the couch
situation: Dilbert lies on a therapist's couch and describes holding a virtual meeting using the cloud. The therapist takes the tech jargon literally, concluding he is already dead and that his soul met in a cloud. Dilbert patiently corrects her that engineers call that an avatar.
punchline: Ordinary tech terms like cloud, virtual meeting and avatar sound like descriptions of the afterlife to a non-technical listener, and Dilbert is stuck translating engineer-speak into plain language.
summary: A therapist hears an engineer's talk of virtual cloud meetings and mistakes it for a spiritual experience of death.

file: 2011/2011-11-24_commerce_service business_unmotivated sales guy_slides are blank_compelling reason_no commission work_budget issues.gif
title: Salesman With Blank Slides Pitch

transcript.speaker: Caption
transcript.text: Unmotivated sales guy

transcript.speaker: Sales Guy
transcript.text: My slides are blank because no one told me what our product does.

transcript.speaker: Sales Guy
transcript.text: And I don't have a compelling reason to find out because I don't work on commission.

transcript.speaker: Sales Guy
transcript.text: If anyone asks why you didn't place an order, would you mind saying you have budget issues?

setting: Conference room during a sales presentation
situation: A salesman stands beside a blank projection screen and admits to the audience that his slides are empty because nobody explained the product to him. He says he has no incentive to learn about it since he isn't paid on commission. He then asks the prospective customers to cover for him by blaming their lack of an order on budget issues.
punchline: The salesman is so unmotivated that he not only gives a pitch with nothing in it but also asks the audience to lie to protect him from blame for the lost sale.
summary: A sales rep with an empty slideshow cheerfully admits he knows nothing about the product and asks his would-be customers to make up an excuse for him.

file: 2011/2011-06-21_approval from cloud_matrix management_office workers_smoke cloud.gif
title: Approval From The Management Cloud

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll need approval from the Cloud.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The Cloud?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It was once called matrix management. But it got so complicated that no one knows who does what.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you approve this?

transcript.speaker: Cloud
transcript.text: What did everyone else say?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he needs approval from "the Cloud," and explains it is the new name for matrix management that became so convoluted nobody knows who is responsible for what. Dilbert then approaches a group of managers, one of whom has a literal cloud for a head, and asks for approval. The cloud-headed manager responds by asking what everyone else said.
punchline: The cloud-headed approver won't decide anything without knowing what everyone else said, showing that nobody in a tangled matrix organization will take responsibility for a decision.
summary: A tangled management structure gets rebranded as a cloud, and the faceless approver simply defers to the opinions of everyone else.

file: 2011/2011-02-13_honesty_less meetings_less micromangemt_managers & supervisors_meetings_more meetings_more with less_business.gif
title: Doing More With Less Means More

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have to learn to do more with less.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Less meetings?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No. We'll need more meetings to figure out how to do more with less.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Less micro-management?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I'll have to watch you more closely than ever to make sure you're doing more with less.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm talking about using less money.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Oh, like a death spiral. Why didn't you just say that in the first place?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's as if you're talking more to say less.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Should we be more like you or less?

setting: Conference room during a management meeting, with a title-card header showing Dogbert on a stool beside a Dilbert projection screen
situation: The Boss announces the team must learn to do more with less. Alice keeps guessing what he wants cut, such as meetings and micromanagement, and he rejects each guess by saying he wants more of both. He finally reveals he only meant spending less money, and Alice points out the contradiction.
punchline: The Boss's 'do more with less' slogan actually means more meetings and more micromanagement, and the only thing he wants less of is money, so he talks at length to say very little.
summary: A manager's cost-cutting slogan turns out to demand extra meetings and closer supervision, with the only real reduction being the budget.

file: 2011/2011-08-10_fraternization_bad haircut_poor font choice_hand sanitizer_substance over style.gif
title: Judging Business Case by Haircut

transcript.speaker: Woman with big hair
transcript.text: I'm judging the quality of your business case by your bad haircut and your poor font choice.

transcript.speaker: Woman with big hair
transcript.text: I plan to use a quart of hand sanitizer when I'm done touching your document.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: I value substance over style.

transcript.speaker: Woman with big hair
transcript.text: How's that working out?

setting: Office meeting room with a desk
situation: A man sits across a desk from a woman with enormous teased hair who is reviewing his business case document. She openly criticizes his haircut and font choice and says she will sanitize her hands after touching his paper. He claims to value substance over style, and she sarcastically asks how that is working out for him.
punchline: The man's claim that he values substance over style is undercut by the fact that his proposal is being rejected purely on superficial style, so her sarcastic question points out that philosophy is getting him nowhere.
summary: A reviewer dismisses a proposal over trivial looks, and when the presenter touts substance over style, she wryly asks how that approach is paying off.

file: 2011/2011-10-07_inventions_thinking_creative_teacher_business card_ideationista_education.gif
title: Ideationista Business Card Creativity Consultant

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired Ken to teach us how to be more creative.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: According to his business card, his title is "Ideationista."

transcript.speaker: Ken
transcript.text: That was some of my best work.

situation: The Boss introduces Ken, a consultant he hired to teach the staff creativity, while Dilbert and a coworker look on. The Boss points out that Ken's business card gives his title as "Ideationista." Ken admits that the made-up title was some of his best work.
punchline: The consultant's only visible creative output is the ridiculous invented job title on his business card, implying he has little real creativity to teach.
summary: A manager proudly hires a creativity trainer whose most inventive accomplishment turns out to be a silly buzzword title.

file: 2011/2011-08-25_anger_thinking_ignorant_backstabbing_die_make changes.gif
title: Dilbert Silently Fumes at Boss

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Customer meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I may correct what Dilbert just said, I'm sure it would be easy to make those changes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You ignorant, backstabbing son of a beach ball.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you saying something inside your head?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Die.

setting: Conference room during a customer meeting
situation: In a meeting with a customer, the Boss contradicts Dilbert and promises the customer that requested changes would be easy. Dilbert silently seethes, thinking insults at the Boss. When the Boss notices his expression and asks if he is saying something in his head, Dilbert denies it while thinking a murderous wish.
punchline: Dilbert cannot voice his anger at the Boss in front of a customer, so he insults him mentally and falsely denies it, thinking 'Die' as the Boss accurately guesses what he is up to.
summary: A boss undercuts his engineer by promising a client easy changes, and the engineer privately wishes him dead while politely denying any complaint.

file: 2011/2011-07-14_cruelty_fraternization_friendship_new engineer_ginat dork_star wars chess set_email_set up date_romantic preference_relationships.gif
title: Dork Matchmaking Goes Wrong

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Have you met the new engineer? He's a gigantic dork. You two would get along great.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll email him to set up a date with you. Is tomorrow good?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Being a dork is not a romantic preference.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He says he'll bring his "Star Wars" chess set.

situation: A coworker sitting at her desk tells Dilbert about the new engineer, calling him a gigantic dork who would be perfect for Dilbert. She offers to email him to arrange a date for tomorrow. Dilbert objects that being a dork is not a romantic preference, but she reports that the engineer has already agreed and will bring his Star Wars chess set.
punchline: The coworker assumes Dilbert's nerdiness makes him a romantic match for any other nerd, and she has already arranged the date despite his objection.
summary: A well-meaning colleague pairs Dilbert with a fellow geek purely on the basis of shared nerdiness and books the date before he can protest.

file: 2011/2011-07-30_exercise & fitness_office workers_using company gym_60 hrs week_paying for itself.gif
title: Gym Pays for Itself, Raise Denied

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, I can't give you a raise because you've been using the company gym during work hours.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I work sixty hours a week! Why did we build a new gym if I'm not supposed to use it???

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You were right. That gym is totally paying for itself.

situation: The Boss tells Ted he can't have a raise because he has been using the company gym during work hours. Ted angrily protests that he works sixty hours a week and asks why the gym was built if he shouldn't use it. Later the Boss, sitting with Catbert, remarks that the gym is paying for itself.
punchline: The gym pays for itself because the company uses it as an excuse to deny raises, saving more money than the gym cost.
summary: A manager turns an employee's use of a new workplace perk into the reason for withholding his pay increase.

file: 2011/2011-11-17_boredom_golf_golf game_boss_talk about game_locked in syndrome_no visitors_sports.gif
title: Golf Stories Threat Backfires Twice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who wants to hear about my golf game?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe someone with locked-in syndrome who doesn't get any visitors.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just for that, I'm going to tell you twice.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: No, please. I'll do anything.

situation: The Boss, holding a golf club, offers to tell everyone about his golf game while Dilbert and Alice stand with coffee mugs. Alice sarcastically says the only audience for it would be a locked-in syndrome patient with no visitors. The Boss punishes her insult by promising to tell the story twice, and she begs him not to.
punchline: Alice's sarcastic insult that only a paralyzed, lonely person would listen backfires, as the Boss treats it as a reason to subject her to the boring golf story twice.
summary: A golf-obsessed manager answers a coworker's snide remark about his tedious stories by doubling the dose, leaving her pleading for mercy.

file: 2011/2011-11-04_comparing a task_criticism_employees_executives_quality is bad_your imagination_time_quality_boss_business.gif
title: Compared To Your Imagination, Quality Bad

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why did this take so long?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're comparing a task — the likes of which has never been done — to your imagination of how long such things should take.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well then, the quality is bad.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Compared to...?

situation: The Boss, seated at his desk holding a paper, asks Dilbert why a task took so long. Dilbert points out that the task is unprecedented, so the Boss is only comparing it to an imagined timeline. The Boss switches tactics and declares the quality bad, and Dilbert asks what he is comparing that to.
punchline: The Boss's criticism has no valid baseline, so when he swaps complaints from speed to quality, he is again judging a unique task against nothing but his own imagination.
summary: When his manager grumbles about a groundbreaking project's duration and then its supposed poor quality, an engineer exposes that both judgments rest on no real standard.
keywords: why did this take so long

file: 2011/2011-06-04_writing_writing systems_press relese_vp of engineering_personal resons_speculate_bieber fever_write fiction.gif
title: Press Release Bieber Fever Fiction

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, all I wanted you to say in the press release is that our VP of Engineering is leaving for personal reasons.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You didn't need to speculate on the reasons.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's lose the part about "Bieber Fever."

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Everyone thinks it's easy to write fiction.

situation: The Boss reviews a press release written by Tina, the technical writer, about the departure of the VP of Engineering. He complains that she was only supposed to say the VP was leaving for personal reasons, but she added speculation, including a reference to "Bieber Fever." Tina responds that people underestimate how hard it is to write fiction.
punchline: Tina made up an absurd reason for the executive's departure and defends it as skilled creative writing, implying she is happy to invent fiction in official company communications.
summary: A writer embellishes an official departure announcement with invented gossip, then complains that her creative talent goes unappreciated.

file: 2011/2011-01-17_anger_engineers_honesty_beginning of decline_salted note_good idea_why don't we format_social product.gif
title: Boss's Social Product Idea Doomed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have a great idea! Why don't we make our product social?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because when you start to understand a concept, it marks the beginning of its decline.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: On a related note, it's never a good idea to ask an engineer a question in the "why don't we" format.

situation: The Boss excitedly proposes making the company's product social, holding it up as a great idea. Dilbert, standing with coffee beside Alice, replies that a concept starts to decline once the Boss begins to understand it. He then warns that asking an engineer a question phrased as "why don't we" invites a blunt, sarcastic answer.
punchline: Dilbert tells the Boss that a trend declines as soon as he grasps it, then sarcastically warns him that "why don't we" questions invite an engineer's blunt reasons why not.
summary: A manager hops on a trendy bandwagon and gets an insulting answer from an engineer who explains why such questions are a bad idea.

file: 2011/2011-05-11_computer software_internet & world wide web_coding_paywall_website_wrote script_new content_idea to eliminate_revenue_lowered costs_technology.gif
title: Wally Deletes Content Instead of Paywall

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, did you finish coding the paywall for our website?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I did something better. I wrote a script to delete any new content as soon as it's posted.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: At bonus time, keep in mind that you're the one who had the idea to eliminate revenue, and I'm the one who lowered hosting costs.

situation: The Boss asks Wally whether he has finished coding a paywall for the company website. Wally, holding his coffee mug, says he did something better: a script that deletes any new content the moment it is posted. He then points out that the Boss's idea eliminated revenue while his own work lowered hosting costs, and suggests this be remembered at bonus time.
punchline: Wally sarcastically presents deleting all website content as a cost-saving achievement, while pinning the revenue-killing idea on the Boss and angling for a bonus.
summary: Instead of building a requested paywall, a lazy engineer automates the destruction of all new site content and claims credit for cheaper hosting.

file: 2011/2011-09-22_joking_questioning_feel free_questions_ghosts have clothes_wedgie.gif
title: Ask Anything: Ghosts and Wedgies

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are there any questions? Feel free to ask anything at all.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why do ghosts have clothes?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If someone gives you a wedgie at the moment you die, will you have it for eternity?

situation: At a meeting, The Boss invites the attendees to ask anything at all. Wally takes him literally and asks why ghosts have clothes, and Dilbert follows up with a question about whether a wedgie received at the moment of death would last for eternity. The Boss looks increasingly unimpressed while the attendees sit around the table.
punchline: When invited to ask anything at all, the employees raise absurd, irrelevant questions about ghosts and wedgies instead of anything related to the meeting.
summary: Given an open invitation to ask questions, the meeting attendees come up with silly philosophical queries about the afterlife.

file: 2011/2011-11-08_next is lie_personnel officers_planning layoffs_questioning_repeat question_communication styles_pattern of talking.gif
title: Repeating the Question Signals a Lie

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you planning layoffs?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Am I planning layoffs?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When you repeat my question it means the next thing you say will be a lie.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Go.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I love your stinkin' guts.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss whether layoffs are being planned, and the boss simply repeats the question back. Dilbert points out that this habit is a tell that a lie is coming next, then invites the boss to continue. The boss responds with an absurdly insincere compliment.
punchline: The boss's flattery is so obviously a deflection that it confirms layoffs are coming and that he is lying to avoid saying so.
summary: A employee calls out his manager's evasive habit of parroting questions before fibbing, and the manager immediately proves him right with empty flattery.

file: 2011/2011-08-28_anger_honesty_meetings_honest opinions_plan_hold back_feedback_monkey eats_fermented fruit.gif
title: Boss Asks for Brutally Honest Feedback

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want your honest opinions on my plan.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't hold back anything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's coworker
transcript.text: Does he mean that?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why don't you find out?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's coworker
transcript.text: Yes, I have some feedback.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Your plan reminds me of what happens when a monkey eats fermented fruit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's coworker
transcript.text: He's all ooh-ooh-ooh and then he falls out of the tree.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that how he looks when he hears honesty?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Beats me. I've never tried it.

situation: The Boss presents a plan on a flowchart and invites his team to give honest opinions without holding back. A coworker takes him up on it and compares the plan to a monkey that eats fermented fruit, acting drunk and falling out of a tree. The Boss fumes with rage while Dilbert and Wally watch.
punchline: Wally admits he has never tried honesty, implying that no one in the company ever gives the Boss genuine feedback, and the one time someone does, he reacts with fury.
summary: A manager begs for candid criticism of his scheme, gets an insulting animal analogy, and turns purple with anger while his team looks on.

file: 2011/2011-12-10_despair_office workers_self respect_prison_goals_slavery_self inflicted_angry_weak.gif
title: Wally's Anti-Motivational Meeting Wisdom

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Self-respect is like a prison for the soul.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Goals are a form of self-inflicted slavery.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sorry I'm late.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That which does not kill us makes us angry and weak.

situation: Wally sits at a conference table holding his coffee mug and delivers a series of bleak, inverted motivational sayings to a coworker. The Boss arrives late to the meeting and Wally greets him with yet another twisted version of a famous quote.
punchline: Wally turns uplifting self-help clichés into cynical anti-wisdom that justifies his own lack of ambition and self-respect, ending with a twisted version of the 'what doesn't kill us makes us stronger' saying.
summary: A coffee-clutching slacker recites a string of upside-down motivational slogans that celebrate low standards and laziness.

file: 2011/2011-05-23_computers & peripherals_internet & world wide web_coupons_email_firewall_malicious complience_downside_dogs of hell.gif
title: Malicious Compliance Unleashes Firewall Hell

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mordac, I'm not getting the coupons by email that I signed up for. Can you dial back the firewall or something?

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Absolutely. There's nothing I enjoy more than malicious compliance with your requests.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is there any downside?

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Unleash the dogs of hell!

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Grrrr

situation: The Boss asks Mordac, the IT security enforcer, to loosen the firewall so he can receive coupon emails. Mordac cheerfully agrees, announcing his love of malicious compliance, and starts typing. When the Boss asks if there's a downside, Mordac shouts for the dogs of hell to be unleashed and the computer growls.
punchline: Mordac gleefully lowers the security for a trivial request and invites catastrophic consequences, because letting the Boss's careless demand through will let all manner of malicious traffic in.
summary: A boss wants his shopping coupons and asks the security gatekeeper to ease the firewall, with disastrous results.

file: 2011/2011-11-28_annoyance_another anonymous email_correlation_employees_link to article_worlds worst boss_business.gif
title: Anonymous Emails About Worst Bosses

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Someone sent me another anonymous email with a link to an article about the world's worst bosses.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I get one of those emails every time I leave your cubicle. Did you think I wouldn't notice the correlation?

transcript.speaker: Thought bubble (Dilbert's coworker)
transcript.text: Correlation does not imply causation.

situation: The Boss visits Dilbert's cubicle and complains that he keeps receiving anonymous emails linking to articles about the world's worst bosses. He says it happens every time he leaves Dilbert's cubicle and accuses Dilbert of thinking he wouldn't notice. Meanwhile, a coworker hiding in the next cubicle sends the email on his phone while thinking about correlation versus causation.
punchline: Dilbert is innocent of the correlation the Boss spotted, because the real sender is a coworker who is sneakily emailing from nearby and thinking that the Boss's logic is flawed even as he proves it wrong.
summary: A suspicious manager blames the wrong employee for sending him mocking emails, while the actual culprit quietly hits send from the neighboring cubicle.

file: 2011/2011-01-20_excitement_interviews_wages_interview_less money_worse job_imagined better_hald day_next useless interview_money.gif
title: Hopeful Interview, Worse Job Offer

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How did your interview go yesterday?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Great!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They offered less money for a worse job. But for half a day I imagined it would be better.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Half a day?! Lucky!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know! I can't wait for my next useless interview!

situation: At the coffee machine, a coworker asks Dilbert how his job interview went. Dilbert cheerfully calls it great, then explains the offer was less money for a worse job, though he enjoyed half a day of imagining it would be better. The coworker envies him for getting even that much hope.
punchline: Dilbert and his coworker are so beaten down by the job market that half a day of false optimism before a disappointing offer counts as a win worth repeating.
summary: A job seeker proudly reports that a bad offer at least gave him a few hours of unfounded hope, which his coworker finds enviable.

file: 2011/2011-12-25_christmas presents_embarrassment_merry christmas_network design meeting_brand of makeup_hid_loobby_elevator_closet for months_creepiness.gif
title: Gift-Wrapped Creepiness at the Elevator

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Merry Christmas, Sarah. This is for you.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: Have we met?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We attended the same network design meeting last April.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I overheard you telling someone in the hallway that you like a specific brand of makeup.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I bought a box of it and kept it in the closet for months.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I came to work early today and hid behind the sculpture in the lobby until I saw you heading to the elevator.

transcript.speaker: Sarah
transcript.text: I didn't know you could gift wrap creepiness.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry. Just act like I'm not here.

characters: Woman with dark red hair (another coworker)
situation: Dilbert gives a wrapped present to a coworker named Sarah who barely knows him. As he explains the details, it becomes clear he eavesdropped on her, bought her favorite makeup, stored it for months, and ambushed her at the elevator after hiding in the lobby. A second woman arrives and joins the awkward wait for the elevator.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt at a thoughtful gift reveals stalker-like behavior, so the present is really a wrapped-up creepy confession, and his apology only makes the situation more awkward.
summary: A socially clueless engineer hands a near-stranger a Christmas present and unwittingly reveals how much he spied on her to pick it out.

file: 2011/2011-10-21_blazers_buying work clothes_female_men's clothing_pantsuit talking_unisex store_unisex suit_women suits.gif
title: The Pantsuit Is Talking

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm buying my work clothes at the unisex suit store.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's no such thing as a unisex suit store.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You always have to be right.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's the pantsuit talking.

situation: Alice tells Dilbert she plans to buy her work clothes at a unisex suit store. Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, flatly insists no such store exists. Alice complains that he always has to be right, and Dilbert replies by blaming her outfit for the attitude.
punchline: Dilbert turns Alice's complaint into a pun by saying her argumentative streak is 'the pantsuit talking', playing on 'the liquor talking' and implying her pantsuit is making her combative.
summary: A coworker's claim about where she shops for suits prompts a quibble, and the argument ends with a quip about her clothing speaking for her.

file: 2011/2011-05-02_exhaustion - tiredness_office workers_peak efficeincy_brain_peak effiency_not working.gif
title: Brain Not Working, Nothing Important

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My brain isn't working at its peak efficiency this afternoon.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Common sense says I should go home early to avoid making any mistakes that would be bad for the company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Unless... nothing I... do is important.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sounds like your brain is back to its peak efficiency.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that his brain is not working well this afternoon and he should go home early to avoid costly mistakes. He then realizes that this logic only holds if his work matters. The boss replies that he sounds like he is thinking clearly again.
punchline: By admitting his work is unimportant, Dilbert accidentally proves his mind is sharp, and the boss's sarcastic reply confirms that nothing he does matters, so he can't leave early.
summary: An employee's excuse to leave early collapses when he concedes his job doesn't matter, and his boss cheerfully declares him fully functional.

file: 2011/2011-07-21_cruelty_embarrassment_not judeg_quality of question_technical.gif
title: Judging People By Their Technical Questions

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: ... And so, that's my question.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I try to not judge people by the quality of the technical questions they ask.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is it working?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not even a little.

situation: A coworker with red hair finishes asking Dilbert a technical question. Dilbert says he tries not to judge people by the quality of their technical questions, then the coworker hopefully asks if his judgment of him is working. Dilbert bluntly says it is not.
punchline: Dilbert claims he doesn't judge people by their technical questions, but admits that his effort to avoid doing so is failing completely, meaning the coworker's question was terrible.
summary: A man's clueless tech question prompts Dilbert to politely claim open-mindedness before admitting he is absolutely judging him.

file: 2011/2011-06-05_absent mindedness_annoyance_status upadte_multitask_one task_doubling rate of failure_useless blob of carbon.gif
title: Multitasking Boss Misses Status Update

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Seriously? You're going to do email while I give my status update?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't worry. I can multitask.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Multitask? You can barely do ONE task properly.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: All you're doing is doubling your rate of failure.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Congratulations on becoming the most useless blob of carbon in the universe.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What? Sorry. I missed that.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I said my project is on schedule.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay. Great.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This totally works for me.

setting: Conference room during a status meeting
situation: Alice gives a project status update while the Boss answers email on his device. When he claims he can multitask, she insults him at length, telling him he is the most useless blob of carbon in the universe. Because he is not listening, he misses it, and she simply reports that her project is on schedule.
punchline: Because the Boss never pays attention to the update, Alice can say anything she likes to him without consequence, which suits Dilbert and Alice just fine.
summary: An inattentive manager reading email during a meeting never hears the insults his employee delivers before she gives a bland all-clear report.

file: 2011/2011-05-26_blaming_quarreling_work independantly_close eyes_fall back_better than other people.gif
title: Trust Fall Without Anyone Catching

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Today you'll learn how to work independently.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In this exercise, I want you to put your arms at your side, close your eyes, and fall backward.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Thud thud

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Thud

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And it's still better than working with other people.

setting: Corporate training session with a stool as a stage
situation: Dogbert, acting as a trainer, stands on a stool and introduces a workshop on working independently. He instructs the attendees to fall backward with their eyes closed and arms at their sides, with no one to catch them. They crash to the floor, shown only by their feet and thud sound effects.
punchline: The painful trust fall with nobody catching them is presented as an improvement over the frustration of teamwork, implying coworkers are even less reliable than the floor.
summary: A trainer leads employees through a backward-falling drill that leaves them sprawled on the ground, then insists that's still preferable to collaborating with colleagues.

file: 2011/2011-05-25_couples_dating_mobile (cell) phones_ex boyfreind_entertainment stabdard_samrtphone_smartphone scale_lying larry_relationships.gif
title: Dating Judged by Smartphone Standards

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I used to compare all men to my ex-boyfriend.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Now I compare all men to the entertainment standard of my smartphone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I only scored a two on the smartphone scale, but I was a solid five compared to someone named "Lying Larry."

setting: Restaurant table on a date, then Dilbert's living room
situation: Dilbert is on a date with a woman who explains that she no longer measures men against her ex-boyfriend but against how entertaining her smartphone is. In the last panel, Dilbert is back home telling Dogbert how the date went, rating himself a two on her smartphone scale.
punchline: Dilbert's date ended up scoring him barely above a liar, because a smartphone is a more entertaining companion than he is.
summary: A woman sizes up her dates by how well they entertain compared with her phone, and Dilbert's dismal score is only rescued by a worse rival.

file: 2011/2011-04-23_announcements_committee decided_file naming_month_year_day_space_temperature_airport_hat size_long meeting_best work.gif
title: Committee's Absurd File Naming Convention

transcript.speaker: Committee member
transcript.text: The committee decided that the file naming convention will start with the date, in the order of month, year, day. . .

transcript.speaker: Committee member
transcript.text: . . . then a space, then the temperature at the airport, and the hat size of the nearest squirrel.

transcript.speaker: Committee member
transcript.text: To be perfectly honest, it was a long meeting and we probably didn't do our best work toward the end.

situation: A committee member announces the company's new file naming convention, which begins sensibly with the date but quickly descends into nonsense, requiring the airport temperature and the hat size of the nearest squirrel. The second panel shows the office building exterior as the absurd rules are read out. He then admits the committee got worse as the long meeting dragged on.
punchline: The committee's rules started out reasonable but degraded into absurdity as meeting fatigue set in, and the speaker casually admits it.
summary: A committee unveils a file naming standard that starts normally and ends in ridiculous requirements, blaming their exhaustion after a marathon meeting.

file: 2011/2011-03-19_belittle subordinates_cruelty_evil intensions_fill in_managers & supervisors_on vacation_fill in for boss_business.gif
title: Alice Relishes Belittling Imaginary Instructions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I need you to fill in for me while I'm on vacation.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yay!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can't wait to belittle my subordinates for not doing the things I only imagined telling them to do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why would you do that?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why would you ask that?

situation: The Boss asks Alice to cover for him while he is on vacation, and she cheerfully agrees. She then gleefully says she looks forward to berating her subordinates for failing to do things she only imagined telling them to do. When the Boss asks why she would do that, she answers with the same question, implying that is simply how managers behave.
punchline: Alice's plan to criticize people for tasks she never assigned is presented as normal management behavior, so she is baffled that the Boss, who does exactly this, would question it.
summary: A stand-in manager eagerly plans to scold her team for failing to read her mind, and deflects the boss's puzzlement by implying it is what bosses do.

file: 2011/2011-09-01_writing_writing materials_executive leadership_money good_pie chart_kitten.gif
title: Dumbing Down for Executives: Money Be Good

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you word that more simply? I need to explain it to the executive leadership.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Money be good. This make more. Oogah!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That was uncalled for.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can replace the pie chart with a kitten.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, asks Alice to reword a document so he can explain it to the executive leadership. Alice types and responds in absurdly primitive caveman-like language. When he objects, she offers to swap the pie chart for a kitten.
punchline: Alice sarcastically implies that executives are so simple-minded that they need caveman grunts and cute animal pictures instead of real information.
summary: Asked to simplify a report for the higher-ups, a programmer answers in grunting caveman speak and offers a kitten picture in place of the chart.

file: 2011/2011-04-08_cartoonists_ventriloquism_writing_hand puppet_data overload_ridiculous_poorly written story_case closed.gif
title: Alice Dismisses Police Report as Bad Writing

transcript.speaker: Police Officer
transcript.text: We have a report of a Pointy-Haired Boss being stunned by data overload, stuffed, and used as a hand puppet.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's ridiculous. It sounds like the plot of a poorly written story arc.

transcript.speaker: Police Officer
transcript.text: It sounds poorly drawn too.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Case closed, right?

situation: Two police officers question Alice about a report that the Pointy-Haired Boss was overwhelmed with data, stuffed, and used as a hand puppet. Alice dismisses the claim as implausible, comparing it to a poorly written story arc. One officer agrees it also sounds poorly drawn, and Alice smugly suggests that settles the matter.
punchline: The strip pokes fun at itself, with the officer admitting the crime sounds 'poorly drawn' and Alice cheerfully using that as an excuse to get off the hook for what was presumably a real incident.
summary: Cops investigating a bizarre hand-puppet attack on the boss accept Alice's argument that the story is too badly written and drawn to be real.

file: 2011/2011-11-27_frustration_gadgets_smartphone interface rage_perfect storm_bad interface design_chubby fingers_poor signal strenth_smashing phone_frustrated_can't survive_lesser of two eveils.gif
title: Smartphone Rage and the Wall

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whoa! Watch out.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've read about this. It's called smartphone interface rage.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's caused by the perfect storm of bad interface design, chubby fingers, and poor signal strength.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He'll get so frustrated that he'll consider smashing his phone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then he'll realize he can't survive without his phone and he'll be twice as frustrated.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We have to do something.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Run as fast as you can into the wall! It will take your mind off of your phone!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes the best you can hope for is that the lesser of two evils is the funny one.

situation: The Boss stomps down the hallway angrily fumbling with his smartphone while Dilbert and Wally watch with coffee mugs. They diagnose his condition as 'smartphone interface rage' and predict he will get even angrier when he realizes he can't live without the phone. When Wally says they have to do something, Dilbert urges the Boss to run headfirst into a wall, and the Boss ends up collapsed on the floor.
punchline: Dilbert cynically 'helps' the frustrated Boss by distracting him with a head-first wall collision, framing it as the lesser evil that at least provides entertainment.
summary: Two coworkers watch their furious boss struggle with his phone and decide the kindest cure is to send him sprinting into a wall.

file: 2011/2011-06-12_computers & peripherals_machinery_office equipment_prototype_traffic_traffic load test_ask lab_didn't ask lab.gif
title: Nobody Asked, So Nobody Knew

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you ask the lab if they have a way to test traffic loads on our prototype?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I met with them for an hour and explained that we need traffic load tests.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But you didn't actually ask if they could do the tests?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well... No... But...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's their job to do the tests, and they would have mentioned it if they didn't have a way to do it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But you didn't ask.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That was the context of the meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If they couldn't do that sort of test they would have mentioned it sometime during our hour together.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you should ask.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! Okay! I'll ask!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you freakin' kidding me?!!!

transcript.speaker: Lab Technician
transcript.text: I wondered why you didn't ask.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether the lab can run traffic load tests on the prototype. Dilbert spent an hour with the lab explaining the need but never actually asked if they could do it, assuming they would have spoken up otherwise. When the Boss tells him to ask, Dilbert storms to the lab, and the technician says he wondered why Dilbert never asked.
punchline: Dilbert's assumption that silence implied capability was shared by the lab, who were also waiting for a question that never came, so the whole hour-long meeting hinged on no one asking the obvious thing.
summary: After a full meeting where the key question was never posed, a worker is sent back to simply ask it and discovers the other side had been waiting for it all along.

file: 2011/2011-06-02_absurdly complicated_financial model_absenteeism_error_excel sheet_stock holders_poison cafeteria.gif
title: Poisoning the Cafeteria for Stockholders

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: According to your absurdly complicated financial model, we can double revenue by increasing absenteeism.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: To be fair, there might be an error or two in the Excel spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe. But I think I owe it to our stockholders to poison the cafeteria just to be sure.

situation: The Boss reads a printout from an employee's overly complicated financial model, which claims revenue will double if employee absenteeism increases. The employee admits the Excel spreadsheet might contain a few errors. The Boss decides to poison the cafeteria anyway, just to test the model.
punchline: The Boss is so eager to trust a dubious spreadsheet that he would harm his own employees rather than risk disappointing stockholders.
summary: A manager hears that a shaky spreadsheet promises a revenue windfall from sick employees and cheerfully decides to make staff ill on purpose to check.

file: 2011/2011-05-29_business ethics_quarreling_major fix_html_website_award_improves morale_glaoting_winner_technology.gif
title: Award for Fix Nobody Understands

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This award goes to Dilbert for coming up with a major fix to our HTML.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't do anything like that. You must be thinking of someone else.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you even know what HTML is?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's like... a website?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... you're giving an award for something you don't understand... to someone who wasn't involved?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What I meant to say is that I give this award to... Alice... for... what she did.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yes! Envy me, you stinkin' losers!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: I don't know why people say this improves morale.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I fixed the HTML!

setting: Office meeting room during an awards presentation
situation: The Boss presents an award to Dilbert for fixing the company's HTML, but Dilbert says he did nothing of the sort. The Boss admits he doesn't know what HTML is, then hastily gives the award to Alice for 'what she did.' Alice gloats and the room descends into a brawl, while Asok, who actually fixed the HTML, is ignored.
punchline: The company hands out an award for work the manager doesn't understand to the wrong person, so the award causes resentment and fighting instead of improving morale, while the person who really did the work gets nothing.
summary: A clueless manager hands out a trophy for a technical fix he can't describe, sparking a fight while the real fixer shouts for recognition.

file: 2011/2011-01-18_losers_meetings_sales personnel_sell to customers_winners sell_low quota levels_ch ching dance.gif
title: Dogbert Teaches Selling Low Quotas

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Sales Training Seminar

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Losers sell to customers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Winners sell the idea of low quota levels to their own bosses.

transcript.speaker: Projection slide
transcript.text: Low... low... low...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now everyone do the cha-ching dance!

setting: Sales training seminar room with a projector screen
situation: Dogbert stands on a stool leading a sales training seminar. He tells the audience that real winners don't sell to customers but instead persuade their own bosses to set low quotas, illustrated by a slide of a hypnotized boss being swung a pendulum. He then tells everyone to do the cha-ching dance while an attendee dances.
punchline: The best way to hit sales targets is to hypnotize or manipulate your own boss into lowering your quota rather than doing the actual work of selling, and the audience celebrates this cynical advice as if it were a triumph.
summary: A sales guru instructs his students that cleverly talking their managers into easy targets beats the hard work of winning over customers.

file: 2011/2011-02-05_embarrassment_frustration_like an idiot_simple solution_stumping dilbert_gladly explin_look like an idiot.gif
title: Condescending Coworker Wins the Insult Game

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There is a very simple solution to the problem that is stumping Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I will gladly explain it to him after this meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're probably wrong, and yet you still made me look like an idiot.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I win!

situation: During a meeting, Dilbert stands holding his phone while a coworker announces in front of the group that there is a simple solution to the problem Dilbert can't solve, and offers to explain it to him afterward. Dilbert points out the coworker is probably wrong but admits he still got embarrassed, and the coworker gleefully declares victory.
punchline: The coworker doesn't care whether his solution is correct; his only goal was to publicly belittle Dilbert, and he counts that as winning.
summary: A smug colleague publicly implies a colleague is too dim to solve a problem, caring only about scoring points rather than being right.

file: 2011/2011-12-06_business ethics_taxes_warren buffet_tax rate_subsidizing mansion_condescending_show appreciation_ceo_high tax_worker.gif
title: Boss Thanks Employee for Subsidizing Mansion

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Warren Buffett says your tax rate is higher than mine.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thank you for subsidizing my mansion. I really appreciate it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A good leader always shows appreciation to his underlings.

situation: The Boss stands beside an employee's cubicle and brings up Warren Buffett's claim that the employee pays a higher tax rate than he does. He then thanks the seated employee for subsidizing his mansion and says he is showing appreciation as a good leader should. The employee grows visibly angrier and grits his teeth.
punchline: The Boss's cheerful gratitude for the employee's higher tax burden is condescending, and he treats his rubbing it in as a mark of good leadership.
summary: A wealthy manager smugly thanks a subordinate for paying more tax than he does, calling this gracious leadership while the worker seethes.

file: 2011/2011-10-23_computers & peripherals_internet & world wide web_down load apps_new phone_primary job_formulas in excel.gif
title: Boss Wants Every App Downloaded

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you show me how to download apps on my new phone?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But that would take time away from my primary job of showing you how to do formulas in Excel.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently the eight times I already taught you weren't enough.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't use Excel often enough to remember from one time to the next.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How often do you expect to download apps?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's hard to say. I just know I want all of them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How many are there?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Four.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to teach him how to download apps on his new phone. Dilbert points out he already spends his time re-teaching the Boss Excel formulas, which the Boss never retains. The Boss then says he wants every app, and Dilbert deadpans that there are only four.
punchline: The Boss, who can't retain basic software skills and has no idea what he needs, wants all the apps, and Dilbert sarcastically reveals that the supposedly vast app universe amounts to just four apps.
summary: A technologically hopeless manager demands lessons on his new phone, only to be told his ambitions are bigger than the pitiful selection of apps available.

file: 2011/2011-11-22_embarrassed of son_family_food service industry_insult_locksmith_mother_named project manger_paying for lunch_restaurants_sons occupation_don't tell freinds.gif
title: Mom Hides Son's Project Manager Job

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mom, the good news I wanted to tell you is that my boss named me Project Manager.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Please keep that to yourself. I tell my friends you're a locksmith.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're paying for your own lunch.

transcript.speaker: Waiter
transcript.text: I'm Ed. I'll be your Project Manager.

situation: Dilbert is having lunch with his mother and proudly tells her he has been promoted to Project Manager. She is embarrassed and asks him to keep it quiet, saying she tells her friends he is a locksmith. Dilbert retaliates by making her pay for her own lunch, while the waiter cheerfully introduces himself as their project manager.
punchline: Even Dilbert's own mother considers 'project manager' so shameful that she would rather claim he is a locksmith, and the waiter's use of the title for serving tables reinforces how low-status it is.
summary: A son's proud career news is met with his mother's shame, so he makes her cover her own meal while the waiter cheerfully borrows the same title.

file: 2011/2011-10-29_doctors' offices_illness_bad case_wahtchamacallit_pills_doctors offcie_doctor_wicked hemorrhoids_feel like progress_medical.gif
title: Pills Cause Hemorrhoids, Feels Like Progress

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: You've got a bad case of whatchamacallit.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: These pills won't fix your underlying problem, but they might give you a wicked case of hemorrhoids.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: And I can treat hemorrhoids, so that would feel like progress.

situation: A doctor gives a vague diagnosis of 'whatchamacallit' to a patient sitting on the exam table. He then offers pills that won't cure the real problem and may cause hemorrhoids. He reasons that since he can treat hemorrhoids, that would at least feel like progress.
punchline: The doctor deliberately prescribes a medication that creates a new, treatable problem so that it looks like he is making progress, satirizing fake productivity and fixing problems you created yourself.
summary: A vague-diagnosing physician hands over pills that fix nothing but conveniently create a new ailment he can then cure.

file: 2011/2011-05-21_consensus_lost and confused_lateness_doesn't work.gif
title: Late Arrival Gets Brutal Meeting Feedback

transcript.speaker: Coworker (green shirt)
transcript.text: There was a consensus in the room that you're not important, so we started without you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker (green shirt)
transcript.text: We hate you for disrespecting us with your lateness and we expect you'll be lost and confused by the rest of this meeting.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: In summary, lateness is one of those things that doesn't work for everyone.

situation: Dilbert sits at the meeting table after arriving late while two colleagues, one of them Alice, address him. The coworker bluntly tells him the group decided he was unimportant and started without him, that they resent his disrespect, and that he will be lost for the remainder. Alice then wraps it up with a bland, corporate-style summary.
punchline: The scathing, openly hostile criticism is capped with a euphemistic summary that pretends lateness merely 'doesn't work for everyone,' contrasting brutal honesty with sanitized corporate speak.
summary: A tardy employee is told point-blank that his colleagues despise his lateness, then the feedback is tidied into a mild, jargon-style conclusion.

file: 2011/2011-03-27_engineering issues_enginner_not a linquist_vague requests_faith in humanity.gif
title: Wally Deflects Vague Review Request

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert by Scott Adams

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wally, can you review this for any engineering issues?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What issues do you think it has?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I don't know. I'm not an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Your request is too vague. You need to tell me what issues I'm looking for!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you just ask me to do what I just asked you to do?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't know. I'm an engineer, not a linguist.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I've suddenly lost all faith in humanity!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: On the plus side, you found an issue.

setting: Office break area near the coffee maker
situation: A coworker asks Wally, an engineer, to review a document for engineering issues. Wally responds by asking the coworker what issues to look for, then calls the request too vague, effectively handing the work back. The coworker is dismayed at Wally's circular dodge.
punchline: Wally's evasive non-answer is itself the 'issue' the coworker was supposedly asking him to find, so losing faith in humanity counts as a success.
summary: A worker's request for a review gets bounced right back by a coffee-sipping engineer who refuses to do the actual work.

file: 2011/2011-12-13_big business_secondhand sales_tablet computer_business_design logo_pay another company_other companies_watch_engineers_degrade_low morale.gif
title: Tablet Business, Outsourced Logo Design

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're going into the tablet computer business.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And by that I mean other companies will make the product and we'll design the logo.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And by that I mean we'll pay another company to design the logo for us.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can we watch?

situation: The Boss announces to Dilbert and Alice that the company is entering the tablet computer business. He then walks the claim back in two steps: other companies will manufacture the product and the company will only design the logo, and finally even the logo will be outsourced to another company. Alice, deadpan, asks if they can watch.
punchline: The company's 'tablet business' amounts to paying someone else to do all the actual work, leaving employees with nothing to do but watch, which Alice sarcastically points out.
summary: A manager's bold product launch shrinks into pure outsourcing until his engineers are reduced to spectators.

file: 2011/2011-01-07_computer software_ignorance (knowledge)_managers & supervisors_business.gif
title: Consultant Says Only 'Blah Blah Cloud'

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a consultant to help us evolve our products to cloud computing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Blah blah cloud. Blah blah cloud. Blah blah cloud. Blah blah cloud.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's as if you're a technologist and a philosopher all in one!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Blah blah platform.

situation: The Boss introduces Dogbert as the consultant he hired to help move the company's products to cloud computing. Dogbert's entire contribution is repeating 'blah blah cloud' over and over, and the Boss is deeply impressed. Dogbert then swaps in 'platform' and the Boss keeps praising him while Dilbert sits by.
punchline: Dogbert gets lavish praise as a technologist and philosopher for reciting meaningless buzzwords, showing that managers can't tell empty jargon from real expertise.
summary: A boss gushes over a consultant whose whole advice is a chant of meaningless tech buzzwords.

file: 2011/2011-02-02_golf_managers & supervisors_rich people_sense of passion_feel different_sports_business.gif
title: Boss Motivates With Greedy Passion

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The experts say I should motivate you by displaying my own sense of passion and purpose.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I love getting rich at your expense... and golfing!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you feel any different?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yup.

setting: The Boss's office, with Dilbert seated across the desk
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that experts advise managers to motivate employees by showing their own passion and purpose. He then enthusiastically announces that his passions are getting rich off Dilbert's labor and playing golf, and asks if Dilbert feels any different.
punchline: The Boss's genuine passion is exploiting his employees and golfing, so sharing it demoralizes Dilbert rather than motivating him, as Dilbert's flat 'Yup' implies.
summary: A manager follows motivational advice to share his true passions, which turn out to be profiting from his staff and playing golf.

file: 2011/2011-07-15_magic_supernatural practices_sacred dance_cucbicle_useful by comparison.gif
title: Sacred Dance Makes Work Look Useful

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It is time for the sacred dance of the cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi-aw-ah-hee hu-ha-ya-ya wa-ha-ya-yi

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That should make everything I do today seem useful by comparison.

situation: Dilbert, alone in his cubicle, announces in a thought bubble that it is time for a sacred dance. He then stomps around chanting like a ritual performer. Afterward he explains he did it so that the rest of his workday will look productive by comparison.
punchline: Dilbert deliberately does something absurd and pointless first so that his ordinary work, however little it accomplishes, will seem valuable next to it.
summary: A lone engineer performs a silly chant-and-stomp routine in his cubicle to lower the bar for how productive the rest of his day will appear.

file: 2011/2011-06-15_frustration_questioning_meeting_questions_blabbing_interuptions_business.gif
title: Can't Get a Word In

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... May I ask one...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Blah, blah, blah blah, blah, blah blah, blah, blah blah, blah, blah blah, blah...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm begging you. Let me ask...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You need to participate more in meetings.

situation: Dilbert tries politely, then desperately, to ask a question in a meeting while a coworker talks nonstop. Alice sits silently with her eyes closed. Afterward, the Boss tells Dilbert he needs to participate more in meetings.
punchline: Dilbert is blamed for not participating in meetings when a dominating talker never lets him get a word in.
summary: A man who can't interrupt a rambling colleague is criticized by his manager for staying quiet.

file: 2011/2011-08-13_annoyance_public speaking_questioning_embrace failures_learn from them.gif
title: Embracing Failure, Then Checking Learning

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We must embrace our failures and learn from them.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's the dumbest thing I've ever heard.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: How's the learning coming along?

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss declares that the team should embrace its failures and learn from them. Alice, scowling and pointing, calls it the dumbest thing she has ever heard. A coworker then asks the Boss how the learning is progressing, implying nothing has been learned.
punchline: The Boss preaches learning from failure but has apparently learned nothing, which the coworker's deadpan question about 'learning progress' exposes.
summary: A manager's motivational slogan about learning from mistakes gets mocked by a colleague who asks for a progress report on that supposed learning.

file: 2011/2011-12-07_meetings_public speaking_let slide_power point_presentation_bored_sleeping audience_low expectations.gif
title: Soul-Crushing Presentation, Low Expectations

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And that's my last slide. Any comments?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You stole an hour of my life. Something inside me died. I will never have another good day.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I went in with low expectations.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: They can't hurt you if you're already dead.

setting: Conference room, then a hallway or break area
situation: Dilbert finishes a slide presentation and asks for comments. Alice, sitting at the table among a dozing coworker and another with his head in his hand, says the hour was a theft of her life and she will never have a good day again. Afterward, a coworker holding a mug says he survived by expecting nothing, and Dilbert, holding his own mug, responds that low expectations can't hurt you if you're already dead.
punchline: Dilbert's presentation was so deadening that the only defense was to be emotionally dead already, which is a bleakly sarcastic take on managing expectations.
summary: After a dreadful slide show leaves the audience drained and asleep, a colleague quips that only the already-dead were safe from its damage.

file: 2011/2011-07-07_office workers_hard work_lateral promotion_new job_old job_money involved_saving it.gif
title: Lateral Promotion Means Double Workload

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like to reward you for your hard work by giving you a lateral promotion.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was going to hire from the outside, but I realized I can make you do the new job plus your old one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is money involved?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes! I'm saving a ton of it!

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is being rewarded with a lateral promotion. He then reveals that Dilbert will simply absorb the new job on top of his old one, sparing the cost of an outside hire. Dilbert asks whether any money is involved, and the Boss cheerfully says yes, but only in the form of savings for the company.
punchline: The 'reward' gives the employee extra work and no extra pay, and the only money involved is what the company saves by not hiring someone.
summary: A manager disguises a plan to pile a second job onto one employee as a generous reward, and the only financial benefit goes to the company.

file: 2011/2011-09-24_anxiety_stress_burned out_gray hair_don't handle stress.gif
title: Burned Out After One Day

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: I'm burned out by this job.

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: Is that a gray hair?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have we met?

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: I started yesterday. I don't handle stress well.

situation: Dilbert stands holding a coffee mug while a stressed coworker with stress clouds over his head complains that he is burned out by his job. The coworker frets over a possible gray hair, and Dilbert, who doesn't recognize him, asks if they've met. The coworker reveals he only started working there yesterday.
punchline: The coworker is already burned out and seeing gray hairs after just one day on the job, showing how toxic the workplace is and how poorly he handles stress.
summary: A brand-new hire is already frazzled and going gray after a single day at the office.

file: 2011/2011-11-25_retail business_service business_buy company's prodcut_pulling teeth_commissions to salary_free from tyranny_customer service_less than ideal_no paperwork.gif
title: Salesman Freed From Customer Service

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want to buy your company's product but it's like pulling teeth with you.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Ha ha! I switched from commissions to a guaranteed salary. I'm free from the tyranny of customer service!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is less than ideal.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: No paperwork for me! Woot! Woot!

situation: Dilbert, a customer, complains that a salesman is making it extremely difficult to buy his company's product. The salesman gleefully explains that he now earns a guaranteed salary instead of commissions, so he no longer has to care about customer service or paperwork. Dilbert is left unimpressed while the salesman celebrates.
punchline: Removing commission incentives makes the salesman so indifferent that he actively avoids making a sale, proving that incentives drive behavior and a salary rewards doing as little as possible.
summary: A buyer struggles to purchase a product from a salesman who is delighted that his new fixed pay lets him ignore customers and avoid paperwork.

file: 2011/2011-08-15_conversation_suspicion_no clue_software works_wear noisier shoes_talk behind back.gif
title: Noisier Shoes Reveal Eavesdropping Coworker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow. The guy who wrote this doesn't have a clue how software works.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: When you talk about people behind their backs, it makes me wonder what you say about ME.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I think we just solved that mystery.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You should wear noisier shoes.

situation: Dilbert and Alice are reading a document and Dilbert criticizes its author as clueless about software. A coworker who has quietly walked up behind them says that Dilbert's talking about people behind their backs makes him wonder what Dilbert says about him. Alice remarks that they have solved the mystery of how he overheard, and Dilbert blames the coworker's quiet shoes.
punchline: Instead of apologizing for badly insulting the author in front of him, Dilbert blames the eavesdropper for sneaking up silently, and Alice notes that this explains why the coworker keeps catching people gossiping.
summary: A stealthy coworker overhears Dilbert trashing a document's author and complains about the gossip, only to be told his silent footsteps are the real problem.

file: 2011/2011-08-20_conversation_interviews_biggest mistake_learned from t_old couch_chewing_starbucks_never tell story.gif
title: Interview Question About Chewed Couch

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Interview question

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Describe your biggest mistake and what you learned from it.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I tried to get rid of an old couch by chewing it into tiny pieces and leaving one handful at a time at Starbucks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And what did you learn?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I learned I should never tell that story.

setting: Job interview at a desk in an office
situation: The Boss interviews a job candidate and asks the classic question about his biggest mistake and the lesson learned. The candidate confesses to an absurd scheme of chewing up a couch and disposing of it piece by piece at Starbucks. When asked what he learned, he says he should never tell that story, which he has just done in the interview.
punchline: The candidate's lesson is self-defeating: by admitting he should never tell the story, he reveals he has just made the same kind of mistake by telling it in the interview.
summary: Asked in a job interview to recount a blunder and its lesson, a candidate shares a bizarre couch-disposal story and concludes that he never should have shared it.

file: 2011/2011-02-14_media_take pledge_give fortune to charity_billionaires_200 million_leave to heir_semi relayed_monkey dna_clones test tube_entertainment.gif
title: CEO Dodges Billionaire Giving Pledge

transcript.speaker: Winged Monkey
transcript.text: The media is asking if you'll take the pledge to give your fortune to charity.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: That pledge is for billionaires! I only have $200 million to leave to my heir!

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: On a semi-related note, find out who keeps putting monkey DNA in my clone's test tube.

situation: A winged monkey in a bellhop-style uniform tells the CEO that the media wants to know if he will take the pledge to give his fortune to charity. The CEO brushes it off, saying the pledge is only for billionaires and he merely has $200 million to leave to his heir. He then tells the monkey to find out who keeps putting monkey DNA in his clone's test tube.
punchline: The CEO's heir is a clone, and the monkey DNA contaminating it suggests the winged monkey assistant is sabotaging or tampering with it, so the CEO is both stingy with his fortune and oblivious to the obvious culprit.
summary: A wealthy executive waves off a charity-giving campaign as beneath his wealth class, then casually asks his monkey assistant to investigate why his clone keeps turning out part primate.

file: 2011/2011-04-07_engineers_managers & supervisors_ventriloquism_finishing projects_early_powerpoint_presentation_executive retreat_dead boss hand puppet_business.gif
title: Dead Boss Hand Puppet Retreat

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: The engineering department is finishing all of their projects early and we don't know why.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell them to do a PowerPoint presentation at the next executive retreat to share their methods.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Now it's my turn to use the dead boss hand puppet!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

setting: Boss's office, then an executive retreat meeting room
situation: An employee reports to the boss that the engineering department is finishing all its projects early and nobody knows why. The boss responds by ordering them to give a PowerPoint presentation at the next executive retreat. At the retreat, an executive gleefully announces it's his turn to use the dead boss hand puppet, which is the dead boss's hair worn on a woman's head, while the others look on.
punchline: The executive retreat apparently features a hand puppet made from a dead boss, implying that engineering's early finishes were achieved by something grisly, and the executives treat the macabre prop as a casual retreat game.
summary: Managers puzzled by speedy engineers invite them to present at a retreat, where the real spectacle turns out to be a gruesome puppet made from a deceased boss.

file: 2011/2011-08-07_business ethics_public realtions firm_persuade media_negative stores_competitor_ethical_public relations form_defaming company_defame.gif
title: Hiring Dogbert to Smear Competitors

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired the Dogbert Public Relations Firm.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: His job is to persuade the media to write negative stories about our competitor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that ethical?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I assure you that your competitor is doing the same thing to you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They're paying a public relations firm a fortune to steer the media toward defaming your company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who did they hire to defame us?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Probably someone awesome.

setting: Conference room, with an exterior shot of a competitor's office building
situation: The Boss announces he has hired Dogbert's public relations firm to get the media to publish negative stories about a competitor. Dilbert asks if that is ethical, and the Boss replies that the competitor is surely doing the same to them. Dilbert wonders aloud who the competitor hired to smear their company, and Dogbert, the very PR firm in question, answers that it was probably someone awesome.
punchline: Dogbert, who profits from the smear campaign, cheerfully admits the rival's hired smear artist is probably just as skilled and effective as he is.
summary: A manager brushes off an ethics concern about a media smear campaign, and the PR consultant he hired cheerfully assumes the rival's hired gun is excellent too.

file: 2011/2011-03-12_work ethic_social network_stategy_global supply chain.gif
title: Social Network for Supply Chain

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can't help you because I'm busy working on a social network strategy for our global supply chain.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That sounds like something that no one wants and no one needs.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's probably why it's taking so long.

situation: At a meeting, Wally declines to help a colleague because he claims to be busy on a social network strategy for the global supply chain. The coworker points out that nobody wants or needs such a thing. Wally calmly replies that this explains why the project is taking so long.
