punchline: Wally treats the project's total lack of demand as the reason for its slow progress, using a pointless assignment as a convenient excuse to avoid real work.
summary: A lazy employee dodges a request by citing a useless buzzword project, then casually admits its pointlessness is what's dragging it out.

file: 2011/2011-07-29_exercise & fitness_office workers_engineers_telomeres_value work_company gym_slacker trap.gif
title: Company Gym Is a Slacker Trap

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're looking for engineers with short telomeres for their age.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's an indication that you value work above exercise.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: But you have a company gym.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's our slacker trap!

setting: Boss's office during a job interview
situation: The Boss interviews an engineering candidate and explains that the company wants to hire people with short telomeres for their age, which he reads as a sign that they prioritize work over exercise. The candidate points out that the company has a gym, and the Boss admits the gym is a deliberate trap to catch slackers.
punchline: The company offers a gym as a perk but secretly uses it to identify and screen out employees who spend time on fitness instead of work.
summary: A manager screens job applicants by biological aging markers, then reveals that the company's fitness center exists only to catch employees who exercise.

file: 2011/2011-02-16_managers & supervisors_move to big building_regular job_so unimprotant_won't be missed_work on something_month_business.gif
title: Building Move Insults Tina's Importance

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, you'll be in charge of our move to the new building.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: That means you think my regular job is so unimportant that I won't be missed if I work on something else for a month.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If it makes you feel any better, this will take longer than a month.

situation: The Boss holding a coffee mug tells Tina she will be in charge of the company's move to a new building. Tina points out that this implies her regular job is unimportant enough that nobody will miss her. The Boss, sipping his coffee, tries to reassure her by saying the move will take even longer than a month.
punchline: The Boss's attempt at comfort makes things worse, since a longer absence just confirms her regular work is considered even less important.
summary: A manager hands a technical writer a lengthy relocation project and unintentionally confirms she is considered expendable.

file: 2011/2011-07-23_competition (psychology)_stop level meeting_confidentail_retribution_every day retribution.gif
title: Confidential Skip-Level Meeting, Scheduled Retribution

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your annual skip-level meeting with my boss is next week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everything you say about me is confidential.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But just to be on the safe side, I scheduled my retribution for every day of the following year.

situation: The Boss stands at Dilbert's cubicle holding a coffee mug and reminds him of his upcoming skip-level meeting with the Boss's own manager. He promises that whatever Dilbert says about him will stay confidential. He then adds that he has already scheduled his retribution for every day of the following year.
punchline: The promise of confidentiality is empty because the Boss has pre-planned a year of punishment, so employees can't safely speak candidly about him.
summary: A manager vows to keep his employee's feedback secret while casually revealing he has planned a full year of payback just in case.

file: 2011/2011-07-27_office workers_collegue_associate_teammate_subordinate_awkward.gif
title: Boss Can't Label Carol Politely

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And this is Carol. She's my...

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Colleague?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Associate?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Teammate?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was going to say "subordinate," but now it's awkward.

situation: The Boss is introducing Carol to a seated coworker and trails off when describing her relationship to him. Carol offers friendlier labels like colleague, associate and teammate, and the Boss rejects each one. He finally admits he meant to say "subordinate" but now finds it awkward.
punchline: The Boss rejects every egalitarian term because he sees Carol strictly as beneath him, and he is only embarrassed because she made him say it aloud.
summary: A manager's introduction stalls when his employee suggests nicer job-relationship words that he shoots down, revealing he thinks of her only as someone below him.

file: 2011/2011-11-14_biology_chemistry_practical jokers_biotech field_giving free flu shots_stem cells_science.gif
title: Flu Shot Turns Coworker Into Pig

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I learned the hard way that a lot of people who work in the biotech field are practical jokers.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I thought my company was giving free flu shots.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Stupid stem cells.

situation: Dilbert sits quietly with a coffee mug while a coworker, who now has a pig's snout and a pair of wings, explains how he ended up this way. He believed he was getting a free flu shot at his biotech company but was actually injected with stem cells by pranksters.
punchline: The coworker accepted a free flu shot from biotech colleagues without suspicion and was transformed into a winged pig, as the 'when pigs fly' idiom comes to life, leaving him to blame the stem cells.
summary: A man with a pig's face and angel wings blames a prankish biotech company for turning a supposed flu shot into a bizarre transformation.

file: 2011/2011-08-02_meetings_standards meeting._represent interests_create standards_mutually exclusive prefrences_laughs.gif
title: Standards Committee Runs on Conflicting Preferences

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Standards meeting

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Each of you has been chosen to represent the interests of your respective companies.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As you know, the best way to create standards is to mash together a bunch of mutually exclusive preferences.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I hope I'm not the only one who joined this group just for the laughs.

setting: Conference room during an industry standards meeting
situation: Dogbert chairs a standards committee at a conference table with representatives from different companies. He explains that the group's job is to merge the incompatible demands of each company into one standard. He then admits he only joined for the entertainment value.
punchline: Dogbert cheerfully acknowledges that standards-making is a doomed exercise in reconciling irreconcilable demands, and that watching the chaos is the only real payoff.
summary: A dog running a standards committee cheerfully describes the process as blending irreconcilable demands, then confesses he's only there for amusement.

file: 2011/2011-08-03_computers & peripherals_gadgets_intergenerational relations_grandpa box_phones_tablets_laptop_text the 90s.gif
title: Young Coworker Mocks Dilbert's Desktop

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Are you getting a lot done on the grandpa box?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The what?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: The people in my generation do our work on our phones and tablets.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I also have a laptop.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'll text the nineties and let them know.

situation: Asok, holding a coffee mug, asks Dilbert if he is getting much done on his old desktop computer, which he calls the grandpa box. He explains that his generation works on phones and tablets. When Dilbert says he also has a laptop, Asok replies that he'll text the nineties to tell them.
punchline: Asok sarcastically implies that Dilbert's technology is so outdated that he must be living in the 1990s, and uses his phone to deliver the insult.
summary: A young intern teases an older engineer about his outdated computer gear, claiming his own generation only needs mobile devices.

file: 2011/2011-05-19_embarrassment_printmaking_printer prowler_spots activity_minions.gif
title: Boss Caught By Printer Prowler

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The printer prowler spots activity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's time to see what the minions are working on.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They're on to me.

setting: Office cubicle area beside a printer
situation: The Boss sneaks up to the office printer, thinking he is secretly checking what his employees are printing. He picks up a page and finds it is a caricature drawing of himself as a donkey, while Dilbert peeks around the cubicle wall watching him.
punchline: The boss's sneaky snooping backfires when he discovers an employee has printed a donkey cartoon of him, suggesting the staff deliberately set a trap for him.
summary: A snooping manager creeps up on the printer to spy on his staff and finds an unflattering donkey portrait of himself waiting for him.

file: 2011/2011-01-28_act nervous_air travel_airport security_guards_more invasive_new pat down_procedures_situations_sleeper cell_terrorits_tsa_molestation.gif
title: Nervous Passenger Gets Invasive Pat-Down

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Airport security

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: Step over here, sleeper cell.

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: Our new pat down procedures might be more invasive than you're used to.

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: Only terrorists act nervous in these situations.

situation: At an airport checkpoint, a guard singles out a passenger by calling him a sleeper cell. The guard warns that the new pat-down procedures are more invasive than usual while a second guard pats the passenger down. When the passenger is practically being pawed and manhandled, the guard declares that only terrorists would act nervous in such a situation.
punchline: Any natural discomfort at an intrusive pat-down is treated as evidence of terrorism, so the passenger cannot win: nervousness gets him suspected, while the invasive search itself is an obviously uncomfortable ordeal.
summary: Airport guards subject a passenger to an intrusive search and then treat his unease as a sign of guilt.

file: 2011/2011-09-02_anxiety_pessimism_approve goal_apathy_plan to fire_unimportant projects.gif
title: Boss's Apathy Means Dilbert's Getting Fired

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you approve my goals for next year?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yeah, whatever.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa! Your apathy about my goals can only mean you plan to fire me within the next year!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ha ha! Now give him unimportant projects.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They all seem that way to me.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss whether he approved his goals for next year, and the boss answers with a bored 'yeah, whatever.' Dilbert panics, reading the apathy as a sign he is about to be fired. Catbert, the evil HR director, gleefully suggests giving Dilbert unimportant projects, and the boss admits all projects seem unimportant to him.
punchline: The boss's indifference isn't a sign of a firing plan but of his general disregard for everything, including all of the work his employees do.
summary: An employee jumps to a grim conclusion about his manager's shrug, only to learn the manager simply finds every project equally meaningless.

file: 2011/2011-11-01_employees_executives_non giant situation_shoulders of giants_non giant_business.gif
title: CEO Stands On Giants' Shoulders

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: As your CEO, if I have seen farther, it is only because I stood on the shoulders of giants.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Plus whatever is going on over here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's sort of a non-giant situation.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: And I haven't had shoulders since I was ten.

situation: At a meeting, the CEO gives a grand speech paraphrasing the line about standing on the shoulders of giants to explain his vision. He then adds that he also relies on whatever is going on nearby, gesturing at the employees at the table. Dilbert and a bald coworker respond with deadpan jabs, noting that they are hardly giants and that the coworker has no shoulders.
punchline: The CEO credits his success to giants but then admits he also leans on his ordinary, unimpressive employees, who sarcastically point out they are not giants and one jokes that he has no shoulders at all.
summary: A boss borrows a famous quote about giants and then clumsily includes his underwhelming staff, who respond with dry self-deprecating humor.

file: 2011/2011-11-23_fraternization_meetings_emails_no one responded_project timeline_consensus nor reality_illusion of progress.gif
title: Project Timeline Mocking and Illusion

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Once again, none of you responded to my emails this past week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I put together a project time line that reflects neither consensus nor reality.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Can I have a copy so I can mock it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No. I'm still enjoying the illusion of progress.

situation: Dilbert complains in a meeting that no one answered his emails all week. In response he has drafted a project timeline on his own, and he admits it matches neither what the team agreed nor what is realistic. Wally asks for a copy so he can mock it, but Dilbert refuses because he wants to keep believing the project is moving forward.
punchline: Dilbert knowingly admits his made-up timeline is fiction and prefers to cling to the comforting illusion of progress rather than let anyone puncture it.
summary: After being ignored by his team, Dilbert invents a fantasy project schedule and guards it from ridicule so he can feel productive.

file: 2011/2011-05-20_computers & peripherals_language_no longer undertsnd_employees_to of touch_technology_gravitons_warp drive_rebalanced_subspace responders_business.gif
title: Boss Hears Star Trek Technobabble

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I no longer understand anything my employees say.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I must be so out of touch with technology that I don't even recognize the words.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I flushed the gravitons out of the warp drive and rebalanced the subspace responders.

setting: Boss's office and an outside view of the office building
situation: The Boss sits at his desk with Catbert nearby and laments that he can no longer understand what his employees say. He concludes he must be hopelessly out of touch with technology. An employee then arrives with a coffee mug and reports fixing something using science-fiction jargon.
punchline: The employee's report is pure Star Trek nonsense, so the boss isn't out of touch at all; the employee is either making things up or the boss's assumption is simply wrong.
summary: A manager blames his own ignorance of technology for not understanding his staff, only to be given an explanation made entirely of sci-fi gibberish.

file: 2011/2011-06-20_employees_gloating_quit working_won lotery_business.gif
title: Wally Already Quit Working Years Ago

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you won the lottery, would you quit working?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I quit working years ago. But I might start gloating if it isn't too hard.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gloating doesn't sound hard.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Can I do it without moving any facial muscles? I have weak eyebrows.

situation: Dilbert walks with Wally, both holding coffee mugs, and asks whether he would quit working if he won the lottery. Wally says he quit working years ago, but might start gloating if it isn't too hard. When Dilbert says gloating isn't hard, Wally asks if he can do it without moving his facial muscles because his eyebrows are weak.
punchline: Wally is so lazy that even gloating, the easiest of activities, is too much effort, and he already does no work at his job.
summary: A lottery question reveals that the idle coworker has long since stopped working and finds even smug gloating too strenuous.

file: 2011/2011-07-20_hardware_internet & world wide web_next week balancing_traffic loads_network_worst wingman_shame.gif
title: Wally's Network Balancing Plan Foiled

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is it okay if I spend the next week balancing traffic loads on our network?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I thought I told you that our hardware vendor already did that.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Worst wingman ever.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Shame is my name!

setting: The Boss's office, then a hallway
situation: Wally asks the Boss for permission to spend a week balancing traffic loads on the network, hoping to get a cushy make-work assignment. Asok, standing beside him, helpfully points out that the hardware vendor already did that work, which kills the plan. In the hallway Wally complains that Asok is the worst wingman ever, and Asok sheepishly apologizes.
punchline: Wally was angling for a week of paid idleness under the guise of a technical task, and honest, eager Asok accidentally sabotaged the scam by telling the truth.
summary: A lazy engineer's bid for a make-work project is derailed when his junior coworker innocently reveals the job was already done.

file: 2011/2011-11-09_anger_envy_big promotion_congratulations_not jealous_good work_art of full body lying.gif
title: Alice Fakes Congratulations Through Gritted Teeth

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Hey, Alice! Did you hear about my big promotion?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Congratulations, Ted. I'm not jealous at all. Keep up the good work.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Sorry about my face. I haven't mastered the art of full-body lying.

situation: Ted approaches Alice and brags about his big promotion. Alice, with a furious scowl and clenched teeth, tells him congratulations and insists she isn't jealous. She then apologizes for her angry face, admitting she can't lie with her whole body.
punchline: Alice's words say she's happy for Ted, but her seething expression gives away her jealousy, and she cheerfully admits as much by apologizing for her face.
summary: A colleague gloats about a promotion and Alice's snarling expression betrays the polite lie she tells him.

file: 2011/2011-11-07_employees_executives_fought boss_get raise_terrific boss_no credible witnesses_business.gif
title: Fighting For Your Raise Unseen

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I fought with my boss to get you a raise but I lost.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm always fighting for you behind the scenes.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're a terrific boss whenever there are no credible witnesses.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thank you.

situation: The Boss tells Alice, who is standing in front of his desk, that he argued with his own boss for her raise but lost, and insists he always champions her behind the scenes. Alice replies that he is only a great boss when nobody can verify it, and he misses the sarcasm and thanks her.
punchline: Alice sarcastically implies his claims of advocating for her are unverifiable and probably false, and the oblivious Boss takes it as a compliment.
summary: A manager claims he valiantly battled for his employee's pay increase out of sight, and she dryly suggests his heroics conveniently happen where no one can confirm them.

file: 2011/2011-04-30_apathy_telephones_get tech support_audio menu_tech support_user manuals_hate customers_apathy thing.gif
title: Menu Tree Outlasts Customer Patience

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I researched how long your customers will stay on the phone trying to get tech support before giving up.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then I designed an audio menu tree that will take them slightly longer than that to reach your tech support.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've seen your user manuals and I assume that you hate your customers' guts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's more of an apathy thing.

setting: Office, consultant's desk facing the boss's desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, explains to the boss that he measured how long customers wait on hold before hanging up. He then built a phone menu that takes just slightly longer than that to reach tech support. He guesses the company hates its customers, and the boss corrects him that it's merely apathy.
punchline: The boss admits he doesn't actively hate his customers; he just doesn't care about them, which is why the deliberately unreachable support line suits him.
summary: A consultant engineers a phone maze designed to make callers give up before they ever reach a human, and the boss shrugs that indifference, not hatred, drives the company's customer service.

file: 2011/2011-01-09_agree_and solution_anger_appearance of differnce_clarity_comprehend both problem_experiencing an illusion_limits of comprehension_wrestling_defective brain.gif
title: You Don't Actually Disagree With Me

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I have to disagree with you, Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, you don't disagree with me.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I don't?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No. You think you disagree with me, but you're mistaken.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're simply experiencing an illusion caused by the limits of your comprehension.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you were able to fully comprehend both the problem and my recommended solution, you would agree with me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So what appears to be a difference of opinion is just you wrestling with your own defective brain.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's no reason to get the rest of us involved in that mess.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you ever noticed that clarity makes people angry?

setting: Office meeting room with a conference table
situation: A coworker says he disagrees with Dilbert, and Dilbert insists the coworker doesn't really disagree but is merely too limited to understand the problem and solution. He tells the coworker to sort out his defective brain without involving everyone else. In the final panel, Dilbert stands alone, and Dogbert looks on from a chair, as he muses that clarity makes people angry.
punchline: Dilbert dismisses any disagreement as the other person's inability to understand him, then smugly blames the resulting anger on his own clarity rather than on his condescension.
summary: Dilbert condescendingly explains that a colleague's objection is only a symptom of his poor understanding, then wonders why his clear thinking upsets people.

file: 2011/2011-04-06_managers & supervisors_ventriloquism_information overload_libertarian_taxidermist_hand hole_work_like puppet_creepy_business.gif
title: Stuffed Boss Worked Like Puppet

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: His brain shut down from information overload, so I asked a libertarian taxidermist to stuff him.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: There's a hand hole in the back so we can work him like a puppet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's sort of creepy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You'll get used to it.

situation: Alice explains to Dilbert that the Boss's brain shut down from information overload, so she had him stuffed by a taxidermist. She reveals there is a hand hole in his back so the team can operate him like a puppet. Dilbert finds it creepy, and Alice tells him he will adapt.
punchline: The Boss was already so brainless and ineffective that turning him into a literal puppet barely changes anything, and the team just accepts it as normal office life.
summary: After the boss's mind gives out under too much data, a coworker has him taxidermied into a hand-operated puppet that everyone is expected to tolerate.

file: 2011/2011-07-26_public speaking_questioning_draw attention_opposite apporach_working.gif
title: Admitting Wrong Numbers In Meeting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And so, as you can see. . .

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: All of the numbers I gave you last week are wrong.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I would have mentioned it sooner, but I don't like to draw attention to myself.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I see that you're taking the opposite approach. How's that working for you?

situation: Dilbert is presenting data on a screen when a coworker seated at the table interrupts to announce that all the numbers he supplied the previous week were wrong. He explains that he didn't speak up earlier because he dislikes drawing attention to himself. Dilbert points out that interrupting the presentation is the opposite of that approach and asks how it's working out.
punchline: The coworker claims to avoid attention, yet he publicly derails the meeting to confess his error, and Dilbert sarcastically calls out the contradiction.
summary: A shy coworker loudly reveals his faulty data mid-presentation, and Dilbert dryly notes that this is hardly a low-profile move.

file: 2011/2011-04-16_computers & peripherals_embarrassment_internet & world wide web_developed app_spare time_awful thing_lees hinest_marketing_business.gif
title: Honest Feedback On Spare-Time App

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I developed this app in my spare time. What do you think?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think you made spare time look like an awful thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you'd like a less honest answer, I can recommend someone in marketing.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I might try that.

situation: A coworker shows Dilbert a smartphone app he built in his spare time and asks for an opinion. Dilbert bluntly says the app is terrible, then offers to point the coworker to someone in marketing if he wants a less honest answer. The coworker takes him up on it.
punchline: Dilbert implies that marketing people will flatter anything, so anyone wanting dishonest praise should go to them.
summary: Dilbert's brutally candid review of a colleague's hobby app ends with a jab that marketing staff will say whatever people want to hear.

file: 2011/2011-01-19_annoyance_interviews_wages_interviewing_salary range_reveal nature of job_current salary_interviewing me_evil or inconsiderate_current job_test the commute_money.gif
title: Interview Reveals Lower Salary Afterward

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks for spending the day interviewing with us. I can now reveal the nature of the job and the salary range.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You know my current salary and yet you wasted my entire day interviewing me for a job that pays less. You are either evil or inconsiderate.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: So... not as good as your current job?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a tie. I'll need to test the commute one more time.

setting: Office interview room, across a desk
situation: After a full day of interviewing Dilbert, an interviewer finally reveals the job details and salary range. Dilbert points out that the job pays less than his current one and that the company knew his salary all along, wasting his day. When asked if it's worse than his current job, he says it's a tie and he needs to test the commute.
punchline: Dilbert's current job is so bad that a lower-paying job is considered equally good, with only the commute left to break the tie.
summary: A job candidate scolds an interviewer for hiding a pay cut until the end of the day, then admits his present job is so dismal the new one merely ties it.

file: 2011/2011-03-21_gloating_managers & supervisors_meetings_alice in charge_better than_business.gif
title: Alice Gloats While Boss Is Away

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Our Pointy-Haired Boss put me in charge while he's gone.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's proof that I'm better than you... and you... and you... and you... and you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Oh look: that's the only thing on my agenda!

situation: Alice, left in charge while the Boss is away, opens a meeting by announcing that her temporary promotion proves she is better than everyone seated around the table, pointing at each coworker in turn. She then looks at her notes and cheerfully notes that this boast is the only item on the meeting agenda.
punchline: Alice has been given authority but has no actual business to conduct, so the meeting exists purely for her to gloat about her status.
summary: Handed temporary authority, a coworker spends the entire meeting rubbing her superiority in her colleagues' faces.

file: 2011/2011-04-25_human body_medicines_vitamin d_inner glow_vitamins_minerals_better than sun.gif
title: Topping Alice's Vitamin D Remark

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Topper

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm in a bad mood. Maybe I need some sun to boost my vitamin D level.

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: That's nothing. Exposure to my inner glow will give you a full range of vitamins and minerals.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're better than the sun?

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: I don't quit just because it's night.

situation: Alice, sitting at a meeting table with Dilbert and a coworker, says she's in a bad mood and might need sun to boost her vitamin D. The coworker, Topper, one-ups her by claiming his 'inner glow' provides a full range of vitamins and minerals. When Dilbert asks if he's better than the sun, Topper boasts that he keeps shining even at night.
punchline: Topper's boastful claim that he outshines the sun because he's available at night is also a thinly veiled, egotistical innuendo about his own supposed greatness.
summary: A self-important coworker tries to outdo a casual remark about sunshine by insisting his own radiance is superior to the sun itself.

file: 2011/2011-02-08_work ethic_charged project_accountants_arsenic based life forms_natural enemy.gif
title: Arsenic-Based Accountant Declares Natural Enemy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Accounting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You charged my project for expenses that aren't mine.

transcript.speaker: Accountant
transcript.text: Let me see that.

transcript.speaker: Accountant
transcript.text: We accountants are arsenic-based life forms. That makes you my natural enemy.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Crumple crumple

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That is not logical.

transcript.speaker: Accountant
transcript.text: Live long and phospher.

setting: Accounting department office, with a green lizard-like accountant seated on a rock at a computer
situation: Dilbert confronts a green, horned, reptilian accountant about expenses wrongly charged to his project. The accountant takes the paper, crumples it, and declares that accountants are arsenic-based life forms and therefore Dilbert's natural enemy. Dilbert objects that this is illogical, and the accountant answers with a Vulcan-style salute and a mangled farewell.
punchline: The accountant dodges the billing complaint by turning it into a sci-fi alien trope, dismissing Dilbert's complaint with absurd pseudo-logic and a parody of Spock's farewell, 'live long and prosper'.
summary: A scaly reptilian accountant answers an expense complaint by claiming to be an alien life form, crumpling the evidence, and bidding the complainer farewell with a Star Trek salute.

file: 2011/2011-02-19_anger_honesty_moving_new offcie_sounds weird_real one_save the attitude.gif
title: A Real Excuse Sounds Fake

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I can't help on your project this week because we're moving to a new office.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: It sounds weird because it's true. I like to throw in a real one every now and then.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: You might want to save that attitude for the next round.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Three coworkers sit at a meeting table. The bald, bespectacled coworker declines to help on a project, citing an office move. When the others react with skepticism, he insists the excuse is genuine and then tells the annoyed coworker to save his attitude for the next excuse.
punchline: The coworker is so used to making up fake excuses that he is offended when someone doubts the rare true one, implying the next excuse will be a lie again.
summary: A habitual excuse-maker gets indignant when his one honest reason for dodging work is met with suspicion.

file: 2011/2011-12-08_conversation_internet & world wide web_seattle_quick meeting_stone age tribe_skype_never used_why fly_telecommunte_airplane.gif
title: Why Fly When Skype Exists

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to fly to Seattle for a quick meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will I be meeting with a newly discovered Stone Age tribe that has never used Skype?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then I'm totally confused.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he must fly to Seattle for a quick meeting. Dilbert asks whether the meeting is with a Stone Age tribe that has never used Skype, the only reason he can imagine for needing to travel. When the Boss says no, Dilbert says he is totally confused.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that in-person travel is only justified when the other party lacks video conferencing technology, highlighting how unnecessary the trip is.
summary: Dilbert wryly questions why he must travel for a brief meeting when video calling would do the job.

file: 2011/2011-05-05_frustration_office workers_solving problem_stadardization policies_high five.gif
title: Congratulating the Boss on Desk Policies

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Congratulations on solving every important problem in the world.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I assume that's what happened. Otherwise, you wouldn't have time to create desk standardization policies.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: High five?

situation: Dilbert stands in front of the Boss's desk holding a coffee mug and sarcastically congratulates him for solving all the world's important problems. He explains that the only reason the Boss could be writing desk standardization policies is that nothing more important is left to do. The Boss scowls while Dilbert cheerfully raises his hand for a high five.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that a manager focused on trivial desk standardization rules must have run out of real problems to solve, then mockingly asks for a high five.
summary: An employee mockingly praises his manager's petty new rules as proof that the planet has no problems left.

file: 2011/2011-10-24_boredom_despair_subject matter expert_judging book.gif
title: Wally Introduced as Expert, Everyone Groans

transcript.speaker: Meeting Leader
transcript.text: Everyone, this is Wally. He's our subject matter expert.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Groan. Uh-oh. Sheesh. Oh well. Ugh.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: People are better than you'd think at judging a book by its cover.

setting: Conference room, then an office building exterior and a hallway
situation: A meeting leader introduces Wally to the group as the subject matter expert. The reaction is shown as a string of groans and sighs floating over an office building. Afterward Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells Dilbert that people are good at judging by appearances.
punchline: Everyone instantly knows from Wally's reputation and appearance that he is useless as an expert, and Wally smugly admits first impressions are usually accurate.
summary: A colleague's grand introduction of Wally as the resident expert draws an immediate chorus of dismay, which Wally himself seems to acknowledge was well founded.
keywords: judging a book by its cover

file: 2011/2011-12-27_anxiety_obliviousness_mentor_hundreds of hour_eagerly absorb_wisdom_hugger.gif
title: Boss Announces Mentoring and Hugging

transcript.text: Good news, Alice. I've decided to be your mentor.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hurk.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll spend hundreds of hours together as you eagerly absorb my wisdom.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hurk.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I've decided to become more of a hugger.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hurk. Hurk. Hurk. Hurk. Hurk.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, cheerfully tells Alice he will be her mentor and that they will spend hundreds of hours together. Alice grows increasingly nauseous with each announcement, and by the time he says he is becoming a hugger she is retching uncontrollably.
punchline: Alice is so horrified by the prospect of being mentored and hugged by her oblivious boss that she physically gags, while he mistakes it for good news being welcomed.
summary: A cheerfully clueless manager announces he will mentor and hug a coworker, who reacts with escalating nausea.

file: 2011/2011-07-08_deterioration_recessions_20%_competitive_industry_involve crime.gif
title: Growing Revenue Through Blinking Crime

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our goal is to grow the top line by 20%.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How will we do that with products that aren't competitive in an industry that isn't growing?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Does it involve crime?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If it does, blink once.

situation: The Boss announces a goal of growing revenue by 20% at a meeting. Dilbert points out the company has uncompetitive products in a stagnant industry, so the goal seems impossible. Wally asks whether the plan involves crime, and Dilbert tells the Boss to blink once if so, as if the Boss were a hostage.
punchline: Since there is no legitimate way to hit the Boss's unrealistic growth target, Dilbert jokes that the only plausible plan is illegal, and asks for a hostage-style blink signal to confirm it.
summary: Faced with an impossible revenue target, the staff wonder whether the secret strategy must be criminal and ask for a covert signal.

file: 2011/2011-10-31_employees_illness_marketing people_brain heals_drank sludge_brain worm_dead in a week_business.gif
title: Asok's Brain Worm Visits Marketing

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Hi-ho, marketing people! I've been transferred into your department until my brain heals.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I drank some industrial sludge. But don't worry— I'll be able to shake it off in a few days.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: A little pollution can't hurt me. I grew up in India. This brain worm will be dead in a week, tops.

setting: Conference room in the marketing department
situation: Asok, holding a coffee mug, cheerfully announces to three marketing employees that he has been transferred into their department while his brain heals. He explains he drank industrial sludge, then reveals a large worm is visibly attached to his head, which he dismisses as harmless. The marketing staff look increasingly alarmed.
punchline: Asok blithely shrugs off a giant brain worm caused by drinking toxic sludge, while the company treats a sick, contaminated employee as a fine fit for marketing.
summary: A cheerful intern with a toxic-sludge-induced brain parasite is parked in marketing and insists a bit of pollution is nothing to worry about.

file: 2011/2011-12-04_car pool_saving planet_steal time_theif_hitch a ride_hero_ride in trunk_pretend_sneaky_leave work.gif
title: Carpool Hero Leaves Meeting Early

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Gotta go. Carpool.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay. See you tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have to go too.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whoa! Sit back down.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why does the carpooler get to leave early?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carpoolers are like heroes that are saving the entire planet.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're more like a thief who is trying to steal time from the company.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What if I hitch a ride home in the carpooler's trunk?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That would make me a hero too.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I only pretend to have a carpool, but you're welcome to ride in my trunk.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Deal!

setting: Conference room during a meeting, then a hallway
situation: An employee leaves a meeting early, citing his carpool, and the Boss lets him go.
