Wally suggests riding in the carpooler's trunk to qualify as a hero, and the employee admits he only pretends to carpool but offers his trunk anyway.
punchline: The Boss's bizarre logic rewards anyone who merely claims a carpool, so Wally games the rule and the 'carpooler' turns out to be faking it too, showing how easily early-leave perks are exploited.
summary: A boss grants early exits to carpoolers as environmental heroes, so a lazy coworker simply finds a way to qualify and slip out too.

file: 2011/2011-06-01_gloating_bad winner_office_co workers.gif
title: The Bad Winner Gloats

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you remember six months ago when I told you you were wrong?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Eee-yore! Eee-yore! Eee-yore!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I just realized I'm a bad winner.

situation: A coworker walks up to Dilbert, who is seated at his computer, and reminds him of an old disagreement. He then waves a piece of paper in Dilbert's face and dances around while braying "Eee-yore!" repeatedly. Once finished, he calmly admits he has just realized he is a bad winner.
punchline: The coworker's loud, childish victory dance is followed by a deadpan admission that he is a bad winner, showing he only noticed his obnoxious gloating after the fact.
summary: A gleeful coworker rubs in a long-ago argument he won, then casually acknowledges how poorly he handles victory.

file: 2011/2011-09-25_competition (psychology)_goals for the year_assignments_average raise_invent nuclear fusion_lack of knowledge.gif
title: Writing Goals Nobody Will Use

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm getting writer's block trying to come up with your goals for the year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just write anything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We both know I'll ignore the goals and work on whatever you assign to me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How will I know if you do a good job if you don't have goals?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Same way as always.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You'll compare your lack of knowledge about what I did to the goals you imagine you might have created if you could have seen the future.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then you'll give me an average raise just like everyone else who didn't invent nuclear fusion.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Works for me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's better to not over-think these things.

situation: The Boss complains that he can't come up with annual goals for Dilbert. Dilbert tells him to write anything, since he'll just work on whatever he is assigned anyway. He then describes how the Boss will evaluate him without real goals, and the Boss happily agrees with the arrangement.
punchline: Annual goals are a meaningless ritual, because the Boss doesn't know what Dilbert actually does and will hand out an average raise regardless, so thinking harder about the goals is a waste of effort.
summary: An employee explains to his clueless manager that yearly goal-setting is an empty exercise and the pay outcome will be the same either way.

file: 2011/2011-09-28_computers & peripherals_office equipment_questioning_wise garbageman_powerpoint slides_only delicious_small does_analogy_works for flies.gif
title: PowerPoint Is Like Garbage Analogy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wise Garbage Man, tell me why PowerPoint slides are so boring.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: PowerPoint is a lot like garbage. It's only delicious in small doses. Too much can kill you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That analogy only works for flies.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Oooh. Look who thinks he's better than flies.

situation: Dilbert asks the wise garbage man why PowerPoint slides are so boring. The garbage man compares PowerPoint to garbage, saying it is only delicious in small doses. Dilbert points out the analogy only works for flies, and the garbage man mocks him for thinking he is better than flies.
punchline: Since garbage is only delicious to flies, the garbage man's analogy implies that people who enjoy PowerPoint in small doses are like flies, and he teases Dilbert for thinking he is above that.
summary: A garbage man offers a flawed comparison between slide decks and trash, and Dilbert's rebuttal gets turned into a jab about flies.

file: 2011/2011-10-08_doctors_employees_medicines_nice guys_paid less_aggressive jerks_offer raise_testosterone injections_illegal_dangerous_unethical_tiny income_business.gif
title: Testosterone Injections For A Raise

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Studies show that nice guys get paid less than aggressive jerks.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should offer your doctor 10% of your next raise if he gives you testosterone injections.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would be illegal, dangerous, and unethical.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Said the man with the tiny income.

setting: Outdoor dirt path with grassy hills
situation: While walking outdoors with Dogbert, Dilbert laments that studies show nice guys earn less than aggressive jerks. Dogbert suggests bribing a doctor with a cut of a future raise in exchange for testosterone injections. Dilbert objects on legal and ethical grounds, and Dogbert counters by pointing out his meager income.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses Dilbert's ethical objections by implying that his low pay is the result of his scruples, so he can't afford to be principled.
summary: Dogbert responds to a complaint about nice guys earning less by proposing a shady medical bribe, then mocks his friend's principles as the cause of his poverty.

file: 2011/2011-11-29_anxiety_death & dying_could go wrong_did go worng_closer to death_creepy.gif
title: Seven Days Closer to Death

transcript.speaker: Unnamed coworker
transcript.text: This past week, everything that could go wrong did go wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Look on the bright side: You're seven days closer to death.

transcript.speaker: Unnamed coworker
transcript.text: Hey! That's true!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's creepy when that works.

situation: At a meeting, a coworker complains that everything that could go wrong went wrong the previous week. Dilbert offers a grim 'bright side' that the coworker is now a week closer to death, and the coworker cheerfully agrees it's true. Wally remarks that it's creepy when such a bleak consolation actually works.
punchline: Dilbert's morbid attempt at cheering someone up, reminding them that death is nearer, actually works, which Wally finds disturbing.
summary: A gloomy coworker is oddly consoled when told that misfortune at least means the end of life is a week closer.

file: 2011/2011-06-16_office workers_teds project_overlap_initiated discussions_create framwork_complementary architectures_leadership.gif
title: Wally's Leadership Means Doing Nothing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, have you done anything to address the overlap of your project with Ted's project?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes. I've initiated discussions to create a framework that would allow us to adopt complementary architectures.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... Nothing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When did we stop calling it leadership?

situation: The Boss asks Wally whether he has done anything about the overlap between his project and Ted's project. Wally answers with a string of buzzwords about initiating discussions and creating a framework for complementary architectures. The Boss translates this as doing nothing, and Wally responds by asking when that stopped counting as leadership.
punchline: Wally's jargon-filled answer amounts to doing nothing, and he cynically suggests that talking about doing something is what passes for leadership in the company.
summary: A manager questions an employee about duplicated project work and gets a pile of jargon that boils down to inaction, which the employee insists is leadership.

file: 2011/2011-12-24_business ethics_retail business_sales trip_dont talk_misleading impression_engineering support_after sale_bag of meat_lying bag of meat.gif
title: Lying Bag of Meat Sales Trip

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to come with me on a sales trip. But don't talk to the customer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your presence is needed to give a misleading impression of how much engineering support we plan to offer after the sale.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I'm nothing but a bag of meat?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No. You're a lying bag of meat.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to accompany him on a sales trip but forbids him from speaking to the customer. He explains that Dilbert's mere presence is meant to falsely suggest the company will provide lots of engineering support after the sale. Dilbert asks if he is just a bag of meat, and the Boss corrects him.
punchline: The Boss's attempt at reassurance actually makes things worse, since he insists Dilbert is not merely a prop but a deceptive one, openly admitting the plan is to mislead the customer.
summary: A manager recruits a silent engineer as a prop to deceive a client about future support, then makes his insult even worse while trying to correct it.

file: 2011/2011-09-19_annoyance_competition (psychology)_tweaks to ideas_fails_claim credit_many forms genius_steaming an oval.gif
title: Heads I Win, Tails You Lose

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I made a few tweaks to your idea.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Now if it fails it was your idea, and if it works I can claim credit.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Genius comes in many forms.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Such as steaming and oval?

situation: A coworker hands Dilbert a paper and says he has tweaked Dilbert's idea. He then cynically explains that he has arranged things so Dilbert takes the blame for any failure while he takes the credit for any success. When he calls this genius, Dilbert sarcastically replies that it is the steaming and oval kind.
punchline: Dilbert implies the coworker's 'genius' is really a steaming pile of excrement, a sarcastic insult to his credit-stealing, blame-shifting scheme.
summary: A colleague boasts about rigging a modified plan so he gets the glory and Dilbert gets the blame, and Dilbert answers with a scatological jab at his supposed brilliance.

file: 2011/2011-04-17_business ethics_language_best shore_off shore_some countries_better than others_racists.gif
title: Bestshore Instead of Offshore Racism

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And we plan to bestshore the production.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We say bestshore now instead of offshore.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that because we never tried to pick the best shore until now?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Of course we tried to pick the best shore!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But we never succeeded because we're incompetent?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All I'm saying is that some countries are better than others!

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: We're racists?

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that the company will now 'bestshore' production rather than offshore it. Dilbert pokes at the logic, suggesting past failures came from incompetence in choosing locations. The Boss defends himself by saying some countries are simply better than others, which leaves the room silent until a coworker concludes the company is racist.
punchline: The Boss's attempt to justify a euphemistic rebranding of offshoring by claiming some countries are better than others accidentally exposes the whole policy as prejudiced.
summary: A manager rebrands outsourcing with a cute new word, then talks himself into sounding bigoted while defending it.

file: 2011/2011-09-03_commerce_optimism_patents_patent infringement_google_apple_microsoft_oracle_nasa_astroid_life span of optimist_technology.gif
title: Patent Lawsuit Brings Asteroid Attack

transcript.speaker: Legal Counsel
transcript.text: Our newest product infringes patents from Google, Apple, Microsoft, and Oracle.

transcript.speaker: Legal Counsel
transcript.text: They've joined forces and hired NASA to nudge an asteroid toward our headquarters.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think we can win this.

transcript.speaker: Legal Counsel
transcript.text: I wonder what the average life span of an optimist is.

situation: A company lawyer tells Dilbert and The Boss that their new product infringes patents held by Google, Apple, Microsoft, and Oracle. Those companies have teamed up and hired NASA to redirect an asteroid at the company's headquarters. The Boss cheerfully claims they can still win, prompting the lawyer to muse about how long optimists live.
punchline: The Boss's baseless optimism in the face of literal planetary destruction draws a sarcastic remark that optimists probably don't live very long.
summary: Tech giants respond to a patent violation by sending an asteroid at the offending company, yet the boss remains upbeat about the outcome.

file: 2011/2011-10-09_anger_frustration_matrix comparing features_skin in game_bang head_cause extra work_value of time_ninja economics.gif
title: Ninja Economics Penalizes Extra Work

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: You know what would be great?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I'd like to see a matrix comparing the features of our past products.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, why don't you pull that together for our next meeting?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would take two days and the matrix would have no practical use.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The problem here is that Ted doesn't have any skin in the game.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I propose that Ted has to bang his head on the table whenever he causes me to do extra work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That will help Ted make better decisions about the value of my time.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Never mind.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ninja economics!

situation: Ted casually asks for a matrix comparing features of past products, and the Boss volunteers Dilbert to build it. Dilbert objects that it would waste two days and be useless, then proposes that Ted must bang his head on the table every time he creates extra work for someone else. Ted withdraws his request.
punchline: Dilbert turns a pointless request into a painful personal cost for the requester, making people who generate busywork finally feel consequences, and cheerfully calls it 'ninja economics'.
summary: When a colleague casually requests a useless report, Dilbert imposes a self-inflicted penalty scheme that makes the request instantly vanish.

file: 2011/2011-06-26_internet & world wide web_monsters_turned feral_engineers_social life_social skills_few weeks_wolfman_howls at inetrnet.gif
title: Engineer Goes Feral Without Meetings

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Steer clear of Darryl. He turned feral.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Feral?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's what happens when engineers don't get invited to meetings.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Darryl's only social life was meetings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He didn't get to use his social skills for a few weeks, and apparently he lost them.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Is it like he turned into a wolfman?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, except he's better at math. And he howls at the Internet, not the moon.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Can we watch?

transcript.speaker: Darryl
transcript.text: How-ooooo can you blog that?

situation: Alice warns Dilbert and Asok to avoid Darryl, an engineer who has turned 'feral' after being left out of meetings for a few weeks. Dilbert explains he lost his social skills from disuse and compares him to a wolfman who howls at the Internet. Asok asks to watch, and the final panel shows a wild-haired, bearded Darryl hunched at his computer howling about blogging while two coworkers peek around the cubicle wall.
punchline: An engineer whose only social outlet was meetings degenerates into a bearded, werewolf-like creature who howls at the Internet instead of the moon, and his coworkers treat it as a spectator event.
summary: A coworker who was shut out of meetings for weeks has reverted to a wild, bearded state, baying at his computer while colleagues gawk.

file: 2011/2011-02-03_budget for a poor job_build software_business ethics_cheap or smart_executives_poor job_return on investment_selling upogardes.gif
title: Buggy Software Pays Better Returns

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If we build our software with no bugs, we can make a 10% return on our investment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But if we do a poor job, we can make a 40% return by selling upgrades and service.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But don't worry. We only have the budget for a poor job.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Phew!

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: I can't remember if we're cheap or smart.

setting: Conference room during a business presentation
situation: Dilbert presents to two executives, showing that flawless software yields only a 10% return while shoddy software earns 40% through upgrades and service. He then reassures them that the budget only allows a poor job anyway. The relieved executives admit they can't tell whether their frugality is deliberate strategy or just cheapness.
punchline: The executives' cheapness accidentally lines up with the more profitable strategy of shipping buggy software, and they can't tell whether they're being clever or just stingy.
summary: A presenter lays out why sloppy software out-earns perfect software, and the relieved decision-makers realize their stinginess may have looked like strategy.

file: 2011/2011-12-14_ignorance (knowledge)_elbonian factory_hysterical blindness_hats_long hats_elbonian_conveyor belt.gif
title: Elbonian Factory Workers Hysterically Blind

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We have a safety problem at our Elbonian factory.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're getting reports of hysterical blindness. They don't know what's causing it.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian worker
transcript.text: I can't see!

setting: The Boss's office, then an Elbonian factory assembly line
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss about a safety problem at the Elbonian factory, where workers are reporting sudden blindness of unknown cause. The final panel shows Elbonian workers on a conveyor belt line wearing tall, heavy hats that cover their eyes, with one shouting that he can't see.
punchline: The cause of the blindness is obvious to the reader, since the workers' enormous hats are pulled down over their eyes, even though the company claims not to know what is causing it.
summary: Management puzzles over mysterious blindness at an overseas plant while the workers' oversized headgear plainly covers their eyes.

file: 2011/2011-05-18_happiness_ignorance (knowledge)_idiot_health benefits_social stigma_healthy_transition_psychology.gif
title: Becoming Happy Idiot for Health

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm considering becoming an idiot so I can get the health benefits of happiness.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It comes with a social stigma, but that's not a problem if I'm not aware that I'm an idiot.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel healthy today, so there's a good chance I already made the transition.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Yep.

setting: Outdoor grassy hills, on a walk
situation: Dilbert walks through the countryside with Ratbert and muses about deliberately becoming an idiot to enjoy the health benefits of happiness. He reasons that the social stigma wouldn't matter if he were unaware of being an idiot. In the last panel he holds Ratbert and suggests he may have already made the transition, and Ratbert agrees.
punchline: Ratbert's blunt 'Yep' confirms that Dilbert's very reasoning shows he is already the oblivious idiot he is contemplating becoming.
summary: A man pondering whether ignorance might buy him a healthier, happier life gets a one-word verdict from his small companion that he is already there.

file: 2011/2011-03-25_deception_managers & supervisors_learn from mistakes_make alits_wrong this year_coincidence_perfromance reviews_management legends_business.gif
title: Mistakes List Before Performance Reviews

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can learn from our mistakes. Let's make a list of the things that each of you did wrong this year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it just a coincidence that our annual performance reviews are due next week?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It would have been the stuff of management legends.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Very nice try.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting, then the Boss's office
situation: The Boss stands at a flip chart labeled "Mistakes" and asks his team to list everything each of them did wrong this year, framing it as a learning exercise. Dilbert points out that the exercise conveniently lands just before annual performance reviews are due. The Boss admits the scheme would have been a legendary management move, and Catbert congratulates him on the attempt.
punchline: The Boss's "learning from mistakes" exercise was really a ploy to gather ammunition for negative performance reviews, and he regrets only that it was caught, not that it was devious.
summary: A manager's cheerful brainstorm about past failures turns out to be a sneaky way to collect evidence against his staff before review season.

file: 2011/2011-07-31_groceries & grocery stores_natural disasters_saving & investment_complete meltdown_financial system_six months_food_water_batteries_gold coins_light on defensive weapontry_protein bars_money.gif
title: Doomsday Prepper Threatens Dilbert's Supplies

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm preparing for the complete meltdown of our financial system.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I've got six months of food and water.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have batteries, flashlights, and gold coins.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm prepared too.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I have your home address.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And I noticed that your preparations are light on defensive weaponry.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can you add some protein bars to the shopping list?

setting: Office break area near the coffee maker
situation: Dilbert and Alice compare their preparations for a total financial system collapse. Dilbert lists batteries, flashlights, and gold coins, while Alice has months of food and water. She then reveals she knows his home address and that he lacks weapons, implying she plans to raid his supplies.
punchline: Alice's casual request to add protein bars to the shopping list reveals she intends to take Dilbert's stockpile by force once society collapses.
summary: Two coworkers swap disaster-survival plans until one calmly hints she'll be showing up armed to claim the other's stash.

file: 2011/2011-10-19_anger_food werewolf_too long_no food_werewolf.gif
title: Hungry Coworker Becomes Food Werewolf

transcript.speaker: Woman in meeting
transcript.text: We'd better wrap up this meeting because Jenny is a food werewolf.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Woman in meeting
transcript.text: When she goes too long without eating, she turns into a werewolf.

transcript.speaker: Jenny
transcript.text: Rrrrr

transcript.speaker: Woman in meeting
transcript.text: It might be too late.

transcript.speaker: Jenny
transcript.text: Ya think?

situation: A coworker urges the group to end a meeting early, warning that Jenny turns into a werewolf when she goes too long without food. Dilbert is confused, and as she explains, Jenny begins growling and visibly transforming. By the last panel she is a snarling werewolf, sarcastically responding to the warning that it may be too late.
punchline: The warning comes too late because the meeting ran so long that Jenny has already turned into a werewolf, and she sarcastically points out the obvious.
summary: A meeting drags on so long that a hungry attendee literally transforms into a snarling beast just as a colleague cautions about her condition.

file: 2011/2011-05-12_annoyance_doctors' offices_medicines_whiny idiots_pill_doctor_exam room_office_treadmill_pass out_medical.gif
title: Doctor Is Sick of Whiners Too

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm sick of listening to whiny idiots. Do you have a pill for that?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: I sure do! I took a handful of them this morning and I feel great in spite of your complaining!!

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: How funny would it be if I make you run on a treadmill until you pass out?

situation: Dilbert sits on the exam table and asks his doctor for a pill that cures his annoyance with whiny people. The doctor cheerfully replies that he took a handful of such pills himself and feels great despite Dilbert's complaining. He then threatens to make Dilbert run on a treadmill until he passes out.
punchline: The doctor turns Dilbert's own whining about whiners back on him, responding with a cheerful, medicated threat of cruel treatment.
summary: A patient hoping for a cure for his irritation at complainers gets a smug doctor who is happily doped up and ready to punish him.

file: 2011/2011-07-05_annoyance_apathy_choosing_comments_two alternatives_recommended option_more expensive.gif
title: Boss Approves Expensive Option Unread

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you read my comments on the two alternatives?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I recommended option two because neither plan will work but option one is way more expensive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I already approved option one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you need any more help, just let me know.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss whether he read the written comments on two proposed plans, and the boss admits he did not. Dilbert explains that he recommended option two because neither plan will work and option one costs far more. The boss reveals he has already approved option one, and Dilbert sarcastically offers further help.
punchline: The boss approved the costlier, doomed plan without reading the advice, making Dilbert's sarcastic offer of more help pointless.
summary: A manager signs off on the pricier of two failing plans before ever reading his employee's warning, leaving the employee to offer weary, sarcastic assistance.

file: 2011/2011-02-11_competition (psychology)_inventions_facebook_robot arm_talented employees_giant condescending facebook.gif
title: Facebook's Giant Condescending Robot Arm

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Facebook has created a giant robot arm to steal talented employees from other companies.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: It's here!!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No, it looks like we got the giant condescending Facebook robot arm instead.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Pat pat

situation: At a meeting table, Catbert tells the Boss and a colleague that Facebook has built a giant robot arm to steal talented employees from other companies. A huge robotic arm bursts through the wall, startling everyone. Instead of grabbing anyone, it just pats the Boss on his bald head.
punchline: The robot arm skips over the Boss because he isn't talented enough to be worth stealing, so it condescendingly pats him on the head instead.
summary: A feared employee-snatching machine from a rival tech giant crashes in and then dismissively pats the boss, leaving his workforce unwanted.

file: 2011/2011-08-22_commerce_new software vendor_form realtionship_take money_ex wife.gif
title: Software Vendor Wants Your Money

transcript.speaker: Software Vendor
transcript.text: I'm your new software vendor. I'm here to form a relationship with you.

transcript.speaker: Software Vendor
transcript.text: That way it will be easy to take half of your money.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does that ever work?

transcript.speaker: Software Vendor
transcript.text: It worked for my ex-wife.

situation: A software vendor in a suit stands over Dilbert's desk and introduces himself as his new vendor, saying he wants to form a relationship. He then explains that this will make it easy to take half of Dilbert's money, comparing the arrangement to a divorce settlement. Dilbert skeptically asks if the tactic works, and the vendor says it worked for his ex-wife.
punchline: The vendor's pitch of building a 'relationship' to extract half of a customer's money mirrors a divorce settlement, and he cites his ex-wife as proof the strategy works.
summary: A salesman cheerfully admits that cultivating a close bond with a customer is just a way to drain their wallet, the same trick his former spouse pulled on him.

file: 2011/2011-07-24_gadgets_scientific equipment_data center_lights out_eliminate problems_moving cables_power cords_ruining everything_speakerphone_humans are germs_science.gif
title: Data Center Speakerphone Banishes Humans

transcript.speaker: Speakerphone
transcript.text: The data center is evolving into a "lights out" operation.

transcript.speaker: Speakerphone
transcript.text: Employees will no longer be allowed in the data center.

transcript.speaker: Speakerphone
transcript.text: We hope to eliminate all of the problems that humans cause by moving cables, unplugging power cords, and ruining everything with their dirt and static.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He makes it sound as if the data center is alive and we humans are nothing but germs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: By the way, who called this meeting and who's on the speakerphone?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you... the data center?

transcript.speaker: Speakerphone
transcript.text: Click

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a bad feeling about this.

situation: Three employees sit around a conference table listening to a voice on a speakerphone announce that humans will be banned from the data center to prevent the problems they cause. Dilbert notes that the voice treats people like germs, then realizes nobody knows who called the meeting or who is speaking. When he asks if the caller is the data center itself, the speakerphone hangs up.
punchline: The data center itself appears to have called the meeting to announce it is eliminating humans, and it hangs up when confronted, implying a machine uprising.
summary: A mysterious speakerphone voice tells staff they are being locked out of the server room, and its abrupt hang-up suggests the facility itself is giving the orders.

file: 2011/2011-12-05_rebellions_riots_violence_rebel army_social justice_iron fisted dictator_billionaire_stain_tank tread_looting_excited animals.gif
title: Dogbert's Rebel Army Recruitment Pitch

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm forming a rebel army.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Count me in! What are we fighting for?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You'll be fighting for social justice and I'll be scheming to become an iron-fisted dictator.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In the long run, I'll be a billionaire and you'll be a stain on a tank tread.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Please, please say there will be looting.

setting: A bare office or room with gray walls and a dotted floor
situation: Dogbert announces he is forming a rebel army, and an eager Ratbert volunteers. Dogbert cheerfully explains that Ratbert will fight for social justice while Dogbert secretly plans to seize power as a dictator, and that Ratbert will end up crushed under a tank. Ratbert ignores the grim fate and only hopes there will be looting.
punchline: Ratbert is so enthusiastic about the chance for looting that he doesn't care he is being used as cannon fodder for Dogbert's power grab.
summary: A scheming dog openly admits he will exploit a gullible follower's revolution for personal power, and the follower only cares about plunder.

file: 2011/2011-06-17_business ethics_inefficiencies_kaizen team_soultions_busy_being ineffcient_ignorance_aggressive type of objectivity.gif
title: Ignorance Rebranded as Objectivity

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I noticed some inefficiencies in another department, so I formed a kaizen team to find solutions.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I asked some of the people in that department to be on the team, but they were busy being inefficient.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: With any luck, my ignorance of their function will be seen as an aggressive type of objectivity.

situation: Wally explains to the meeting, with the Boss and Dilbert seated beside him, that he formed a kaizen improvement team to fix another department's inefficiencies. The department's own staff declined to join because they were busy being inefficient. Wally then hopes that his total lack of knowledge about their work will be mistaken for bold objectivity.
punchline: Wally is trying to spin his complete ignorance of the department as a virtue, passing off cluelessness as aggressive objectivity.
summary: A lazy employee launches an improvement team for a department he doesn't understand and hopes his cluelessness will pass for impartial insight.

file: 2011/2011-09-30_deception_hypocrisy_open door policy_suggestions_not importnat_extra work.gif
title: Open Door Policy, Closed Mind

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thanks for the suggestion, Asok.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm going to ignore it because you're not important to my career and I don't like doing extra work.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm confused. Why do you have an open-door policy?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How can you leave if the door isn't open?

situation: Asok brings a suggestion to the Boss, who thanks him politely and then candidly admits he will ignore it because Asok is unimportant to his career and acting on it means extra work. Asok, confused, asks why the Boss bothers having an open-door policy, and the Boss says the door is open so Asok can leave.
punchline: The Boss's open-door policy exists only to let employees exit after being dismissed, not to encourage genuine feedback.
summary: A manager cheerfully admits he'll disregard an underling's idea, then explains his welcoming policy is really just a way to usher people out.

file: 2011/2011-06-11_boredom_despair_mind numbing tesk_stop thinking.gif
title: Craving Mind-Numbing Work to Stop Thinking

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can't wait to finish this mind-numbing task. . .

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So I can start another mind-numbing task.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I really need to stop thinking.

situation: Wally sits alone at his desk holding papers, thinking in thought bubbles across three panels. He says he is eager to finish a dull task only so he can begin another equally dull one. He then concludes that what he really wants is to stop thinking altogether.
punchline: Wally is so disillusioned that he finds mindless busywork appealing because it spares him from having to think, implying that his job is soul-crushing and his own thoughts are worse than the drudgery.
summary: A weary employee reveals that he welcomes tedious work simply because it lets his brain switch off.

file: 2011/2011-05-07_computers & peripherals_embarrassment_process order_middle ages_stinging sarcasm_faxed copy_1950's_happy time_bob in procurement.gif
title: Sarcasm Wins a Faxed Contract

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bob in Procurement

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I need the signed original contract to process your order.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because we're in the Middle Ages?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Ouch! Your stinging sarcasm has embarrassed me into saying I will accept a faxed copy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are we good now?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Absolutely, because the 1950s is a happy time.

setting: Bob's desk in the procurement department
situation: Bob, a dinosaur-like procurement employee, insists Dilbert provide a signed original contract before he can process an order. Dilbert sarcastically compares this to the Middle Ages, which embarrasses Bob into accepting a faxed copy instead. Dilbert asks if they're settled, and Bob cheerfully confirms.
punchline: Bob concedes only to a slightly less outdated requirement, accepting a fax, and is proud of it because he happily lives in the 1950s.
summary: A procurement clerk demanding paper originals is shamed into accepting a fax, which is hardly more modern.

file: 2011/2011-05-16_computers & peripherals_frustration_coding_users specifications_technology.gif
title: Boss Announces Changed Specs Too Late

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did I remember to tell you before you finished the coding that the user's specifications changed?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aaaiii-yiiii-yiiii-yiiii-yiiiiii!!!!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, no-ish?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Bam! Bam! Bam!

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, casually asks Dilbert whether he mentioned that the user's specifications changed before the coding was finished. Dilbert screams in horror and then repeatedly bangs his head on his desk while the Boss looks on, unbothered.
punchline: The Boss obviously failed to tell Dilbert about the changed requirements until after the work was done, and his vague 'no-ish?' shows he is oblivious to the wasted effort and Dilbert's despair.
summary: A manager breezily admits he forgot to mention that the requirements had changed, driving his programmer to a head-banging breakdown.

file: 2011/2011-03-04_competition (psychology)_exhibitions_barf bag_consumer electronics show_new product cooler than anything_weighs an ounce.gif
title: Dilbert's Barf Bag Trade Show Trip

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I see you have your giant-sized barf bag. You must be going to the consumer electronics show.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yup.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Every time I see a new product that is cooler than anything we're working on, I'll go to the bag.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: At the show

transcript.speaker: Exhibitor
transcript.text: And it only weighs one ounce!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: FOOMP!!!

setting: Office hallway, then a consumer electronics trade show
situation: A coworker notices Dilbert carrying a huge barf bag and guesses he is heading to the consumer electronics show. Dilbert explains he plans to throw up whenever he sees a product better than anything his company is building. At the show, an exhibitor demonstrates a slim, feather-light gadget and Dilbert promptly buries his face in the bag.
punchline: Dilbert expects so many competitors' products to be superior to his own company's that he needs a giant barf bag, and the exhibitor's impressive gadget sets him off right away.
summary: A man brings an oversized sick bag to a gadget expo because he expects rival inventions to make him feel physically ill about his own employer's lagging products.

file: 2011/2011-11-21_computers & peripherals_machinery_office equipment_software maintence_indispensible_zeberpupin system.gif
title: Indispensable Software Patch Guy

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I successfully installed a software maintenance patch to the Zeberpupin system.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'd show you, but it's just a bunch of zeroes and ones.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The word you're trying to think of is "indispensable."

situation: At a meeting table, Wally tells the Boss and Dilbert that he installed a maintenance patch. He says he can't show any evidence because it's only zeroes and ones, then calmly sips coffee and tells the Boss that the word he is searching for to describe him is 'indispensable.'
punchline: Wally claims credit for work nobody can verify and uses the incomprehensibility of technical work to present himself as indispensable.
summary: A smug employee takes credit for an unverifiable technical chore and prompts his manager to praise him as irreplaceable.

file: 2011/2011-10-28_business ethics_illness_industrial sludge_drank_has tail_lower iq points_bright future_quality assurance_marketing_zip line guide_business.gif
title: Sludge Drinker Has Bright Future

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's been like this since our CEO made him drink a glass of our industrial sludge at a press conference.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It lopped a few points off his I.Q., but he still has a bright future in quality assurance or maybe marketing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And with his new tail he'd be an awesome zip line guide.

situation: Dilbert and Wally, holding coffee, stand beside a dazed, twitchy coworker (Asok) who was forced by the CEO to drink industrial sludge at a press conference. Wally says the sludge lowered his IQ but he could still work in quality assurance or marketing, and in the last panel the coworker has grown a tail.
punchline: The poisoned employee's mental decline and mutation barely matter, since his lowered IQ still qualifies him for quality assurance or marketing, and his new tail gives him a useful side career.
summary: After being made to swallow toxic factory waste for a publicity stunt, a coworker is left dim and tailed, and his colleagues cheerfully list the jobs he is now suited for.

file: 2011/2011-03-20_laziness_meetings_buddha jogging_reliability stats_data does not exist_random numbers_deep understanding of reality.gif
title: Wally's Fake Data Philosophy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, get me the reliability stats for our previous model.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I am fairly certain the data does not exist.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally can show you how to get it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Come with me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You start by typing random numbers into a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Then what?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Then you're done.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: All business data is intentionally misleading. I just take it to the next level.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: A deep understanding of reality is exactly the same thing as laziness.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Click click click click click

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That can't be right.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Have you ever seen a statue of Buddha jogging?

situation: In a meeting, the Boss asks Asok for reliability statistics on the previous model. Asok says the data doesn't exist, so the Boss sends him to Wally, who teaches him to simply type random numbers into a spreadsheet. Wally justifies his laziness with a faux-philosophical claim about enlightenment.
punchline: Wally dresses up his laziness and data fabrication as profound wisdom, arguing that enlightened beings never exert effort, as proven by the absence of jogging Buddha statues.
summary: A young engineer is taught by his laziest coworker to fabricate missing data with made-up numbers, justified by a pseudo-spiritual rationalization.

file: 2011/2011-04-10_anxiety_stress_meltdown cubicle_theoretical workload limit_brains full_becomes overdue_projects overdue_tasks_urgent_funny noise_missed dead line.gif
title: Theoretical Workload Limit Brain Meltdown

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meltdown in cubicle 459540!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's Ted. He must have reached his T.W.L.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: His what?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Theoretical workload limit. In layman's terms, his brain is full.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It starts when just one of your projects becomes overdue.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You end up spending all of your time explaining why you didn't get it done.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That makes all of your other projects overdue. When every task becomes urgent, your brain can't decide what to do next.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Brains make a funny noise when they shut down.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Poink

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Uh-oh. I just missed a deadline.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: And so it begins.

situation: Dilbert explains to coworkers that Ted has suffered a meltdown after hitting his 'theoretical workload limit.' He describes how one overdue project leads to endless explanations, making every other project overdue until the brain shuts down. As he finishes, a coworker announces he just missed a deadline, implying the cycle is starting again.
punchline: The same overload cascade Dilbert describes as the cause of Ted's brain shutdown is already beginning in another coworker the moment he misses a deadline.
summary: A fully loaded employee collapses at his desk, and a colleague's lecture on how overdue work snowballs is interrupted by the next victim's first missed deadline.

file: 2011/2011-03-17_air travel_cash payment_college freind_cost & standard of living_expensive_friendship_relationships.gif
title: Paying Friend Not to Invite

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: My best friend from college keeps bugging me to visit her. The flight will cost a small fortune.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Try offering her a cash payment of half the estimated cost of the trip if she agrees to stop inviting you.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You don't have any friends, do you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hear they're expensive.

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker
situation: A coworker complains that her college friend keeps inviting her to visit and the flight is costly. Dilbert suggests paying the friend half the trip cost to stop inviting her. The coworker deduces he has no friends, and he replies that he hears friends are expensive.
punchline: Dilbert justifies his lack of friends by claiming friendships cost too much, treating relationships purely as a financial burden.
summary: A coworker's travel dilemma prompts Dilbert to propose buying her way out of a friendship, revealing his own cost-cutting view of companionship.

file: 2011/2011-02-21_engineers_laziness_project budget_new technology_slow learner_expensive.gif
title: Slow Learner or Just Expensive

transcript.speaker: Project Manager
transcript.text: You used the entire engineering portion of my project budget just learning the new technology.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I'm sorry things didn't work out for you.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Some say I'm a slow learner, but I like to think of myself as expensive.

situation: A project manager complains to an engineer that the whole engineering budget was burned just on learning a new technology. The engineer offers a flat, insincere apology about things not working out for the manager, then sips from a mug and quips that he'd rather be seen as expensive than as a slow learner.
punchline: The engineer reframes his own incompetence as a high price tag, showing no accountability and treating the blown budget as a point of pride.
summary: Confronted about a budget drained by training himself on new tools, an engineer shrugs it off by calling himself costly instead of slow.

file: 2011/2011-08-11_business ethics_taxes_sociopth_victimless crime_insider information_hedge fund_split profit_tax people.gif
title: Sociopath Pitches Insider Trading Scheme

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The great thing about being a sociopath is that everything feels like a victimless crime.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you give me some insider information for my hedge fund, I'll split the profit with you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Think of it as a tax on people you don't know.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's the best kind!

situation: Dogbert stands on the Boss's desk and explains that being a sociopath makes every crime feel victimless. He then offers to split hedge fund profits if the Boss supplies insider information. The Boss happily agrees once Dogbert frames it as a tax on strangers.
punchline: The Boss enthusiastically embraces insider trading because it only harms people he doesn't know, comparing it to his favorite kind of tax.
summary: A scheming dog talks his boss into illegal stock tips by recasting the fraud as a levy on faceless strangers.

file: 2011/2011-04-24_fraternization_joking_agenda_know anything_important he is_like his jokes_late for dinner_jokes_table_meeting_laughter_business.gif
title: Faking Laughter For Important Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The first thing on the agenda. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hold on. I don't know anything about this guy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's the difference?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to know how important he is.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I pretend to like his jokes? Should I nod in agreement no matter what he says?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can call me anything. Just don't call me late for dinner.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope I didn't waste that.

situation: At the start of a meeting, Dilbert interrupts the Boss to say he doesn't know who the attendee is, explaining he needs to know how important the man is. He then openly wonders whether he should pretend to like his jokes and agree with everything he says. The Boss responds with a corny joke and Dilbert laughs uproariously, then worries he wasted the effort.
punchline: Dilbert openly admits he calibrates his flattery to someone's rank, then fakes enthusiastic laughter at a stale joke and worries the sucking-up was wasted if the person turns out to be unimportant.
summary: A man pays an exaggerated, rank-dependent laugh to an old dinner joke and then frets that his insincere flattery might have been squandered.

file: 2011/2011-12-18_declare failure_explaining things_frustration_incompetence_office workers_partial victory_platform upgarde_teds brain_trapped.gif
title: Ted's Brain Is Where Knowledge Dies

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted can explain what you need to do before the platform upgrade.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No he can't.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ted's brain is where knowledge goes to die.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's not good at explaining things.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The knowledge might be in his brain, but it's trapped there.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Unfortunately, Ted's incompetence is so unbelievable that you literally DON'T believe me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In time, you will assume that Ted taught me well but I forgot all of it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm doomed before I start. Let's just declare failure and move on.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That works for me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Partial victory.

setting: Office hallway and Dilbert's cubicle area
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to get instructions for the platform upgrade from Ted. Dilbert insists Ted is useless at explaining anything, but realizes the Boss won't believe him and will later blame Dilbert for forgetting what Ted taught him. He suggests declaring failure up front, and the Boss readily agrees.
punchline: Dilbert realizes he will be blamed for the project's failure no matter what, so getting the Boss to agree to declare failure in advance counts as a small win.
summary: Knowing his boss will blame him for Ted's useless instructions, Dilbert talks the boss into conceding defeat before the project even begins.

file: 2011/2011-01-27_fear_rodents_transcontinental journeys_elbonia_too cold_airplanes_operate_underground route_fly_switzerland_swear system_sewerside mission_warm jacket_rat hammer.gif
title: Sewer Trek to Elbonia

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I need you to go to Elbonia. It's too cold for airplanes to operate there, so you'll need to use the underground route.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Fly into Switzerland and follow the sewer systems from there. Stick to the side of the sewer where it's dryer.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: It's a sewerside mission!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll need a warm jacket and a rat hammer.

situation: The Boss orders Asok to travel to Elbonia on a business trip. Because it is too cold there for planes, he must fly to Switzerland and then crawl through the sewer system, keeping to the drier side. Asok cheerfully calls it a sewerside mission, and the Boss tells him to bring a warm jacket and a rat hammer.
punchline: The Boss casually assigns a miserable, dangerous sewer journey as routine business travel, and the naive Asok responds with enthusiasm, with the rat hammer revealing the grim reality.
summary: A manager sends a junior employee on an absurd trip to a frozen foreign country by way of rat-infested sewers, and the employee treats it like an adventure.

file: 2011/2011-12-22_anminals_greed and corruption_money_pay to protest_peaceful protest_permit_protest movements_rebellions_to protest.gif
title: Protest Permit Turns Into Payoff

transcript.speaker: Protester
transcript.text: I'm staging a peaceful protest against your greed and corruption.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you have a permit to protest here?

transcript.speaker: Protester
transcript.text: No. How much do they cost?

transcript.speaker: Protester
transcript.text: I'm winning this, right?

setting: A living room with a large green armchair
situation: An orange protester holding a blank sign announces a peaceful protest against Dogbert's greed and corruption. Dogbert, seated in his armchair, asks whether the protester has a permit. When the protester asks how much permits cost, Dogbert takes his money, and the protester hands over cash while hopefully asking if he is winning.
punchline: The protester, trying to fight greed and corruption, ends up paying Dogbert for a 'permit', which is exactly the corrupt behavior he was protesting, yet he naively believes he is winning.
summary: A demonstrator denouncing a fat cat's graft ends up cheerfully paying him a fee for the right to complain.

file: 2011/2011-04-27_eliminate redundencies_internal process_irony_task force.gif
title: Duplicate Task Forces Against Redundancy

transcript.speaker: Green-shirted colleague
transcript.text: I started a task force to eliminate redundancies in our internal processes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Really? I'm doing the same thing.

situation: At a meeting, a colleague in a green shirt announces he has started a task force to eliminate redundancies in internal processes. Dilbert replies that he is doing the very same thing. In the last panel the Boss buries his face in his hands while the two others sit with arms crossed, having realized the absurdity.
punchline: Two people independently launching task forces to eliminate redundancy is itself a redundancy, which makes the effort self-defeating.
summary: Two coworkers realize they have each launched a separate initiative to cut duplicated effort, creating exactly the duplication they wanted to remove.

file: 2011/2011-03-29_fake press relases_new green technology_scientist_2040 power home_refrigerator door_science.gif
title: Fake Green Energy Press Releases

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm writing fake press releases for imaginary new green energy technologies.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Scientists say that by 2040 you will be able to power your entire home with the breeze from your refrigerator door.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now how will I know which green breakthroughs are real?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Seriously? You think there are real ones?

situation: Dogbert sits at a laptop and tells Dilbert he is writing fake press releases about imaginary green energy technologies, then reads out an absurd example about powering a home from a refrigerator door breeze. Dilbert asks how he will tell real breakthroughs from fake ones, and Dogbert incredulously asks whether he thinks any are real.
punchline: Dogbert implies that all green energy breakthrough announcements are as fanciful as his fakes, so there is no real ones to distinguish.
summary: A dog cheerfully fabricates absurd clean-energy announcements and then scoffs at the idea that the genuine ones are any more believable.

file: 2011/2011-02-25_context_contracts_harvest organs_holes in contract_software contract_signed contract_holes in torso.gif
title: Software Contract Harvests Dilbert's Organs

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Company lawyer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I signed a software contract without getting your input because I was in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now the software company claims they can harvest my organs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you see any holes in their contract?

transcript.speaker: Company Lawyer
transcript.text: They mention holes... in the context of your torso.

situation: Dilbert admits to the company lawyer that he signed a software contract in a hurry without consulting legal. He hands over the contract, explaining that the vendor now claims the right to harvest his organs, and asks whether it has any loopholes. The lawyer reads it and deadpans that the only holes it mentions are the ones to be made in Dilbert's torso.
punchline: Asked for legal loopholes in the contract, the lawyer points out the only holes mentioned are the surgical ones in Dilbert's body, a grim reminder of what happens when you skip legal review.
summary: After carelessly signing a vendor agreement, Dilbert learns from his lawyer that the fine print literally entitles the vendor to cut him open.

file: 2011/2011-05-10_computers & peripherals_gadgets_4g products_goodness_competetive_g stands for.gif
title: Rebranding 4G Products as 8G

transcript.speaker: Man with phone
transcript.text: For competitive reasons, we've rebranded all of our 4G mobile products as 8G.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm curious what the marketing department thinks the "G" stands for.

transcript.speaker: Man in yellow tie
transcript.text: Guess what doesn't mean "goodness."

situation: At a meeting, a man holding a phone announces that all 4G mobile products have been rebranded as 8G to stay competitive. Dilbert wonders what marketing thinks the "G" stands for. In a cubicle, a coworker answers that it is not "goodness" while a seated colleague looks on.
punchline: Marketing renamed 4G to 8G just to sound twice as good, even though the "G" stands for "generation" and not "goodness", so the rebrand is meaningless and misleading.
summary: A company doubles the number on its phone technology label purely for marketing appeal, and a coworker points out the letter never meant what they assume.

file: 2011/2011-11-16_different_employees_goals_work little_year ahead_your goals_my goals_business.gif
title: Employee's Goals: Do Less, Avoid Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When I asked for your goals for the coming year, I had something different in mind.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not "work as little as possible while avoiding the wrath of the Pointy-Haired Troll."

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Don't call them MY goals if you mean YOUR goals.

situation: The Boss reads an employee's written goals for the coming year and complains that they are not what he wanted. The goals amount to working as little as possible while avoiding the Boss's anger. The employee, standing with a coffee mug, replies that the Boss shouldn't call them 'my goals' if he really means his own goals.
punchline: The employee points out, sarcastically, that the boss only wants him to adopt the boss's goals, so asking for the employee's goals was a pretense, and the employee's honest goals are to do as little as possible.
summary: A manager is disappointed that a worker's yearly objectives amount to slacking off, and the worker coolly points out that the manager only wants his own aims restated.

file: 2011/2011-11-11_employees_executives_ignorance (knowledge)_technical details_idea_deciosns_people involved_pale and poorly dressed_business.gif
title: Boss Judges Ideas by People

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop right there. Don't tell me the technical details of your idea.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I make my decisions based on what I know about the people involved.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You know less about me than you know about my idea.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is your idea pale and poorly dressed?

situation: Dilbert comes to pitch an idea, but his boss cuts him off and refuses to hear the technical details. The boss claims he decides based on knowing the people involved, so Dilbert points out the boss knows even less about him than about the idea. The boss responds by asking whether the idea is pale and poorly dressed, revealing that his only impression of Dilbert is his appearance.
punchline: The boss's entire knowledge of Dilbert amounts to a stereotype of his looks (pale and poorly dressed), exposing how shallow his people-based decision-making really is.
summary: A manager who refuses to hear an idea because he trusts his judgment of people turns out to know nothing about the employee beyond his appearance.

file: 2011/2011-09-13_deception_electronic mail_answer email_signal to noise_technical problem.gif
title: Email Too Noisy to Read

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You didn't answer my email.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I tried to read it but the signal-to-noise ratio was too low.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So it's sort of a technical problem?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay.

setting: Office, in front of a cubicle wall
situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, complains that Dilbert never answered his email. Dilbert explains that he tried to read it but the signal-to-noise ratio was too low. The Boss reframes this as a technical problem, and Dilbert simply agrees.
punchline: Dilbert politely insults the Boss's rambling, content-free email by using technical jargon, and the Boss misses the insult and treats it as an IT issue, which Dilbert happily lets him believe.
summary: Dilbert dodges blame for ignoring a rambling email by using engineering jargon that the clueless Boss mistakes for a technical fault.

file: 2011/2011-10-11_angry rich guy_buy small companies_mergers & acquisitions_obscenely profitable_prosperity_suck good will_universally despised.gif
title: Acquiring Goodwill From Angry Founder

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our company is obscenely profitable but universally despised.

transcript.speaker: Projected Man
transcript.text: Grrrr

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our plan is to buy a smaller and more popular company, take their name, and suck out their goodwill like a monkey on an orange.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Please welcome their founder, Bradley. He's the angriest rich guy you'll ever meet.

situation: The Boss presents to his staff, explaining that the company is hugely profitable but disliked by everyone. His plan is to acquire a smaller, more popular company, adopt its name, and drain its goodwill. He then introduces the founder of the target company, who is seen scowling and growling.
punchline: The company intends to buy goodwill by parasitically absorbing a beloved brand, and the founder it is acquiring is visibly furious about it.
summary: A manager reveals a plan to fix his hated but wealthy firm by swallowing a likable startup and borrowing its reputation, while the bitter founder glares from the audience.

file: 2011/2011-01-23_sales personnel_friendship_allegiance_relationships.gif
title: Frendor: Friend Plus Vendor Stalker

transcript.text: Dilbert, this is Alan. He's a frendor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's not just a friend, and not just a vendor. He's something in between.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He'll laugh at your jokes and invite you to golf.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Some people are bothered by this conditional type of "affection."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But it's better than the nothing you have now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now you've done it. You turned your frendor into a stalker.

The Boss explains Alan will flatter Dilbert and invite him to golf, then Dilbert admits he has already chosen a competitor. Alan turns into a persistent stalker, and Dilbert privately admits he enjoys the attention.
punchline: Dilbert, who has no real friends, finds that the fake affection of a spurned salesman is still flattering enough to enjoy, even when it becomes stalking.
summary: A boss brings in a salesman who pretends to be a buddy to win business, and when Dilbert rejects him the pursuit turns creepy yet oddly flattering to the lonely engineer.

file: 2011/2011-02-24_cats & kittens_computer software_contracts_harvest organs_signed_software services_save lives.gif
title: Organ Harvester Over Software Agreement

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: There's a guy in the lobby who says he's here to harvest your organs.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Apparently, you signed a software services agreement without fully understanding it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, at least I can save lives.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: He said something about his cat's birthday.

situation: A coworker tells Dilbert that a man in the lobby wants to harvest his organs. She explains it's because he signed a software services agreement without fully understanding it. Dilbert consoles himself that at least his organs will save lives, but she adds that the man mentioned his cat's birthday.
punchline: Dilbert's hope that his forfeited organs will serve a noble purpose is crushed by the revelation that the harvester wants them for a frivolous reason, his cat's birthday.
summary: A careless software contract turns out to hand a stranger the rights to Dilbert's body parts, and the sliver of comfort he finds in it is undone by the trivial reason behind the claim.

file: 2011/2011-01-12_engineers_vaccinnations_wicked case_disease_heat_every seven years_kill me!.gif
title: Pon Farr Strikes Office Meeting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My doctor says I have a wicked case of pon farr. It's when Vulcans and engineers go into heat every seven years.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm pretty sure I don't care, but let me check my calendar just in case...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Someone kill me! Now! Now! Now!

situation: Dilbert tells his coworkers at a meeting table that he has pon farr, the Vulcan mating fever that supposedly also afflicts engineers every seven years. Alice dismissively checks her calendar on her phone. She discovers that her own seven-year cycle is due, and she panics and begs to be killed.
punchline: Alice sarcastically claims not to care about Dilbert's condition, but her calendar reveals she is also an engineer in her own seven-year heat, and she is horrified.
summary: A coworker's cheerful announcement of a Vulcan-style mating fever turns personal when a colleague's calendar shows she is next.

file: 2011/2011-08-04_complaining_conversation_reflexive urge_diagree_counter point_software can't be changed.gif
title: Reflexive Disagreement Gets Ridiculous Software Claim

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Everything you said is right, but I have a reflexive urge to disagree with you.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: If you don't mind, I'm going to make a ridiculous counterpoint just to get it out of my system.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, but don't be creepy about it.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Software can't be changed.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Ahhh... that's good.

setting: Office, at a desk or conference table
situation: Asok admits to Dilbert that although Dilbert is right about everything, he feels a compulsive need to argue. He asks permission to make a ridiculous counterpoint to purge the urge. Dilbert tells him not to be creepy, and Asok blurts out that software can't be changed, then sighs with relief.
punchline: The obviously absurd claim that software can't be changed is treated as a harmless release of tension, with Asok's blissful sigh making it sound faintly indecent, while also mocking the kind of objection people often raise in real software discussions.
summary: A junior engineer must voice a deliberately silly objection to purge his urge to contradict a colleague, and sighs with pleasure when he does.
keywords: get it out of my system

file: 2011/2011-01-25_tax incentives_capital investments_pursue opportunities_over burdened staff_divert resocurces_top priorities.gif
title: Tax Incentives Divert Overburdened Staff

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The government announced tax incentives for new capital investments.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's great. Now we can pursue marginally attractive opportunities with our overburdened staff.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Is he always like this?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll just divert resources from our top priorities.

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: At a meeting, a green horned colleague reports that the government has announced tax incentives for new capital investments. The Boss cheerfully decides to chase marginally attractive opportunities using the already overburdened staff. The colleague asks Dilbert if the boss is always like this, and Dilbert confirms it while the boss announces he will pull resources from top priorities.
punchline: The boss treats a mere tax incentive as a reason to chase mediocre opportunities, cheerfully sacrificing the company's real priorities and exhausting his staff in the process.
summary: A boss responds to a government tax break by loading overworked employees with weak new projects at the expense of what actually matters.

file: 2011/2011-10-20_commerce_credit_forbidden knowledge_change to dotted lines_made of ink.gif
title: Dotted Lines and Forbidden Knowledge

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Change all of the lines to dotted.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're not made of ink.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why'd I just get chills?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Me too. It feels like some sort of forbidden knowledge.

situation: The Boss reads from a document and instructs Dilbert to change all the lines to dotted, as if it were a drawing or org chart. Dilbert objects that they are not made of ink, which implies the two of them are cartoon characters drawn with lines. Both feel an eerie chill at having stumbled onto a meta-level truth.
punchline: Dilbert accidentally points out that they are comic characters drawn in ink, and the two of them sense that they have brushed against forbidden knowledge about their own fictional existence.
summary: A routine request about line styles in a document leads two cartoon coworkers to a spooky glimpse of their own fictional nature.

file: 2011/2011-04-09_inventions_managers & supervisors_portal_parallel uiverse_more prodcutive_universe_cops_alice killed boss_business.gif
title: Alice Disposes of Boss Through Portal

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I created a portal to a parallel universe. My success was possible because Alice killed our boss so we are all more productive.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Step aside. The cops have been sniffing around and I need something from the other universe.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Look on the bright side, Asok. Some other universe just got a lot more productive.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Gaaa!

setting: Office lab with a parallel-universe portal
situation: Asok proudly explains that his portal to a parallel universe succeeded because Alice killed their boss, which made everyone more productive. Alice shoves him aside because the police are investigating and she needs to retrieve something from the other universe. She then pushes the boss's head through the portal and tells a horrified Asok that another universe just became more productive.
punchline: Alice gets rid of the incriminating evidence by shoving it into another universe, and treats it as a favor since the boss's absence boosts productivity there too.
summary: A scientist's portal to another universe becomes a handy way for a murderous coworker to dump the evidence, with a grim silver lining for the universe next door.

file: 2011/2011-07-11_anxiety_frustration_implications_offend by complimenting_rational.gif
title: Offended By Compliments To Others

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You offended me when you said Ted did a great job. It implied that I'm unimportant.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you saying I can offend you by complimenting other people?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Exactly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, you're very rational today.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Thank you!

setting: Office break area, with coffee mugs in hand
situation: Alice complains that Dilbert offended her by praising Ted, because it implied she is unimportant. Dilbert checks that she really means she can be offended by compliments given to other people, and she confirms it. Dilbert then turns to Wally and says he is being very rational today, which Wally happily accepts.
punchline: Dilbert's compliment to Wally is itself an insult to Alice's absurd logic, since by her own rule praising Wally implies she is unimportant, and Wally cheerfully misses that he is being used as a contrast.
summary: A colleague takes offense at praise given to someone else, and her coworker responds by flattering a third person, proving her convoluted rule.

file: 2011/2011-08-26_frustration_laziness_writing materials_pile_busget numbers_print again_think murder.gif
title: Boss Refuses Pile, Dilbert Contemplates Murder

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need your latest budget numbers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I put them on that pile yesterday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't have time to look through a pile. Go print it out again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How many times per day is it okay to think about murder?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm up to six and it's only lunchtime.

setting: Boss's office, then a lunch table in the office
situation: The Boss demands Dilbert's latest budget numbers. Dilbert says he already left them on the boss's pile of papers, but the Boss refuses to look through the pile and orders him to print them again. At lunch, a frustrated Dilbert asks his coworkers how often it is acceptable to think about murder, and Wally says he's already at six.
punchline: The Boss's laziness makes Dilbert so frustrated that he jokes about homicidal thoughts, and Wally's casual reply shows that everyone at the company feels the same way.
summary: After being told to reprint a document his boss was too lazy to find on his own desk, Dilbert wonders aloud about the daily limit for violent fantasies, and a coworker cheerfully reports his own tally.

file: 2011/2011-02-04_bad time_governments unemployment stats_look for job_managers & supervisors_new job_employment_business.gif
title: Unemployment Statistics Thrown at Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The government's new unemployment statistics are out.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Crumple crumple

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Poink!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's still a bad time to look for a job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah. I got that.

situation: The Boss announces that the government's new unemployment statistics are out while crumpling up the report. He tosses the paper ball at Dilbert, hitting him in the head. He then tells Dilbert it's still a bad time to look for a job, and Dilbert says he already understood.
punchline: The Boss's way of delivering the grim jobs report is to crumple it up and throw it at Dilbert, an insulting gesture that makes his point, that employees are stuck and have no leverage, without any words needed.
summary: A manager pelts his employee with a wadded-up jobs report to remind him that quitting is not a realistic option.

file: 2011/2011-03-15_gloating_meetings_idea_rejected idea_being impractical_take credit_noticing_implied your a moron_appreciated.gif
title: Stealing Credit While Insulting You

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I thought of your idea a year ago and rejected it for being impractical.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you just take credit for my idea and diss it at the same time?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Thanks for noticing.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He also cleverly implied that you're a moron.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It feels good to be appreci-ated!
