situation: At a meeting table, a coworker announces that he thought of Dilbert's idea a year ago and rejected it as impractical. Dilbert points out that he just claimed credit for the idea and dismissed it at once, and the coworker happily confirms it. Another attendee adds that he also implied Dilbert is a moron, and the coworker says he enjoys being appreciated for it.
punchline: The coworker is delighted that Dilbert recognizes his clever combination of stealing credit and insulting him, treating the insult as a talent worthy of praise.
summary: A smug colleague claims an idea as his own while trashing it, then basks in praise when his double-dealing is noticed.

file: 2011/2011-05-27_mobile (cell) phones_surveillance_security_employee locator device_smarthone_questions_text to yourself.gif
title: Smartphone Rebranded As Employee Locator

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Security says your employee locator device isn't turned on.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My what?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think you call it a smartphone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I might have some questions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Put them in a text to yourself. I'll read them later.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that Security has noticed his employee locator device is switched off. When Dilbert asks what that is, the Boss says it is what Dilbert would call a smartphone. Dilbert says he has questions, and the Boss brushes them off, telling him to text them to himself to be read later.
punchline: The company is casually admitting that employees' smartphones double as tracking devices, and the Boss dismisses any concerns about it by suggesting Dilbert send his questions to himself, which means they will never be answered.
summary: A manager reveals that the company views staff phones as tracking tools and shrugs off the resulting privacy worries.

file: 2011/2011-09-08_computer software_computers & peripherals_conversation_risk assessment tools_communicate_enhance sector.gif
title: Jargon Speaker Can't Communicate

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We need to enhance our sector-relevant support for a suite of integrated risk assessment tools.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you understand?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe. Is your point that you don't know how to communicate?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh. Then I didn't get it.

setting: Office, with an exterior shot of the building in the middle panel
situation: A coworker delivers a sentence packed with meaningless business jargon about risk assessment tools and asks Dilbert if he understands. Dilbert guesses the real point is that the coworker can't communicate, and the coworker says no, so Dilbert concludes he simply didn't get it.
punchline: Dilbert's polite deduction implies the jargon-filled statement is so incomprehensible that the only sensible explanation is the speaker's poor communication, yet the speaker never grasps the insult.
summary: A buzzword-spouting colleague is gently told, through a faux-innocent question, that his unintelligible speech is the real problem.

file: 2011/2011-12-11_meetings_office workers_focus areas_sense of humor_dumb enogh_misunderstood man_angry idiot_selling it.gif
title: 25 Focus Areas Must Be Joke

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: These are our 25 focus areas for next year.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ha ha! Good one.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Sometimes I think you have no sense of humor and then ZING!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think it's real.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It can't be real. No one would be dumb enough to think we can focus on 25 areas.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Don't worry. I've got this.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: This misunderstood man is a brilliant comedian. He is only pretending to be an angry idiot.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're totally selling it.

situation: The Boss announces 25 focus areas for next year, and a coworker assumes it is a joke and laughs, praising his sense of humor. Dilbert says it is real, but the coworker insists no one could be that dumb, then explains to the others that the Boss is a brilliant comedian pretending to be an angry idiot.
punchline: The coworker is so convinced the Boss's absurd strategy must be a joke that he reinterprets the Boss's real anger and stupidity as a comedic performance, and the Boss is oblivious enough to accept the compliment.
summary: A manager's wildly unrealistic plan is mistaken for satire by his staff, who then interpret his genuine fury as expert acting.

file: 2011/2011-05-04_business ethics_saving & investment_intentional billing errors_honest mistakes_maintain bonuses_pipelien_new errors_pension algorythm_money.gif
title: Billing Errors Keep Bonuses Flowing

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Once again, our only profitable line of business is "intentional billing errors."

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: It started as a series of honest mistakes. Now it's the only way we can maintain our bonuses.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do we have anything better in the pipeline?

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: R&D is testing some new errors for our pension algorythm.

setting: Corporate boardroom meeting, with an exterior shot of the office building in the middle panel
situation: Three executives sit at a conference table reviewing the company's finances. One admits that the only profitable business is deliberate billing errors, which began as accidents and now sustain executive bonuses. The Boss asks if anything better is in development, and is told that R&D is testing new errors for the pension calculations.
punchline: The company has turned fraud into its core product and is eagerly developing new ways to cheat customers, now extending to pension funds, all to protect executive bonuses.
summary: Company leaders matter-of-factly discuss how overcharging customers by design has become their main income source and brainstorm fresh ways to defraud pensions.

file: 2011/2011-02-26_contracts_relations between the sexes_women_ignorantly signed_legal strategy_affadavit_attractive women_have cooties.gif
title: Cooties Affidavit Legal Strategy

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: The contract that you ignorantly signed gives them the right to harvest your organs.

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: Your best legal strategy is to get sworn affidavits from attractive women saying you have cooties.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Heck yes, I'll sign it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was hoping this would be harder.

setting: A lawyer's office, then outside an office building, then a hallway
situation: Dilbert learns from his lawyer that a contract he carelessly signed lets the other party harvest his organs. The lawyer advises him to collect sworn affidavits from attractive women stating he has cooties, and a woman readily agrees to sign one. Dilbert is quietly dejected that it was so easy.
punchline: Dilbert's thought bubble reveals he is disappointed that an attractive woman so eagerly agrees to swear he has cooties, because he was hoping it would be harder, which underscores his poor standing with women.
summary: A lawyer's odd advice to prove Dilbert is unattractive leads to a woman cheerfully signing a statement that he is unappealing, to his private dismay.

file: 2011/2011-08-18_meetings_need input_worked backward_due date.gif
title: Deadline Needs Input Two Weeks Ago

transcript.speaker: Project Manager
transcript.text: I worked backward from the project due date and calculated that we'll need your input on this date.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have me finishing two weeks before I start.

transcript.speaker: Project Manager
transcript.text: Let's schedule a time to talk about that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure. How about two weeks ago?

situation: A project manager hands Dilbert a schedule he built by working backward from the project due date. Dilbert points out that the schedule requires him to finish his work two weeks before he is even able to start. The manager suggests scheduling a meeting to discuss it, and Dilbert replies that the meeting should have happened two weeks ago.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically proposes meeting in the past, since the manager's impossible schedule would only work if time travel were possible.
summary: A planner's backward-calculated timeline demands work that should already have been done, so the engineer sarcastically offers a meeting slot in the past.

file: 2011/2011-10-10_money_prices_aggressive jerks_underpaid nerdling_give her a raise_nice employees.gif
title: Aggressive Jerks Get The Raises

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I read that aggressive jerks get paid more than nice employees.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Step aside, underpaid nerdling!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remind me to give her a raise, and I don't know why.

situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, mentions a study saying aggressive jerks earn more than nice employees. Alice immediately shoves him aside, spilling his coffee, and calls him an underpaid nerdling. The Boss, who witnessed it, tells someone to remind him to give her a raise without understanding why he wants to.
punchline: Alice's rude, aggressive behavior instantly proves the study right, as the Boss rewards it with a raise while being oblivious to his own bias.
summary: Right after hearing that pushy people earn more, Dilbert gets shoved aside by a coworker whose bullying promptly earns her a raise from the clueless boss.

file: 2011/2011-02-28_afterlife_death & dying_international economic integration_secure a long term supply_rare earth_metal_rare earth metals_dying_reincarnating_20% chance_born chinese.gif
title: Consultant Recommends Dying and Reincarnating

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our consultant will tell us how we can secure a long-term supply of rare earth metals for our products.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: China has most of the rare earth metals. Try dying. And reincarnating. There's a 20% chance that you'll be born Chinese.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's Plan B?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If the only part that goes wrong is the Chinese part, you can try dying again.

situation: The Boss announces that a consultant, Dogbert, will explain how to secure a long-term supply of rare earth metals. Dogbert says China controls most of them and absurdly recommends dying and being reincarnated as Chinese. When the Boss asks for a Plan B, Dogbert says to simply die again if the reincarnation fails.
punchline: The consultant's absurd, useless advice to die and be reborn Chinese, with a backup plan of dying repeatedly, mocks consultants who charge for impractical recommendations and the lack of real options against China's rare earth dominance.
summary: A consulting dog solves a company's metal-supply worries by suggesting everyone die and come back as citizens of the country that owns the resource.

file: 2011/2011-08-21_anxiety_mobile (cell) phones_telephones_rings after 4pm_caller id blocked_ignore call_email_horrible issue_hate life_torture coworker.gif
title: Dread of the After-Four Phone Call

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ring

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's never good when my phone rings after 4 pm.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ring

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Caller ID is blocked. Someone must know that I would ignore the call if I knew who it was.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If it weren't urgent, it would be email.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This must be some sort of horrible issue that will cause me to work all night.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It stopped. There's still a chance that I'll be okay unless my cell phone. . .

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Bzzz

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! I hate my life!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're right. That was funny.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now I'll text him.

situation: Dilbert's desk phone rings late in the afternoon from a blocked number, and he spirals into dread that it means an emergency that will keep him working all night. When the ringing stops he hopes he's safe, until his cell phone buzzes and he panics. The final panel reveals Alice and Wally were the ones calling him as a prank.
punchline: Dilbert's anxious catastrophizing was being deliberately provoked by coworkers Alice and Wally, who found his panic funny and are now escalating by texting him.
summary: Coworkers amuse themselves by tormenting a jumpy colleague with anonymous phone calls and then a text message.

file: 2011/2011-09-15_anger_debates_more aggressive_blaming others_lack of success_keeping from work.gif
title: Aggressively Blaming Dilbert For Failure

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've decided to become more aggressive in blaming others for my lack of success.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: For example, you're keeping me from working right now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No I'm not.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't have time to stand here and argue with you all day!

setting: Office hallway, near the coffee area
situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, tells Dilbert he is going to blame others more aggressively for his lack of success. He immediately accuses Dilbert of keeping him from working. When Dilbert denies it, Wally angrily claims he has no time to argue.
punchline: Wally's accusation is absurd since he is the one standing around talking with a coffee, and he ends up blaming Dilbert for the very argument he is starting, showing how little work he actually does.
summary: A coffee-clutching coworker vows to pin his failures on others and promptly turns on the nearest colleague, then storms off the argument he created.

file: 2011/2011-06-07_public speaking_financial model_complicated_formula errors_management_figures support_schemes for career development_life is ridiculous.gif
title: Excel Model Riddled With Errors

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: My financial model in Excel is so complicated that I assume it's riddled with formula errors.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: But that's okay because management only uses the results when the figures support their schemes for career advancement.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Uh-oh. I just realized that my life is ridiculous.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have hand-outs?

setting: Conference room during a slide presentation
situation: A mustached employee presents a complicated financial model on a whiteboard diagram, openly admitting it probably contains formula errors. He explains that management only uses the results when they back up their own career plans. He then realizes his life is ridiculous, while the Boss, unfazed, simply asks if there are handouts.
punchline: The presenter has an existential crisis over the meaningless, manipulated nature of his work, and the Boss completely ignores it, caring only about handouts.
summary: A presenter confesses his spreadsheet is probably full of mistakes that nobody cares about, has a moment of despair, and gets a trivial request in response.

file: 2011/2011-09-12_deception_flattery_suspicion_manipulate_full benefit_wisdom_george clooney.gif
title: Manipulating the Boss Behind You

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We can manipulate the Pointy-Haired Menace into picking the right plan by comparing it to the worst alternatives.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But then we wouldn't get the full benefit of his wisdom.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is he behind me?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It might be George Clooney. I can't tell them apart.

situation: Dilbert proposes tricking the boss into choosing the right plan by presenting it next to terrible alternatives. Alice points out that this would waste the boss's supposed wisdom. The boss, who has been standing behind Dilbert listening, asks whether she is talking about him, and Alice sarcastically claims she can't tell him apart from George Clooney.
punchline: Alice's insincere, absurd flattery pretends the boss could be mistaken for the handsome movie star, a transparent lie to cover for having been caught mocking him.
summary: Colleagues plotting to steer their manager toward a good decision get caught in the act and respond with ridiculous compliments.

file: 2011/2011-08-06_business ethics_clubs_meetings_society for the preservation of evil ideas_file patents_sue for infringement_embezzle_entertainment.gif
tags: society for the preservation of evil ideas
title: Society for Preserving Evil Ideas

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Welcome to the monthly meeting of "The Society for the Preservation of Evil Ideas."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our goal for the coming year is to convince companies to file absurdly broad patents and sue each other for infringing.

transcript.speaker: Member in devil costume
transcript.text: How do we make money from that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Beats me. I'm just here to embezzle your dues.

setting: A conference table at a meeting of a secret society
situation: Dogbert chairs the monthly meeting of the Society for the Preservation of Evil Ideas, attended by members in red devil costumes and a man in a white shirt and tie. He announces a goal of getting companies to file absurdly broad patents and sue each other. A devil-costumed member asks how the society profits from that.
punchline: Dogbert admits he has no real plan for making money from the scheme and is only there to embezzle the members' dues, making the society itself the real scam.
summary: A dog running a club for villainous schemes pitches a patent-trolling strategy, then confesses his true motive is simply stealing the membership fees.

file: 2011/2011-11-15_cruelty_deception_trust and stupidity_demonstrates question_difference.gif
title: Wally Demonstrates Trust Versus Stupidity

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wally, is there any difference between trust and stupidity?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hold that thought. I'll be right back.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Oh.

situation: A young coworker asks Wally whether there is any difference between trust and stupidity. Wally tells him to hold that thought and he'll be right back, then walks off. The coworker keeps standing there holding his coffee mug, waiting, until he realizes Wally is never coming back.
punchline: By telling him to wait and never returning, Wally lets the coworker's own gullible waiting prove that trust and stupidity can be the same thing.
summary: A naive coworker's philosophical question is answered by a brush-off he foolishly believes, proving the point without a word.

file: 2011/2011-09-21_complaining_conversation_failed to hold attention_resist turge_check email.gif
title: Checking Email During Conversation Standoff

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Your topic of conversation has failed to hold my attention.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can no longer resist the urge to check my email while you talk.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You'd better not be emailing me now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This isn't over.

setting: Office, in front of plain pink background
situation: Alice tells Dilbert that his conversation is boring her and pulls out her phone to check email while he talks. Dilbert responds by pulling out his own phone and glaring at her, while Alice suspects he is now emailing her. The exchange turns into a tense, petty standoff.
punchline: Alice rudely admits she is bored and checks her email mid-conversation, but she is instantly offended when Dilbert does the same thing back, showing her double standard.
summary: A woman openly ignores a coworker for her phone, then bristles when he retaliates by doing exactly the same thing.

file: 2011/2011-02-06_annoying music_buying deciosn_clutter design_cubicle_eacape_images_look ugly_ne wpordcut_no information_portfolio_stock holders_website_work till death_technology.gif
title: Gustav's Portfolio Website Sabotages Product

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, work with Gustav to get our new product explained on our website.

transcript.speaker: Gustav
transcript.text: Here's what I have so far.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's awful.

transcript.speaker: Gustav
transcript.text: Excuse me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's no information. It's all images and annoying music.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: People make buying decisions based on what they read. This gives them nothing.

transcript.speaker: Gustav
transcript.text: If I clutter the design with useful information, it will look ugly, and I won't be able to use it in my portfolio.

transcript.speaker: Gustav
transcript.text: I need that portfolio to get a job at a better company. Please help me escape.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You'll probably work here until you die in your cubicle no matter what the website looks like.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you help Gustav?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, but it wasn't a good day for our stockholders.

setting: Conference room and office, with a title panel showing Dogbert presenting at a projector screen
situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert to help Gustav, a web designer, with a product website. Dilbert finds the site is all flashy images and music with no useful information, but Gustav explains he wants it purely as a portfolio piece to land a better job elsewhere. Dilbert bluntly tells him he'll be stuck at the company regardless, and later admits to the Boss that the help didn't go well for shareholders.
punchline: Dilbert's cruel honesty crushes Gustav's hope of escaping, implying the demoralized designer wrecked the product website and hurt the company's stock.
summary: A web designer cares only about making a pretty showpiece for his résumé, and when Dilbert tells him he's trapped anyway, the company pays the price.

file: 2011/2011-03-05_exhibitions_honesty_relations between the sexes_chat me up_mammary filter_trade show_free stuff_job orders.gif
title: Trade Show Mammary Filter

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: At the trade show

transcript.speaker: Booth Woman
transcript.text: Are you actually interested in this product or are you just trying to chat me up?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The show is too big to see everything, so I use a mammary filter to decide who I talk to.

transcript.speaker: Booth Woman
transcript.text: You use a what?

transcript.speaker: Booth Woman
transcript.text: Do you have any free stuff or job offers?

situation: Dilbert is visiting a trade show booth where a female representative asks whether he is really interested in the product or just flirting. He candidly explains that he picks which booths to visit using a 'mammary filter'. The woman, unfazed, asks whether he has any free stuff or job offers.
punchline: Dilbert's blunt admission that he chooses booths based on female staff is met with the woman's own mercenary filter: she only cares about what perks or jobs he can give her, so both are shallowly using each other.
summary: A woman at an exhibition booth challenges a visitor's motives, and after his awkwardly honest answer she reveals she is just as calculating about what she can get from him.

file: 2011/2011-12-01_obliviousness_obstinacy_office workers_whiteboard_conference room_prohject timeline_zombie reflex mode.gif
title: Janitor's Zombie Mode Threatens Timeline

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't clean the whiteboard in the conference room. It has my project timeline.

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: I can't promise that. I slip into a sort of zombie reflex mode when I do this job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I envy you.

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: Would you like a few minutes to say goodbye to your timeline?

setting: Office hallway outside the conference room
situation: Dilbert asks the janitor not to erase the whiteboard in the conference room because it holds his project timeline. The janitor admits he can't promise that, since he goes into a zombie-like reflex mode while cleaning. Dilbert says he envies him, and the janitor calmly offers Dilbert a few minutes to say goodbye to the timeline.
punchline: The janitor's detached, unthinking approach to his work is so bleak that Dilbert envies it, and the janitor treats the destruction of the project timeline as an inevitability to be mourned politely.
summary: A custodian warns an engineer that he operates on autopilot while cleaning and offers him a moment to bid farewell to the doomed project plan on the whiteboard.

file: 2011/2011-08-24_anxiety_conversation_discussion_valuable input_hear alarm.gif
title: Boss Crashes Customer Meeting, Dilbert Hears Alarm

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When are you meeting with the customer? I'll join you to add my valuable input.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Slurp

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does everyone hear that alarm or is it only in my head?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can stay all afternoon.

situation: The Boss offers to attend Dilbert's upcoming customer meeting so he can contribute his supposedly valuable input. Dilbert sits silently while the Boss sips his coffee, then clutches his head in alarm. The Boss cheerfully adds that he can stay all afternoon.
punchline: Dilbert hears an alarm in his head because he knows the Boss's participation would be disastrous, while the Boss obliviously offers even more of his time.
summary: A manager volunteers to tag along to a client meeting, and his employee reacts with visible dread.

file: 2011/2011-07-04_interviews_ignorant and bored_hired_awesome tech skills_management genius.gif
title: Hiring Someone Because Nobody Killed Them

transcript.speaker: Candidate
transcript.text: You're ignorant and ridiculous. I'm bored. Are we done here?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're hired. You must have awesome technical skills or else someone would have killed you by now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't tell if I'm a management genius or just lazy.

setting: Office conference room during a job interview, then the boss's office
situation: A job candidate insults the interviewer, calling him ignorant and ridiculous and saying he's bored. Instead of rejecting him, the Boss hires him, reasoning that he must have great technical skills or someone would have killed him already. Afterward the Boss holds a coffee mug and wonders aloud whether he is a management genius or simply lazy.
punchline: The Boss uses absurd reasoning to justify hiring an obnoxious candidate, and then admits he can't tell whether his lazy shortcut is actually good management.
summary: A rude interviewee gets offered the job on the strength of a bizarre survival-based assumption, leaving the boss unsure whether his hiring instincts are brilliant or just sloth.

file: 2011/2011-04-28_anxiety_confused_emails accounts_internet & world wide web_might snap_pin code_too many passwords_user names_chaos_crazy_lose it_mental_breakdown_overload_technological_psychology.gif
title: Password Recovery Needs Another Password

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Password Recovery Service

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: I have so many passwords and email accounts and user names that I don't know what goes to what.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: I'm lost. If you can't help me I think I might snap.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No problem. What's your password recovery pin code?

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Snap!

setting: Dogbert's office desk, at his password recovery service
situation: A frazzled client visits Dogbert's Password Recovery Service because he has too many passwords, email accounts and user names to keep track of. He says he might snap if he can't be helped. Dogbert cheerfully asks for his password recovery pin code, which is one more thing to remember, and the client snaps.
punchline: The recovery service itself demands yet another secret code to remember, which pushes the overwhelmed client over the edge.
summary: A man drowning in logins seeks help from a recovery service, only to be asked for yet another code, which breaks him.

file: 2011/2011-07-13_cruelty_deception_ignorance (knowledge)_helicopter from kit_link to website_too dumb_pliers.gif
title: Helicopter Kit for the Dumb Boss

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You should build your own helicopter from a kit. I'll send you a link to the website.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's only dangerous for people who are too dumb to know how dumb they are.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is it as easy as it sounds? I have pliers.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yes!

situation: Alice, seated at her desk, urges the Boss to build a helicopter from a kit and offers to send him the website link. She then notes it is only dangerous for people too dumb to realise how dumb they are. The Boss, clearly one of those people, asks if it's easy and mentions he owns pliers, while Alice thinks 'Yes!' with a grin.
punchline: Alice sets the Boss up to endanger himself, and his overconfident reply proves he is exactly the kind of person the warning applies to, which she gleefully encourages.
summary: A scheming employee talks her clueless manager into assembling a flying machine at home, delighted that his misplaced confidence will do the rest.

file: 2011/2011-03-13_costs compared to alternatives_doing nothing_expensive plan_honesty_managers & supervisors_business.gif
title: Boss Dumps Explanation on Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: I can't sign off on this plan. It's too expensive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You heard me say that doing nothing will end up costing you twice as much, right?

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you understand that this is your only alternative?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have another meeting. Maybe Dilbert can explain it to you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... Okay. I'll try.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: My boss doesn't understand that costs should be compared to alternatives.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Teamwork means you can't pick the side that's right.

setting: Conference room during a meeting with a client
situation: A client refuses to approve an expensive plan even though The Boss insists that doing nothing would cost twice as much. The Boss leaves for another meeting and hands the explaining to Dilbert, who then hears the client complain that his own boss fails to compare costs with alternatives. The client's boss overhears and fumes, leaving Dilbert caught between the two sides.
punchline: Dilbert realizes that being on the team means he can't agree with the client, who is actually right, so teamwork forces him to side with the wrong party.
summary: A client's reasonable objection puts Dilbert in the awkward spot of defending his own side when the other party's logic is better.

file: 2011/2011-01-22_newspapers_wages_managers & supervisors_business_money.gif
title: Stopping the News Instead of Raising Pay

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I just saw in the news that Google gave an engineer millions of dollars. I'm underpaid!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll speak to our director of human resources and see how I can fix this situation.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Really?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How can we stop news?

situation: Alice tells the Boss she is underpaid after reading that Google gave an engineer millions of dollars. The Boss promises to talk to the director of human resources, and she is hopeful. He then asks Catbert, the HR director, how they can stop news.
punchline: Instead of addressing the underpayment, management plans to suppress the news that makes employees aware of their low pay, which is a ridiculous and cynical fix.
summary: A worker asks for a raise after seeing a rival's lavish pay, and her boss responds by trying to eliminate the source of the information.

file: 2011/2011-09-10_cruelty_thinking_creative person_bad at math_analytical skills_permanent.gif
title: Creative Person Means Bad at Math

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I like to think of myself as a creative person.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And by that you mean you're bad at math and you don't have any analytical skills.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it permanent?

situation: Asok tells his colleagues he considers himself a creative person. Alice translates this as meaning he is bad at math and lacks analytical skills. Dilbert then deadpans a question about whether the condition is permanent.
punchline: Dilbert treats Asok's lack of analytical ability as if it were a medical condition, coldly asking whether it can be cured, which delivers a double insult.
summary: A self-described creative type gets his claim decoded as mathematical incompetence, and a coworker piles on by asking if the affliction is lasting.

file: 2011/2011-04-04_managers & supervisors_brain overload_detailed answer_broken_decison_nodding_sensing opportunity_business.gif
title: Overloaded Boss Nods, Alice Sees Opportunity

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Now you've done it. He has brain overload from your unnecessarily detailed answer.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Great. He's totally broken and we need a decision today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is he nodding yes?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm sensing an opportunity here.

situation: Dilbert has given the Boss an overly detailed answer, and the Boss is now slumped in his chair, mentally frozen. Alice complains that a decision is needed today, then notices the Boss's head is bobbing as she pushes on it. She decides to exploit the moment by treating his movement as agreement.
punchline: Alice decides to manipulate the incapacitated Boss's head to make it look like he is nodding yes, so she can claim he approved the decision.
summary: With the boss mentally shut down, a coworker spots a chance to fake his approval by moving his head herself.

file: 2011/2011-04-13_appeal_bad person_business ethics_comparison shopping_guilt_molt_prevents competitors_raising prices.gif
title: Justifying Products for Poor Shoppers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our products only appeal to people who aren't good at comparison shopping.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I justify it because our existence prevents competitors from raising prices.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Am I a bad person?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I molt a little bit every time you talk.

situation: Dilbert admits to Catbert that his company's products only attract customers who are bad at comparison shopping. He then offers a rationalization that the company keeps competitors from raising prices, and asks Catbert whether he is a bad person. Catbert, visibly shedding fur, answers that he molts whenever Dilbert speaks.
punchline: Catbert dodges the ethical question and implies Dilbert's self-serving rationalizing is so repellent it physically disgusts him.
summary: After rationalizing a business that preys on careless shoppers, Dilbert seeks moral reassurance from a cat who responds with fur-shedding disgust.

file: 2011/2011-10-25_big business_meetings_succession plan_awesome and charismatic_replace you_bag of moss.gif
title: Replace You With Moss

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: We need a succession plan. I'm so awesome and charismatic that the company would be in trouble if I were to leave.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I wouldn't worry about it. It's not as if you invented anything. We could replace you with a bag of moss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He got quiet.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: See? Moss can totally do that.

situation: At a meeting, a bald executive boasts that the company needs a succession plan because he is so awesome and charismatic. Alice replies that he never invented anything and could be replaced by a bag of moss. He falls silent, and Alice points out that this proves moss could do his job.
punchline: The executive's sudden silence proves that a bag of moss could fill his role, since it too would just sit there quietly.
summary: A self-important executive demands a succession plan, and a colleague shuts him up by suggesting a bag of moss could replace him.

file: 2011/2011-01-15_cruelty_managers & supervisors_couldn't be worse_bad idea_funny_project is bad idea_business.gif
title: Punished For Being Right

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's everything going?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It couldn't be worse.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was the only person who said this project is a bad idea. Then you assigned it to me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's funnier when I make them say it.

transcript.speaker: Unknown
transcript.text: Grrrr

situation: The Boss stops by Dilbert's cubicle and asks how things are going. Dilbert complains that after he alone warned the project was a bad idea, the Boss assigned the project to him. Walking away, the Boss thinks that he enjoys it more when employees spell out their own misery.
punchline: The Boss deliberately asks questions he already knows the answers to, because he gets amusement from making his employees voice their frustration after he has punished them for honesty.
summary: A manager cheerfully checks in on the employee he stuck with a doomed project, savoring the complaint he knew was coming.

file: 2011/2011-08-23_commerce_fraternization_creepy new vendor_did laundry_creepy_made sandwhiches.gif
title: Creepy Vendor Overly Friendly Relationship

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our new vendor is creepy. He's trying to form a relationship with me.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: I went to your house and did your laundry. You're welcome.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How creepy could it be?

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: I made us sandwiches. You're out of mayo.

setting: Office, where two coworkers stand holding coffee mugs
situation: Dilbert complains to a coworker that a new vendor is creepy because he is trying to build a relationship with him. The vendor suddenly appears behind Dilbert and cheerfully announces that he broke into Dilbert's house to do his laundry, then that he made sandwiches there and noticed Dilbert is out of mayo. The coworker, who had asked how creepy it could be, is left to see the answer.
punchline: The vendor's attempt at relationship-building has crossed into stalking and trespassing, and he is completely oblivious to how creepy that is, answering the coworker's question in the worst way.
summary: A salesman eager to win a client's business shows up unannounced with domestic favors that reveal he has been inside the man's home.

file: 2011/2011-06-09_absent mindedness_computers & peripherals_unix servers_new servers_new names.gif
title: Server Names Only in My Mind

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This week I renamed all of the Unix servers to make them easier to remember.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In phase one, the new names exist only in my mind. I won't know if they're easy to remember until next week.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Next week

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How are the new server names?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't know what you're talking about.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting, then a hallway the following week
situation: In a meeting with the Boss and Dilbert, Wally announces he renamed all the Unix servers to make them easier to remember. He explains the new names exist only in his head, so he can't judge them until next week. The following week, Dilbert asks how the new names are working and Wally has forgotten the whole thing.
punchline: Wally's plan to make server names memorable fails immediately because he forgets he renamed them at all, undermining the supposed improvement and implying he did nothing useful.
summary: A lazy engineer claims to have improved server names by keeping them secret in his head, then promptly forgets the entire project.

file: 2011/2011-12-02_frustration_joking_project staus update_improve listening skills_repeating.gif
title: Boss Repeats Alice's Words Badly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I need your project status update by end of day.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ahleth, ah wan yer proja thatuth updah, fuh-fuh-fuh.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm trying to improve my listening skills by repeating what people say.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, asks Alice for her project status update by end of day. Alice answers with a garbled, mangled imitation of his request, then explains that she is practicing her listening skills by repeating what people say.
punchline: Alice's sarcastic, nonsensical mimicry of the Boss mocks his request and the self-improvement jargon he might use, while giving him a flimsy excuse he can't easily object to.
summary: Alice responds to a deadline demand by parroting it back in gibberish and claiming it's listening practice.

file: 2011/2011-03-07_envy_exhibitions_technology trade show_so huge_illusion_great cup holder.gif
title: Shrunken Dilbert Becomes Cup Holder

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What happened to you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I went to a technology trade show.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The event was so huge that it made me feel small. But it's just an illusion.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: For an illusion, you make a great cup holder.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dude. Not cool.

situation: Dilbert sits at the conference table looking tiny, and Wally asks what happened to him. Dilbert explains that a huge technology trade show made him feel small, insisting it's only an illusion. Wally then sets his coffee mug on top of the shrunken Dilbert and uses him as a cup holder.
punchline: Dilbert claims his shrinking is just an illusion, but Wally treats it as real by using him as a coaster, and Dilbert's flat objection shows he feels belittled both literally and figuratively.
summary: After a giant tech expo leaves him literally miniature, a coworker takes advantage by parking a drink on him.

file: 2011/2011-10-22_crimes_criminals_elbonian_minister of commerce_leave no eveidence_connects crime_bribe him_kill him.gif
title: Bribe, Kill, Then Eliminate The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to bribe an Elbonian Minister of Commerce and leave no evidence that connects the crime to our company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The only way to do that is to bribe him and kill him at the same time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I did not think this through.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And obviously I'll need to do you first.

setting: The Boss's office, with the Boss at his desk and Dogbert as consultant
situation: The Boss asks Dogbert to bribe an Elbonian Minister of Commerce without leaving any evidence tying the crime to the company. Dogbert explains that the only way to leave no evidence is to kill the minister at the same moment as bribing him. The Boss realizes his request has dark implications, and Dogbert adds that the Boss himself would have to be eliminated first.
punchline: Leaving no evidence of a crime logically means eliminating everyone who knows about it, including the Boss who ordered it.
summary: A manager's request for a perfectly untraceable foreign bribe leads his consultant to conclude that every witness, himself included, must be removed.

file: 2011/2011-11-05_embarrassment_obliviousness_hired consultant_less confident_overconfident people_don't recognize mistakes_didn't know studies_feel like idiot.gif
title: Consultant Teaches Boss Less Confidence

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a consultant to teach us how to be less confident.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that because research has shown that overconfident people don't recognize their own mistakes?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now I feel like an idiot because I didn't know about those studies.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I did him first.

situation: The Boss announces to the meeting that he hired a consultant to teach the team to be less confident. Dilbert asks whether it's because research shows overconfident people can't recognize their mistakes, which leaves the Boss feeling like an idiot. Dogbert, the consultant, quietly says he already got the Boss first.
punchline: Dogbert, the consultant, has already succeeded in making the Boss less confident before the training even begins, apparently by exploiting the Boss's own ignorance.
summary: A boss hires a consultant to cut down overconfidence, only to have his own cluelessness exposed by the consultant himself.

file: 2011/2011-02-18_employees_engineers_revenge_loud talker_chronic faltualator_seating arrangements_cubicle arrangements_sound_noise_business.gif
title: Engineered Revenge Through Cubicle Placement

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Office relocation

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Your floor plan puts me between a loud talker and a chronic flatulator.

transcript.speaker: Facilities Planner
transcript.text: I could move you to a cubicle between a guy who clears his throat all day and a woman who laughs too much.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is this because I once said you aren't smart enough to be an engineer?

transcript.speaker: Facilities Planner
transcript.text: Look what I engineered.

situation: Alice complains to the woman who designed the new floor plan that she has been placed between a loud talker and a chronic flatulator. The planner offers an alternative that is just as annoying. Alice wonders if this is payback for once saying the planner wasn't smart enough to be an engineer.
punchline: The planner proves she is an engineer by deliberately designing an exquisitely annoying seating arrangement as revenge for Alice's insult.
summary: A woman who was once told she wasn't engineer material gets even by cleverly designing her critic's miserable new workspace.

file: 2011/2011-11-30_employees_secretaries (office)_manually entered data_entire weekend_die monster!_business.gif
title: Weekend Data Entry Wasted Effort

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I manually entered all of the employee data you wanted. It took the entire weekend.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I probably should have told you I no longer need it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Die! Die! Die! You inconsiderate monster!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you really enter all of the data?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe. Let's call it a tie.

situation: An employee tells the Boss she spent her entire weekend manually entering the employee data he asked for. The Boss casually admits he no longer needs it, and she lashes out at him in fury. He then asks whether she really did the work, and she coyly suggests she may not have, calling it even.
punchline: Alice's rage at the Boss's thoughtlessness is undercut when she hints she may have lied about doing the work, so both have wasted each other's time and effort.
summary: A worker who claims to have sacrificed her weekend for a pointless task gets her revenge by leaving it unclear whether she did the work at all.

file: 2011/2011-01-29_terrorists_work ethic_elbonian leftists_kidnapped_ransom demands_three pack tube socks_carton milk_six yams_making life nightmare_gives in to kidnappers.gif
title: Ransom Demands Too Trivial to Pay

transcript.speaker: Caller (off-panel)
transcript.text: Elbonian leftists kidnapped Asok. They have ransom demands.

transcript.speaker: Caller (off-panel)
transcript.text: They want a three-pack of tube socks, a carton of milk, and six yams.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you could buy that stuff on your way home.

transcript.speaker: Woman on phone
transcript.text: You're making my life a nightmare! Just keep him!

characters: Woman on phone (Asok's contact, likely Alice or a coworker)
setting: Office cubicle, with the phone call heard over an exterior view of an office building
situation: A woman in a cubicle takes a phone call from Elbonian leftists who have kidnapped Asok. The Boss listens while holding his coffee mug, and the kidnappers' ransom demand turns out to be a bizarre list of groceries. The Boss suggests she simply pick the items up on her way home, and she angrily tells the kidnappers to keep Asok.
punchline: The kidnappers' ransom demands are so mundane that the Boss treats them as a shopping errand, while the woman on the phone is so fed up with Asok that she would rather let the kidnappers keep him.
summary: Kidnappers demand a humble grocery list for an employee's release, and the exasperated coworker would rather abandon him than shop.

file: 2011/2011-07-16_customer survey data_marketing_design_engineering secret_business.gif
title: Marketing Hoards Survey Data, Engineering Hoards Timeline

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: The customer survey data is for marketing's eyes only.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Design the next release and we'll tell you if it's what everyone wanted.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: How long will that take?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's an engineering secret.

situation: A marketing employee tells Dilbert that customer survey data is off-limits to engineers. He then instructs Dilbert to design the next release blind and promises to judge afterward whether it matches what customers wanted. When he asks how long that will take, Dilbert answers with the same secrecy.
punchline: Dilbert turns marketing's information hoarding back on them by refusing to share the schedule, since they refuse to share the data needed to do the job.
summary: A marketer who withholds customer data from engineers gets a taste of his own medicine when asked for a delivery estimate.

file: 2011/2011-05-14_death & dying_estate plan_inherit stuff_option_powerful incentive_saving & investment_wills_money.gif
title: Dogbert Names Himself Dilbert's Heir

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I took the liberty of updating your estate plan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This gives you a powerful incentive to kill me so you can inherit my stuff.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If it makes you feel any better, that option has always been on the table.

situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he has updated Dilbert's estate plan, apparently naming himself as the heir. Dilbert reads the document and points out that Dogbert now has a strong motive to kill him. Dogbert reassures him that murder was already something he was considering.
punchline: Dogbert's attempt at comfort reveals that he has always been willing to kill Dilbert, so the new estate plan changes nothing.
summary: A scheming dog rewrites his owner's will in his own favour, then cheerfully admits that homicide was always an option.

file: 2011/2011-04-19_radiation_capital for testing_handset radiation_tumor_stan.gif
title: Stan Found a Cheaper Way

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Which one of you asked for capital for testing handset radiation?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That was Stan. And you told him to find a less expensive way to do it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Which one of you is Stan?

situation: The Boss sits at a meeting table and asks who requested funding to test cell phone handset radiation. Dilbert reminds him that it was Stan, and that the Boss himself told Stan to find a cheaper way. In the last panel the Boss asks which person is Stan, and Stan, seated at the end, looks on nervously.
punchline: The Boss has forgotten who Stan is, and the implication is that Stan's cheaper way of testing radiation may have been using himself as the test subject, leaving him looking unwell.
summary: A manager hunts for the employee who wanted money to test phone radiation, then fails to recognise the very man he told to economise.

file: 2011/2011-05-24_computers & peripherals_internet & world wide web_firewall down_viruses_spyware_tuberculosis_zombies_deposed dictator_iphone 3gs_army of mole people.gif
title: Firewall Down, Mole People Arrive

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our firewall is down. Some bad stuff is getting through.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How bad?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So far we've seen viruses, spyware, tuberculosis, zombies, a deposed dictator, and an iPhone 3GS.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Buzzzz

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Update: An army of mole people from another dimension has tunneled through.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Keep me informed.

situation: Dilbert reports to the Boss that the company firewall is down and bad things are getting through. He lists an escalating series of intrusions, mixing real IT threats with absurd ones like zombies and a deposed dictator. A buzzing phone brings an update that an army of mole people from another dimension has arrived, and the Boss just asks to be kept informed.
punchline: The Boss responds to an interdimensional invasion with the same detached, hands-off non-reaction he gives to routine problems, showing he doesn't grasp the severity of anything.
summary: A security breach report escalates from computer malware to supernatural invaders while the manager remains completely unfazed.

file: 2011/2011-08-19_debates_discussion_email_objecting_hallucination of plan_defensive_narrowed problem.gif
title: Email Objections and Hallucinated Plans

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you see my email objecting to your plan?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, but I saw your email objecting to what I assume is your hallucination of my plan.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You seem defensive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have we narrowed down the problem to me?

situation: A coworker holding a folder asks Dilbert whether he saw an email objecting to his plan. Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, replies that he saw an email but it objected to a plan he never made. When the coworker says Dilbert seems defensive, Dilbert asks sarcastically whether the blame has now been pinned on him.
punchline: Dilbert points out that his coworker is attacking a misunderstood version of his plan, then sarcastically notes that the coworker is deflecting the blame onto him by calling him defensive.
summary: A colleague's criticism of a plan that was misread leads to an argument where being accused of defensiveness is treated as a way of making the other person the problem.

file: 2011/2011-01-13_anger_engineers_lust_pon farr cycle_irreversible urge_mating season_engineer mating season_spawn_prodcut_unnecessary steps_rarely happens_specifications_vague.gif
title: Engineers Mating Cycle Ends in Arguing

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Did you hear that Dilbert and Alice are on the same Pon Farr cycle?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Every seven years, engineers have an irresistible urge to mate. Their spawn would be the product of two engineers.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: There's a reason it rarely happens

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your plan has unnecessary steps!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Your specifications are vague!

situation: Carol tells Alice that she and Dilbert are on the same Pon Farr cycle, the Star Trek reference to a Vulcan mating urge, and explains that engineers feel an irresistible urge to mate every seven years. In the final panel Dilbert and Alice, both visibly agitated and with Alice's hair wild, are shown criticizing each other's plans and specifications instead.
punchline: Two engineers can't get past nitpicking each other's work long enough to mate, because they critique everything like a technical document.
summary: A coworker predicts that two engineers in sync will be driven together by nature, but they only manage to trade design-review complaints.

file: 2011/2011-12-23_big business_cost & standard of living_green goals_recycling bins_company documents_corporate secuirty_blue recycling bins_same policies.gif
title: Contradictory Recycling and Security Policies

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: To reach our green goals, employees must always use the blue recycling bins for company documents.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: To satisfy our corporate security guidelines, never put company documents in the blue recycling bins.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You read those same policies to us last week.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I don't know how to get rid of them.

situation: Phil, the horned-hair manager, reads out a policy requiring company documents to go in the blue recycling bins for environmental reasons. He then reads a security policy that forbids putting company documents in those same bins. Dilbert points out he already read both policies last week, and Phil admits he has no idea how to dispose of the documents.
punchline: Two corporate policies, one for green goals and one for security, directly contradict each other, leaving no acceptable way to dispose of company documents.
summary: A manager announces two rules that cancel each other out, then shrugs when asked how anyone is supposed to obey both.

file: 2011/2011-10-27_big business_business ethics_public speaking_spit take_industrial sludge_intern will drink.gif
title: Boss Makes Intern Drink Sludge

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I will prove our industrial sludge is safe by forcing an intern to drink a glass of it.

transcript.speaker: Offscreen Audience Member
transcript.text: That's stupid. We want to see you drink it yourself.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: See if you can reach that guy in the second row with a spit take.

setting: A press conference or public speaking event with a podium and microphone
situation: The Boss stands at a microphone beside a nervous intern and announces he'll prove the company's industrial sludge is safe by making the intern drink a glass of it. A heckler in the audience demands that the Boss drink it himself. He sips it, and then spits it out toward an audience member.
punchline: The Boss's reaction to drinking the sludge shows it is clearly not safe, which undermines his public claim and reveals his willingness to endanger others rather than himself.
summary: A manager tries to publicly demonstrate the safety of toxic waste by sacrificing a junior employee, but when forced to try it himself he reveals the truth.

file: 2011/2011-01-08_critics_employees_laziness_big picture guy_lesser minds_managing_implementing_not getting it_business.gif
title: Big Picture Guy Wants Criticizing Job

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've decided to become more of a big picture guy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Lesser minds can do the managing and implementing while I criticize them for not "getting it."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... you want to get paid to be a jerk?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Said the implementer.

situation: Wally sits at a meeting table with Dilbert and the Boss and announces he wants to become a big picture guy. He explains that this means letting others do the managing and implementing while he criticizes them for not understanding his vision. Dilbert points out that this amounts to being paid to be a jerk, and Wally retorts that this is exactly what someone who does the actual work would say.
punchline: Wally dismisses Dilbert's accurate accusation by pointing out that only a lowly implementer would object to a job that consists of criticizing people who do the real work.
summary: A lazy employee proposes to upgrade himself to visionary status so he can fault everyone else for failing to grasp his ideas, and brushes off a colleague's objection as typical of the doers.

file: 2011/2011-09-26_employees_violence_burt nount_started yesterday_sneezed away_business.gif
title: Sneeze Blows New Hire's Head Off

transcript.speaker: Burt Nount
transcript.text: Hi. My name is Burt Nount. I started here yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Sneeze coming.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Aaachooo!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I gotta warn you, they come in threes.

situation: A new employee introduces himself to a coworker with big brown hair, who warns him that a sneeze is coming. Her enormous sneeze blasts his head clean off his body. Standing over his headless body, she casually warns him that her sneezes come in threes.
punchline: The woman warns the new hire about her next two sneezes only after the first one has already blown his head off, so the warning is far too late to help him.
summary: A new hire's friendly introduction ends abruptly when a coworker's sneeze decapitates him, and she offers a belated warning about more to come.

file: 2011/2011-02-12_dating_inventions_dead end job_developing an app_spare time_lottery ticket_odds of success_relationships.gif
title: Lottery Tickets Beat Dilbert's App

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It might look as if I'm in a dead-end job, but I'm developing an app in my spare time.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Here's a lottery ticket. I just doubled your odds of success.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I bought two for myself so I don't need to make an app.

setting: A restaurant table on a date
situation: Dilbert sits across from a woman on a date and tries to impress her by saying his dead-end job is just a stopgap while he builds an app in his spare time. She hands him a lottery ticket, saying she has doubled his odds of success. She adds that she bought two for herself, so she doesn't need to develop an app.
punchline: She implies that Dilbert's app has about the same chance of making him rich as a lottery ticket, so buying tickets is an equally good plan with far less effort.
summary: A man's boast about his side-project app is deflated when his date treats his chances of striking it rich as no better than a lottery win.

file: 2011/2011-01-11_engineers_honesty_viruses_honest opinions_causing problems_medical records_engineer_classified as disease_vaccination_engineering.gif
title: Engineering Classified as a Disease

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't stop voicing my honest opinions. It's causing problems at work.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: According to your medical records, you're an engineer. We classify that as a disease now.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! You haven't had your Pon Farr vaccination.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it warm in here?

situation: Dilbert, sitting half-undressed on an exam table, tells his doctor that he can't stop voicing his honest opinions at work. The doctor checks his records, discovers he is an engineer, and declares that engineering is now classed as a disease. He then panics that Dilbert has skipped his Pon Farr vaccination, and Dilbert turns red and flushed.
punchline: Engineers are treated as carriers of a disease, and the Star Trek reference to Vulcan mating fever (Pon Farr) implies engineers are logical, emotionless Vulcan-like creatures who are about to be overcome by their biological urges.
summary: A doctor diagnoses a patient's blunt honesty as the symptom of being an engineer, then alarms himself by realizing the patient is overdue for a shot against a Star Trek-style mating frenzy.

file: 2011/2011-02-15_business ethics_program website_collect browser hostory_invent device_sense of right and wrong.gif
title: Website Spying Needs Ethics Removal Device

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How hard would it be to program our website to collect browser history from our visitors?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, first I'd need to invent some sort of device that reverses my sense of right and wrong.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... are we talking about a week... or a month?

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how difficult it would be to make the company website secretly collect visitors' browser history. Dilbert replies that he would first need a device to reverse his sense of right and wrong. The Boss ignores the ethical objection and only asks how long the project will take.
punchline: The Boss completely misses Dilbert's sarcastic point that the request is unethical and treats it as a mere scheduling question.
summary: Asked to build a privacy-invading feature, an engineer sarcastically cites his conscience as an obstacle, and his oblivious manager just wants a time estimate.

file: 2011/2011-12-20_employees_interviews_tools for job_resource_agree to disagree_business.gif
title: Are You a Tool or Resource?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Question four: Do you have the tools to do your job?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: That depends. Do you consider yourself a tool?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm a resource.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Let's agree to disagree.

setting: Office meeting table during a question-and-answer session
situation: The Boss reads from a list of questions to an employee who is drinking coffee, asking whether he has the tools to do his job. The employee snidely replies by asking if the Boss considers himself a tool. The Boss insists he is a 'resource', and the employee says they should agree to disagree.
punchline: The employee calls the Boss a 'tool' (an idiot) through wordplay, and the Boss's feeble defence that he is a 'resource' gets him politely but pointedly contradicted.
summary: A manager's routine survey question gets turned into an insult when the employee suggests the manager himself is the problem.

file: 2011/2011-05-30_quarreling_suspicion_work ethic_work independantly_boss_preemptive strike_project update.gif
title: Preemptive Complaint About Boss Distrust

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can't work for a boss who doesn't trust me to work independently!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is this a preemptive strike so I won't ask why you didn't turn in a project update?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And more distrust. How do you live with yourself?

situation: Wally storms into the boss's office holding a coffee mug and angrily complains that the boss doesn't trust him to work independently. The boss calmly suspects Wally is trying to deflect from the fact that he never submitted a project update. Wally doubles down, treating the boss's reasonable suspicion as further proof of distrust.
punchline: Wally turns the boss's justified question about a missing project update into another offense, using indignation about distrust to dodge accountability.
summary: An employee tries to pre-empt scrutiny of his missing report by loudly accusing his manager of not trusting him.

file: 2011/2011-11-12_boredom_business ethics_boost morale_pretending to be intereted_overkill_unemployement_brain_fallout_yawn hole.gif
title: Boss Fakes Interest in Employee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm here to boost your morale by pretending to be interested in you as a human being.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But it's probably overkill since unemployment is around 9% and you're not likely to quit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Still, it's nice to...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's enough! I don't want my brain to fall out of my yawn hole.

situation: The Boss visits Dilbert's cubicle holding a coffee mug and openly announces he is only pretending to care about Dilbert to boost morale. He admits it's unnecessary because high unemployment means Dilbert won't quit. When Dilbert tries to say it's still nice, the Boss cuts him off because listening is too boring.
punchline: The Boss can't even sustain his fake interest in an employee for a few seconds, bluntly admitting that morale efforts are pointless when workers are trapped by a bad job market.
summary: A manager cheerfully admits his show of caring is insincere and unneeded given the weak job market, then shuts down his employee's reply out of sheer boredom.

file: 2011/2011-07-22_ignorance (knowledge)_interviews_managers_dumb decions_particpate.gif
title: Study Participation Proves Manager's Dumbness

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm doing a study to find out which managers make dumb decisions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Would you like to participate?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't see why not.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And we're done.

situation: Dogbert stands on the Boss's desk with a clipboard and announces he is conducting a study to identify which managers make dumb decisions. He invites the Boss to participate, and the Boss cheerfully agrees without hesitation. Dogbert immediately declares the study finished.
punchline: By willingly volunteering for a study of managers who make dumb decisions, the Boss instantly demonstrates that he is exactly the type being studied.
summary: A dog researcher gets his data instantly when a clueless executive eagerly signs up for an investigation of poor managerial judgment.

file: 2011/2011-05-31_annoyance_office buildings_open workspace_environemnt_crying baby spunds_more distractions.gif
title: Open Office Needs More Distractions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company is considering moving from cubicles to an open workspace environment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Great idea. Can we add some crying babies and the sound of water dripping?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're being stupid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I'll be smarter when I have more distractions.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that the company may replace cubicles with an open workspace. Dilbert sarcastically suggests adding crying babies and dripping water to the noise. When the Boss calls him stupid, Dilbert replies that he will be smarter once he has more distractions.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically turns the Boss's insult around by claiming that more distractions will make him smarter, mocking the idea that open offices help productivity.
summary: A manager floats tearing down cubicle walls, and a sarcastic engineer proposes extra annoying noises to complete the experience.

file: 2011/2011-08-09_gloating_meetings_non stop talking_trophy_participating_too much self esteem.gif
title: Trophy For Participating In Meeting

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We're out of time and we accomplished absolutely nothing, thanks to your non-stop talking.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: When do I get my trophy for participating?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Someone was raised with too much self-esteem.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Watch me walk!

situation: At the end of a meeting, a colleague complains that nothing was accomplished because Asok talked non-stop. Asok cheerfully asks when he gets his participation trophy. Dilbert remarks that Asok was raised with too much self-esteem, and Asok proudly stands up and announces 'Watch me walk!'
punchline: Asok is so full of unearned self-regard that he treats Dilbert's insult as a cue to show off, even asking to be praised for the simple act of walking away.
summary: A meeting derailed by one chatty coworker ends with him begging for a participation award and then seeking applause for leaving the room.

file: 2011/2011-10-30_gloating_ignorance (knowledge)_internet & world wide web_digital media curation_trendy jargon_ignorance on dsiply_not worthy_curation means.gif
title: Digital Media Curation Jargon Backfires

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My role is digital media curation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Am I supposed to know what that means?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ha ha! I look down on you for not understanding my trendy jargon.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your ignorance is on display for all to see!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Leave this meeting now! You are not worthy!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you could just tell us what curation means.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Fine. Let's try that.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It means um... um...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is it too late for me to overlook your ignorance and move on?

situation: A coworker introduces his job title as digital media curation. When Dilbert asks what it means, the coworker mocks him for not knowing the trendy jargon and tries to throw him out of the meeting. When Dilbert asks him to explain the term, the coworker realizes he cannot define it himself.
punchline: The coworker who smugly belittled others for not knowing his buzzword turns out not to know what it means himself, so he hastily asks to forget the whole thing.
summary: A man who sneers at a colleague for not grasping his fashionable job title is stumped when asked to explain it.

file: 2011/2011-06-19_embarrassment_walkways_minute_meeting_walk and talk_barely concentrate_prove underling wrong_business.gif
title: Walking and Talking Ends Badly

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have a minute?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm on my way to a meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Follow me. We'll walk and talk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't see how this can possibly work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can barely concentrate when you're sitting perfectly still.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When you add the extra complexity of walking, it's like asking a squirrel to land a 747.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Must... prove underling... wrong...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: BONK!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't know that being right could feel so good.

situation: Dilbert asks the Boss for a minute, and the Boss suggests they walk and talk on the way to a meeting. Dilbert insults the Boss's ability to concentrate, saying walking will overload him. The Boss, determined to prove Dilbert wrong, walks headfirst into a door and ends up on the floor.
punchline: The Boss's spite-driven attempt to prove he can multitask backfires and proves Dilbert exactly right, which Dilbert happily savors.
summary: Goaded by an insult about his limited focus, a manager tries to prove he can walk and talk at once and promptly knocks himself out on a door.

file: 2011/2011-11-19_employees_ignorance (knowledge)_fire wally_can't risk_zeberpupin system_only one_program_business.gif
title: Wally's Job Security: Zeberpupin System

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want to fire Wally, but I can't risk it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He says he's the only one who can program the Zeberpupin system.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Are you sure that's true?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It must be. No one else has even heard of it.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells Catbert he wants to fire Wally but fears losing the only person who can program the Zeberpupin system. Catbert asks whether that is really true. The Boss takes the lack of anyone else having heard of the system as proof that Wally is indispensable.
punchline: The Boss treats the fact that nobody has heard of the system as evidence that only Wally can program it, when it more likely suggests Wally invented the system to protect his job.
summary: A manager holds off on firing a lazy employee because he believes the man's claim of unique expertise in a system nobody else has ever heard of.

file: 2011/2011-07-02_frustration_quarreling_bullying behavior_confirmation bias_delusional witch.gif
title: Documenting Your Bullying, Allegedly

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Let's begin the meeting, but be aware that I am documenting all of your bullying behavior.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... I'm not even close to being a bully, but now your confirmation bias will make everything I say sound like bullying to you.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click click click click

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Can you repeat the part after you implied that I'm a delusional witch?

situation: Tina opens a meeting by announcing she is documenting Dilbert's bullying behavior. Dilbert protests that he isn't a bully but points out that her confirmation bias will make anything he says seem like bullying. Tina types his words into her phone and asks him to repeat the part where he implied she is a delusional witch.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to defend himself by naming her bias is itself an insult, which Tina immediately records as proof of the bullying he denies.
summary: A coworker who is logging a colleague's supposed harassment turns his clumsy self-defense into fresh evidence against him.

file: 2011/2011-07-18_big business_business ethics_class_more efficient_government contract_stuffed deer.gif
title: Efficiency Class Hurts Government Billing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This class will make me more efficient.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't want you to be more efficient. You're working on a government contract and billing by the hour.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
