transcript.text: Now go bill them for the time you stood here and stared at me like a stuffed deer.

setting: The Boss's office in a cubicle-filled workplace
situation: Dilbert asks his boss to approve a training class that would make him more efficient. The boss refuses because Dilbert is on a government contract billed by the hour, so efficiency would reduce revenue. The boss then tells him to bill the client for the time he spent standing there staring blankly.
punchline: The boss opposes efficiency because hourly billing on a government contract rewards wasted time, and he cynically tells Dilbert to bill the taxpayer even for the awkward conversation.
summary: A boss rejects a productivity course for his employee because slower work means bigger invoices to a government client.

file: 2011/2011-05-08_business ethics_suspicion_features for product_overstaffed_spare time_job description_healthy raise_highest performance rating.gif
title: Spare Time Reveals Overstaffing Fear

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In my spare time I created some awesome new features for our product.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gaaaa!!!! Shut the door!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You fool! If my boss finds out you have spare time, he'll think we're overstaffed!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can never speak of these awesome new features again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm confused. You told me I need to go above and beyond my job description to get the highest performance rating.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's just something I say to keep you from getting a healthy raise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... I lose no matter what I do?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: For what it's worth, you're doing better than our customers.

setting: Office, the Boss's cubicle and doorway
situation: Dilbert proudly tells his boss he built some great new product features in his spare time. The boss panics, shuts the door, and forbids him from mentioning it because it might make the department look overstaffed. When Dilbert points out the boss told him to go above and beyond, the boss admits that was only a ploy to avoid giving raises.
punchline: Dilbert is punished for showing initiative and denied raises however he behaves, and the boss's only consolation is that Dilbert is treated better than the company's customers.
summary: A worker's extra effort is suppressed by a boss who fears headcount cuts and admits that encouraging it was merely a way to withhold raises.

file: 2011/2011-06-22_annoyance_frustration_buy in_cleaner_windows don't open.gif
title: Circular Approval Makes Jumping Tempting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't get buy-in for my project because our CEO hasn't approved it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I can't get our CEO to approve it until I have buy-in from all of the divisions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: On the plus side, now I understand why the windows in our building don't open.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: It's cleaner.

situation: Dilbert stands before the seated Boss and explains that his project is stuck in a circular approval trap: the divisions won't buy in until the CEO approves, and the CEO won't approve until the divisions buy in. He remarks that he now understands why the building's windows don't open, and the Boss cheerfully says it's cleaner.
punchline: Dilbert implies the windows are sealed to stop employees from jumping out in despair over bureaucratic dead ends, and the Boss obliviously or callously says it's about cleanliness.
summary: After describing an impossible chicken-and-egg approval loop, an employee darkly jokes about why office windows are sealed, and his boss misses or dismisses the implication.

file: 2011/2011-11-06_interviews_suspicion_job interview_brand online_blog_tweets_facebook_credit_criminal record_transcripts_refrences_external stuff_attitude_yrine test_dna test_tanning bed_mri_psychology.gif
title: Interviewer Knows Everything About Candidate

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Job interview

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I researched your personal brand online.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: My what?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I looked at your blog, your tweets, and your Facebook page. I googled your name and followed every link.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I checked your credit, criminal record, school transcripts, and references.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But that's just the external stuff.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Exactly. It's my attitude that counts!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I mean I also have the results of your urine test.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, and apparently some of your sample landed in a DNA test kit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And that tanning bed you used last week was actually an MRI.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's your attitude now?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Harder to fake.

situation: The Boss interviews a job candidate and reveals that he has researched the candidate's online presence, credit, criminal record, and school records. When the candidate says his attitude is what counts, the boss escalates by revealing he has urine test results, a DNA sample, and even secretly scanned him with an MRI disguised as a tanning bed.
punchline: After being subjected to invasive surveillance and testing, the candidate admits his attitude is now harder to fake, since he has been stripped of any ability to hide anything.
summary: A hiring manager's background check grows absurdly invasive until the applicant concedes there is nothing left to pretend about.

file: 2011/2011-04-29_annoyance_anxiety_internet & world wide web_password recovery_password_pin code_user name_code word_complicated planet_floyd_first person_breath_jump_outer psce.gif
title: Password Overload Launches Floyd Into Space

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Password Recovery Service

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you trying to recover a password, pin code, user name, pass code or code word?

transcript.speaker: Floyd
transcript.text: I hate this stupid complicated planet! I am so out of here!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: And that is how Floyd became the first person to hold his breath and jump into outer space.

situation: A frustrated customer named Floyd visits Dogbert's Password Recovery Service, where Dogbert rattles off a long list of credentials he might be trying to recover. Floyd, fed up with the complexity of modern life, shouts that he is leaving the planet. A caption then shows him floating in outer space, having literally held his breath and jumped off the Earth.
punchline: The sheer number of passwords, PINs and codes people must remember is so maddening that a man would rather leap into the vacuum of space than deal with it.
summary: A man driven to despair by the endless pile of logins and codes decides to escape the world altogether, and the strip shows him drifting into space.

file: 2011/2011-02-09_mobile (cell) phones_text message_auto correction feature_weather holds_rude fresco_auto correction_feature.gif
title: Autocorrect Garbles the Boss's Text

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: I got your text message and I burped the grope plow armistice as you requested.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should turn off the auto-correction feature on your phone.

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: If the weather holds, I'll flail the rude fresco tomorrow.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: Three men sit at a table while a balding coworker reports on a task he did after receiving a text message, but his words are complete nonsense. Dilbert suggests the sender turn off the auto-correction feature on his phone. The coworker then replies with another nonsensical sentence, showing his own phone is garbling his messages too.
punchline: The person blaming autocorrect for gibberish is himself speaking gibberish, so the real problem is that nobody can communicate clearly and everyone is nodding along anyway.
summary: A coworker's reply is so full of absurd phrases that Dilbert blames phone autocorrect, yet the nonsense keeps coming.

file: 2011/2011-07-19_dating_gadgets_mobile (cell) phones_dilbert_twitter_world has judged_dont exist_ghost_blocking tv_relationships.gif

situation: At a social gathering, Dilbert introduces himself to a woman who immediately asks how many Twitter followers he has. When he admits he has none, she coldly declares that the world has judged him. At home, Dilbert complains that it's as if he doesn't exist, and Dogbert, sitting in an armchair, quips that he is blocking the TV.
punchline: Dilbert laments feeling nonexistent without followers, and Dogbert sarcastically says that for someone who supposedly doesn't exist, he sure blocks the TV well.
summary: A stranger dismisses Dilbert for having no online audience, and his pet mocks his claim of invisibility by pointing out he's in the way of the television.

file: 2011/2011-04-11_fraternization_internet & world wide web_friends with ghoats_real freinds_imaginary ones_idea is ridiculous_ridiculous idea_facebook freinds.gif
title: Facebook Friends Are Imaginary Too

transcript.text: How many friends do you have on Facebook?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Seven hundred. Why?

setting: The Boss's office, across his desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss to develop a product that lets people feel they are friends with ghosts. The Boss dismisses the idea, saying people only want real friends. Dogbert asks how many Facebook friends he has, and the Boss proudly answers seven hundred without seeing the point.
punchline: The Boss's 700 Facebook friends are hardly real friendships, so he already pays for the illusion of friendship he just called ridiculous.
summary: A boss scoffs at a pitch for fake ghost friends, then unwittingly reveals that his hundreds of online friends are just as illusory.

file: 2011/2011-06-18_anxiety_work ethic_worry_indispensible_fired_useless_riskier_toe clip_20 years of service.gif
title: Indispensable Versus Useless Job Security

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, should I try to become indispensible so I won't be fired?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No. Indispensible people end up working too hard because they can't risk showing anyone else how to do what they do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Being useless seems riskier.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Have you seen the tie clip I got for 20 years of service?

situation: Dilbert asks Wally whether he should make himself indispensable to avoid being fired. Wally warns that indispensable people overwork because they can never train anyone else. Dilbert says being useless seems riskier, and Wally answers by showing off the tie clip he received for 20 years of service.
punchline: Wally's long career of doing as little as possible has been rewarded with a trivial tie clip, implying that being useless is actually a safe strategy for keeping a job.
summary: A worried Dilbert is advised by Wally that being irreplaceable means endless work, while Wally's own long, lazy tenure proves slacking is perfectly survivable.

file: 2011/2011-04-22_cruelty_office workers_mindless task_intern_time_little value_jump out_nice way to say.gif
title: No Nice Way To Insult Intern

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: There probably was a nice way to say that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It didn't jump out.

situation: Dilbert walks up to Asok, who is seated at his computer, and warns that there is no nice way to say what he is about to say. He then bluntly hands Asok a mindless task, telling him that as an intern his time has very little value. Asok replies that a nicer phrasing surely existed, and Dilbert admits he simply didn't think of one.
punchline: Dilbert uses the excuse that no nice phrasing existed, but he admits he just didn't bother to find one, revealing his casual cruelty toward the intern.
summary: A senior engineer insults a young intern while handing him grunt work, then shrugs off the rudeness as a failure to think of better wording.

file: 2011/2011-03-14_apathy_executives_work ethic_enginner_no budget_emailed_ceo_social network_global supply chain.gif
title: Social Network Steals All Project Funding

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... you e-mailed our CEO and asked for funds to build a social network for our global supply chain.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No one wants that. But it sounds good, so he moved all of our project funding to your dumb idea.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And... you will produce nothing.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Said the engineer with no budget.

situation: Dilbert confronts a coworker who emailed the CEO asking for money to build a social network for the global supply chain. Because the idea sounded trendy, the CEO moved all the company's project funding to it, leaving Dilbert with nothing. Dilbert says the coworker will produce nothing, and the coworker calmly sips his coffee and retorts that Dilbert is the engineer with no budget.
punchline: The coworker, having successfully captured all the funding with a buzzword-laden pitch nobody wants, mocks Dilbert for being the one left with no budget to produce anything.
summary: A trendy but unwanted idea pitched to the CEO hoovers up every project's funding, and its smug author gloats over the engineer he just left broke.

file: 2011/2011-12-21_business ethics_wealth_ceo_good job_50 million dollar bonus_not motivated_bad genes_inequality_dosaprity_ceo and worker_unfair wages_crazy money_slave wages_more work_no rewards_money.gif

transcript.text: More work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: Alice asks the Boss what the CEO receives for doing a good job and is told it's a fifty million dollar bonus. When she asks what she gets for doing a good job, he says more work. She then asks why she might be unmotivated, and he blames her genes.
punchline: The Boss cluelessly attributes Alice's lack of motivation to bad genes rather than the obviously lopsided reward system where the CEO gets millions and she just gets extra work.
summary: A worker contrasts her reward for excellence with the boss's executive payout, and her manager pins her low morale on heredity instead of the pay gap.

file: 2011/2011-09-29_dont know_flashdrive_gadgets_hand_illness_where its been_data.gif

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: Asok walks up to Dilbert's desk and offers him a flash drive containing data. Dilbert recoils, saying he doesn't know where it has been. Asok hopes Dilbert means the drive and not his hand, and Dilbert admits he meant the drive but now wonders about the hand too.
punchline: Dilbert's germophobic remark about the flash drive accidentally prompts Asok to point out that his own hand is just as suspect, and Dilbert agrees.
summary: A coworker's offer of a data-filled USB stick gets rejected as unsanitary, and the conversation turns to whether the hand holding it is any cleaner.

file: 2011/2011-04-14_ignorance (knowledge)_laziness_seven layers of management_lead company_unknowingly_bad idea_input to avoid_ceo_middle management.gif
title: Seven Layers Between Me and Reality

transcript.speaker: CEO

situation: A bald CEO tells a subordinate he intends to insert seven more layers of management between them. He explains that his goal is to run the company while knowing nothing about it. When the subordinate objects that this is a bad idea, the CEO says that this kind of honest feedback is precisely what he wants to avoid.
punchline: The CEO is deliberately building bureaucracy to insulate himself from honest feedback, and the subordinate's warning proves the plan is working exactly as intended.
summary: A chief executive wants a tower of middle managers so he can run the firm in blissful ignorance and never hear criticism.

file: 2011/2011-02-20_lying_budget meeting_cfo_precious budget dollars_competeing_dots are staffed_professional liars_call marketing_finace.gif

file: 2011/2011-06-03_anger_debates_internet & world wide web_outsiurcing_racist_restrooms_debate_internet_learn debate_technology.gif

Dilbert calmly points out that the coworker's debating style looks like something learned online, and the coworker asks how he could tell.
punchline: The coworker's absurd, straw-man accusation is exactly the kind of bad-faith argument found in internet debates, and he fails to realize he has just proved Dilbert's point.
summary: A colleague hurls a wildly unfounded accusation at Dilbert, who diagnoses the debating technique as one picked up from online arguments.

file: 2011/2011-12-29_conversation_employees_executives_on line class_develop charisma_change the world_die from stree_health issues_business.gif

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

The Boss delivers a rousing-sounding speech that promises world-changing achievement but admits employees will die of stress-related illness. The Boss feels pleased with his performance and Dilbert agrees he captured it perfectly.
punchline: The Boss's attempt at inspirational charisma accidentally reveals his true management philosophy: exploiting employees until their health fails, and Dilbert sarcastically confirms it is authentic.
summary: A manager's practice motivational pitch turns out to be an honest confession of how burnout-inducing his leadership really is.

file: 2011/2011-08-31_complaining_conversation_get mad_point out dumb_helpful_doctor_dogbert_medical.gif

transcript.text: I'm kind of like a doctor.

situation: Dilbert sits outside with Dogbert and muses aloud about why people get angry when he tells them how dumb they are. He insists he is only being helpful and compares himself to a doctor diagnosing a problem. Dogbert reveals he tuned out of the conversation long ago.
punchline: Dogbert admits he stopped listening long before, implying Dilbert's self-righteous lecture is as tedious as the insults that annoy everyone else.
summary: After justifying his habit of calling people stupid as a kind of medical service, Dilbert learns his only listener tuned him out ages ago.

punchline: Despite Asok's absurdly impressive credentials, the coworker reduces him to his ethnicity, showing how workplace prejudice overlooks individual achievement.
summary: A boastful engineer lays out a spectacular academic résumé, only for a colleague to summarize his whole background with a single stereotyped label.

file: 2011/2011-02-10_executives_meetings_dogbert_consulting_facebook_china_irrelevant_breakout groups_fantasize_being relevant.gif

punchline: The 'comprehensive list' leaves only one possible answer for the company, so the consultant sarcastically proposes a group exercise in fantasizing about being relevant.
summary: A consultant's three-item chart leaves one honest answer for the client's company, so he assigns a group activity in pretending it isn't true.

file: 2011/2011-07-09_lying_optimism_projections_realistic_optimistic_near death_hallucination_luci dream.gif

punchline: Dilbert admits his forecasts are essentially delusional, and the Boss cheerfully relabels them as 'most likely', showing management will accept absurd numbers if given a respectable-sounding label.
summary: When asked about the quality of his forecasts, an engineer confesses they are pure fantasy, and his manager simply rebrands them as the likely outcome.

file: 2011/2011-07-10_anger_quarreling_mastered art_being useless_next level_toxic_toxic people_complain_personal problems.gif

file: 2011/2011-12-12_thinking_worry_no probelms_insane_universe_nail waiting for hammer_pre frontal cortex_anticipation_too smooth_mysteriously calm_uncomforatbale.gif

situation: Dilbert talks with Wally over coffee, confessing he is anxious because nothing has gone wrong today. punchline: Wally's deadpan reply implies that anxious foreboding is what you get from using your prefrontal cortex, so being less rational would be easier, and it comically endorses Dilbert's paranoia.
summary: A man who is uneasy over a suspiciously trouble-free day is told by his coworker that the brain's rational center is overrated.

file: 2011/2011-09-23_annoyance_conversation_dating_micromanaging_boss_god work_just listen_insulting_insuate_relationships.gif

Dilbert responds with the tactless suggestion that she try doing good work so her boss won't feel the need to hover. summary: Instead of sympathizing with his date's complaint about a hovering boss, Dilbert implies she is at fault and then sees from her glare that he blundered.

summary: A job seeker's willingness to put in extreme hours is used by the interviewer as proof of poor judgment, leaving him unsure how to answer anything.

file: 2011/2011-06-08_friendship_gadgets_mobile (cell) phones_shoulder holder_jealousy is attractive_relationships.gif

transcript.text: I invented a shoulder holder for my phone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I felt bad keeping my best friend in my pocket.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Jealousy is not attractive.

situation: Dilbert shows Dogbert a shoulder-mounted holder he invented for his cell phone, explaining that he felt bad keeping his phone, which he calls his best friend, in his pocket. In the last panel Dogbert, who has been sitting on the dresser, is holding a smoking toy ray gun and looks put out. Dilbert tells him that jealousy is not attractive.
punchline: Dilbert treats his phone as his best friend and tells Dogbert, who has apparently zapped the phone out of jealousy, that jealousy is unattractive, which pokes fun at how attached people are to their gadgets.
summary: An inventor affectionately mounts his phone on his shoulder and scolds his dog for resenting the gadget.

file: 2011/2011-04-02_complaining_communication skills_poor skills_random numbers_spreadsheet_clarify_listening skills.gif
title: Random Numbers For Unclear Requests

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: This isn't what I wanted.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your communication skills are so poor that I gave up trying to understand what you wanted and instead put some random numbers on a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Why didn't you just ask me to clarify?!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently your listening skills need work too.

situation: A requester complains that the spreadsheet Dilbert delivered is not what she wanted. Dilbert admits he knew that, explaining he couldn't decipher her vague request and just filled it with random numbers. She asks why he didn't ask for clarification, and he replies that she evidently didn't listen.
punchline: Dilbert turns the blame back on the requester, implying he did ask for clarification repeatedly and she never listened, so her complaint about his work is really a failure of her own communication.
summary: After delivering a deliberately meaningless spreadsheet to a person who couldn't explain her needs, Dilbert deflects her criticism by pointing out her own poor listening.

file: 2011/2011-01-21_prosperity_competition (psychology).gif
title: Niche Player Sounds Strategic Enough

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're not creative enough to create whole new markets, the way Apple does.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And we're not powerful enough for a fast follower strategy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What we need is a sexy, strategic-sounding name for crumb-snatching.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Niche player?

setting: Conference room in a corporate office
situation: The Boss tells colleagues at a meeting that the company lacks the creativity to invent new markets like Apple and the clout to be a fast follower. He concludes they need an impressive-sounding label for simply grabbing leftovers. Dilbert offers 'niche player' as the term.
punchline: Corporate jargon like 'niche player' is just a flattering euphemism for a company that can only scavenge the scraps larger competitors leave behind.
summary: A meeting admits the company is neither innovative nor strong, so it hunts for a glamorous phrase to dress up picking up leftovers.

file: 2011/2011-07-03_questioning_shopping_hardware_powerpoint deck_boss_ambiguity_mumbling_change subject_badger for answer_too many questions.gif
title: Boss Dodges Dilbert's Clarifying Questions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you look at this bid and let me know if I can order the hardware?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you saying yes I can order the hardware, or yes you'll look at it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mumble, mumble.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need your input on my PowerPoint deck.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So far, in response to my request, you've given me ambiguity, mumbling, and a change of subject.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you prefer that I badger you for an answer until you get angry, or should I return to my cubicle and resume being ineffective?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You ask too many questions.

setting: Office, Dilbert's cubicle and the Boss's desk
situation: Dilbert asks his boss to review a hardware bid so he can place an order, but the boss gives a vague one-word answer. When Dilbert asks for clarification, the boss mumbles and then changes the subject to his own PowerPoint deck. Dilbert lays out the boss's evasions and asks whether to badger him or give up, and the boss just complains that Dilbert asks too many questions.
punchline: The boss responds to a perfectly reasonable request for clarity by blaming the employee for asking too many questions, showing he never intended to give a real answer.
summary: A manager sidesteps an employee's attempt to get a simple approval and then blames him for being too inquisitive.

file: 2011/2011-09-18_conversation_discussion_hijack conversations of subordinates_imperious interuptus_load and testing.gif
title: Imperious Interruptus: Bosses Hijack Conversations

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...Then we can do the load testing and...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm invoking the right of Imperious Interruptus.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In layman's terms, it is the right of all bosses to hijack the conversations of subordinates.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I will now turn my back to you and speak with Alice as if you don't exist.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do not leave. Do not chime in. Just awkwardly stand there.

transcript.speaker: Another Boss
transcript.text: Imperious Interruptus!

transcript.speaker: Another Boss
transcript.text: Behold my power to make two underlings stand awkwardly while I hijack this conversation!

transcript.speaker: Another Boss
transcript.text: Have you heard my speech about how we're not level conscious at this company?

situation: Dilbert is discussing load testing with Alice when the Boss interrupts, announcing his supposed right to hijack subordinates' conversations. He turns his back on Dilbert to talk to Alice and orders Dilbert to stand there silently. A second, taller boss then repeats the move on the Boss, leaving the Boss and Dilbert standing awkwardly.
punchline: The Boss gets a taste of his own medicine when a higher-ranking boss hijacks his conversation and makes him stand silently, while hypocritically giving a speech about not being level conscious.
summary: A boss claims a made-up privilege to barge into a chat and ignore one employee, only for an even higher boss to pull the same trick on him.

file: 2011/2011-12-26_christmas presents_sweaters_ugly sweater_lose a bet_gift from mom_hideous sweater.gif
title: Wearing the Ugly Sweater Once

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What's up with the ugly sweater? Did you lose a bet?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This? Oh, right. It was a gift from my mom. I'm wearing it once in case she asks me later.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did you know it was hideous before I told you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Snork

setting: Office break area by the coffee maker
situation: Alice notices Dilbert's ugly sweater at the coffee machine and asks if he lost a bet. Dilbert explains it was a gift from his mom and he's wearing it just once in case she asks about it later. Alice asks if he knew it was hideous before she pointed it out, he answers 'Maybe,' and Wally snorts into his coffee mug.
punchline: Dilbert's vague 'Maybe' reveals he knew exactly how awful the sweater was and is only wearing it once so he can truthfully tell his mom he wore it.
summary: A man grudgingly wears a hideous gift sweater a single time to cover himself with his mother, and a coworker's blunt question gets a wry non-answer.

file: 2011/2011-04-03_executives_interviews_ceo's interview series_company priftable_credit_overpaid and useless_dumb employees_highest bidder_blackmail_interview.gif
title: Dogbert's Hostile CEO Interview Series

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's CEO interview series

transcript.text: I don't like people.

transcript.text: What makes your company so profitable?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is that another way of saying you're overpaid and useless?

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: No! They're smart!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But not as smart as you?

transcript.text: Who's going to see this?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No one, assuming you're the highest bidder.

setting: A CEO's office, framed by a presentation screen showing the Dilbert logo in the opening panel
situation: Dogbert, holding a microphone, interviews a CEO for his interview series and asks pointed questions about why the company is profitable. Each answer the CEO gives is twisted by Dogbert into an insult, and the CEO grows increasingly nervous. In the last panel the CEO asks who will see the interview, revealing Dogbert's blackmail scheme.
punchline: Dogbert's interview series is really a blackmail racket: the footage will only stay unpublished if the embarrassed CEO pays the most.
summary: A talk-show dog grills a rattled executive with insulting follow-ups, then reveals the unflattering footage is for sale to the highest bidder.

file: 2011/2011-01-04_sagas_supernatural beings_anxiety.gif

situation: Seated at a meeting table, Alice complains to Tina that she can't concentrate because Tina reminds her of a creature. She explains that Tina has a Bilbo Baggins look that is distracting her. Alice then asks to be warned if a walking stick comes her way, implying she might lash out.
punchline: Alice is so thrown by a coworker's resemblance to a hobbit that she suggests she may need to be warned before she attacks her with a walking stick, implying a hostile reaction.
summary: A prickly coworker blames a colleague's hobbit-like appearance for ruining her focus, then hints that violence with a cane may follow.

file: 2011/2011-10-12_employees_office workers_worked at home_work tonight_leaving early_work late_business.gif
title: Counting Home Hours Before Leaving Early

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Leaving early?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you count the two hours I worked at home when I woke up, and the two hours I'll work tonight, you'll come out way ahead today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How will I come out if you do all of that plus work late here?

situation: Dilbert is heading out with his bag when The Boss checks his watch and asks if he is leaving early. Dilbert justifies it by adding up the work he did at home that morning and the work he will do that evening. The Boss responds by asking why Dilbert wouldn't do all of that and also stay late at the office.
punchline: The Boss, unmoved by Dilbert's time-accounting, shows that his real expectation is for employees to give more and more unpaid hours, so any extra work only raises the bar.
summary: An employee tries to excuse an early departure by tallying his off-site hours, only to have his manager treat the extra effort as a reason to demand even more.

file: 2011/2011-03-31_created cold fusion_jar with light bulb_more news_camera guy.gif
title: Camera Guy Debunks Cold Fusion

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Press conference

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As you can clearly see, I have created cold fusion.

transcript.speaker: Camera Operator
transcript.text: That's not cold fusion. It's just a jar with a light-bulb.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's some more news: No one cares what the camera guy thinks.

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: It's free energy!

setting: A press conference with a table, a jar and reporters
situation: Dogbert holds a press conference to announce that he has created cold fusion, showing a jar with a lightbulb. The camera operator points out that it is merely a jar with a lightbulb. Dogbert dismisses him, and the excited reporter announces that it is free energy.
punchline: The media ignores the one person who states the obvious truth and eagerly runs with the sensational false claim, showing how easily the press and public are fooled.
summary: A scam artist dog passes off a bulb in a jar as a scientific breakthrough, and the gullible press embraces it over the one skeptic who spots the trick.

file: 2011/2011-03-30_hold press conference_introduce cold fusion_breakthrough_lightbulb_wires plugged_low opinion_jar with frosted glass_overkill.gif

transcript.text: You have a low opinion of people.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I considered using a jar with frosted glass, but it seemed like overkill.

situation: Dogbert announces he is ready to present a cold fusion breakthrough to the press. Dilbert inspects the device and sees it is only a lightbulb in a jar, plugged into a wall outlet. Dogbert admits he barely tried to disguise the fake.
punchline: Dogbert's sham invention is so crude that he didn't bother hiding the wires, because he assumes the public is gullible enough to fall for it anyway.
summary: A scheming dog plans to unveil a laughably fake energy device, assuming the audience is too foolish to notice the deception.

file: 2011/2011-04-26_business ethics_health insurance_reduce expenses_radiation dosimeters_wrongness_policy.gif

punchline: The employees' passive-aggressive staring tactic fails because the clueless Boss has no conscience to be shamed into reversing the unsafe, cost-cutting policy.
summary: Workers try to shame their boss with a silent group stare after he makes them pay for their own radiation safety badges, but he remains unmoved.

file: 2011/2011-07-17_big business_business ethics_career path_warn you_maximum career potential_less embarrassing car_ne wocmpany_ceo_huge nbonus_conversation.gif
title: Honest Career Advice Backfires on Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to talk about my career path.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you sure?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... Yes, I'm sure.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't say I didn't warn you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're within 20% of your maximum career potential.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your future will be just like the present, except you'll be older and you might own a less-embarrassing car.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you go to a new company, you'll like it at first, but in time you'll realize every place is the same.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! Take back the truth!!! Lie to me! Lie to me!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe someday our CEO will make such a huge bonus that he'll want to share some of it with you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate you!

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: Dilbert asks his boss to discuss his career path, and the boss warns him he might not like the answer. The boss then candidly tells Dilbert he is near his career ceiling, his future will be no different from the present, and changing companies won't help. Dilbert begs to be lied to, and the boss's only comfort is a far-fetched hope of a CEO bonus trickling down.
punchline: The boss's brutally honest career advice is bleak and demoralizing, and he points out he did try to warn Dilbert, implying that the truth about corporate careers is something nobody really wants to hear.
summary: An employee seeking career guidance gets a relentlessly honest reality check about his dismal prospects and begs his manager to go back to lying.

file: 2011/2011-08-30_debates_discussion_ognorant_arrogant_reading comprehension_logic.gif

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: A coworker accuses Dilbert of writing an ignorant and arrogant email while a third colleague sits nearby. Dilbert responds by insulting the coworker's reading comprehension, then proposes using logic to settle who is right. Each reply is labeled as another bad decision, and the coworker grows angrier.
punchline: Dilbert escalates the argument with insults and an appeal to logic, which only makes an emotional coworker angrier, showing that 'rational' debate rarely works on someone who is already upset.
summary: Dilbert keeps making things worse when a colleague criticizes his email, countering with an insult and then an offer to settle it with logic.

file: 2011/2011-06-25_despair_recessions_unemployment_fix your lips_job satisfaction_all time low.gif

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh no!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ha ha! Fix your lips!

situation: Catbert stands on the Boss's desk and announces, in a mock-alarmed tone, that employee job satisfaction is at an all-time low while unemployment is high. The Boss laughs and tries to imitate the concern. His 'Oh no!' comes out flat, and Catbert laughs and tells him to fix his lips.
punchline: The Boss thinks he is joking about caring, but his face and voice show he actually doesn't, and the grim economic news means he has no incentive to improve morale because unhappy employees can't easily leave.
summary: A sarcastic cat and a smirking manager trade fake expressions of worry over miserable workers who can't escape because jobs are scarce.

file: 2011/2011-04-21_managers & supervisors_questioning_suspicion_schedule meetings_excuse_do nothing_disbelief_scheduling meetings_business.gif

situation: Dilbert asks the Boss for permission to have Carol help him schedule a batch of meetings. The Boss refuses because Carol would treat the small task as a reason to do nothing else all week. Dilbert sarcastically asks if he may simply stare in disbelief, and the Boss tells him to get back to scheduling.
punchline: The Boss's objection implies that the task is trivial yet Carol would milk it for a week, while he is oblivious to Dilbert's sarcasm and just orders him back to work.
summary: A manager vetoes a colleague's help with a simple scheduling chore because she would stretch it out, then brushes off his employee's incredulous stare.

file: 2011/2011-12-30_excitement_gloating_awesome bob_dry cleaner_flying wing suit.gif

The coworker's phone rings, and she relays that Bob is late because the dry cleaner couldn't remove sushi stains from his flying wingsuit. The Boss responds with enthusiasm, finding even this excuse awesome.
punchline: The Boss is so starstruck by Awesome Bob that he treats an ordinary lame excuse for lateness as impressive, simply because it involves a flying wingsuit and sushi.
summary: A starstruck manager hears that his hero is late for their meeting over a laundry mishap with an extreme-sports outfit and cheers it as impressive.

summary: A manager brags about his company's eco-friendly values, casually threatens to trade away the applicant's children for carbon offsets, and later laments that the applicant wasn't more gullible.

file: 2011/2011-09-04_administrative agencies_control_data_delay_frustration_manipulate_meetings_time_two weeks.gif

transcript.text: Six or seven days, tops.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I need it in three days, not a week.

summary: A frustrated colleague tries to pin Wally to a three-day deadline but he keeps inflating the timeline until she surrenders and moves her whole meeting.

file: 2011/2011-09-17_commerce_competition (psychology)_hate new product_customers_fake revenue projections_engineer_stronger company_engineering.gif

punchline: Rather than face a realistic analysis that every outcome is bad, management would prefer to silence the engineer and be comforted by made-up financial numbers.
summary: An engineer lays out the grim odds for a new product, and his superiors react by seeking fictional good news instead of dealing with the problem.

file: 2011/2011-03-02_farmers & farm workers_work ethic_manage issues_align org. activities_stakeholder_real work_farm.gif

file: 2011/2011-09-20_commerce_joking_market share_increase market share_good sense of humor.gif

file: 2011/2011-06-14_cruelty_frustration_idea_never work_reject hypothesis_self doubt.gif
title: Dilbert Insults Critic's Intelligence

transcript.text: Your idea will never work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At what point did you reject the hypothesis that you're too dumb to understand how good the idea is?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm becoming even less of a people person.

setting: Conference room, then a hallway or break area
situation: A coworker at a meeting table dismisses Dilbert's idea as unworkable. Dilbert responds with a cutting question suggesting the critic may simply be too dumb to appreciate it. Afterwards, holding a coffee mug beside Wally, Dilbert remarks that he is getting worse with people.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic put-down shows he is aware that his blunt, insulting reaction to criticism is making him even worse at dealing with people.
summary: After having his proposal shot down, Dilbert fires back with a scathing question and then admits his social skills keep declining.

file: 2011/2011-09-16_conversation_language_positive feel_power cables_insulated.gif
title: Positive Phrasing Shocks Customer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Avoid saying "unfortunately" when you talk to customers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Say instead, "As it turns out." That has a more positive feel.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As it turns out, our power cables aren't as insulated as we had hoped.

setting: Conference room, then a customer meeting
situation: At a meeting, the Boss coaches the team to replace the word 'unfortunately' with 'as it turns out' when speaking to customers because it sounds more positive. Dilbert applies the advice by telling a customer about faulty power cables. The customer stands there electrocuted, hair on end and smoking, still holding the cable.
punchline: Positive-sounding phrasing can't soften the reality of a dangerous product defect, as the electrocuted customer shows.
summary: After being coached to sound upbeat with customers, Dilbert cheerfully admits a product flaw to a client who has just been zapped by faulty cables.

file: 2011/2011-06-30_apps_gadgets_mobile (cell) phones_new smartphone_tongue on flagpole_victime of good marketing_voice reception.gif
title: Smartphone Victim of Good Marketing

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Check out my new smartphone!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The voice reception is a bit weak, but I can usually make a call if I keep my tongue on a flagpole.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You might be a victim of good marketing.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It has apps!

situation: A coworker proudly shows Alice her new smartphone, then admits its call reception is so poor she can only make calls with her tongue on a flagpole. Alice points out she may have fallen for slick marketing, and the coworker dismisses the criticism by saying the phone has apps.
punchline: The coworker accepts an absurdly bad phone, one that barely works as a phone, because of the lure of apps, proving Alice's point about marketing's power.
summary: A gadget enthusiast brags about a smartphone that can barely make calls, and defends it with the magic word apps when a skeptical colleague calls her a marketing victim.

file: 2011/2011-01-26_commerce_economic policy_utax incentives_projects_tax savings_executive bonuses_stimulate economy_trickle on your heads_trickle down theory_poker night.gif
title: Trickle Down Becomes Trickle On

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've decided to use the new tax incentives on the projects we were going to do anyway.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The tax savings will go toward executive bonuses, which stimulate the economy via the "trickle on your heads" theory.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's called the "trickle down" theory.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not on poker night.

situation: The Boss tells Alice and Dilbert that the company will claim new tax incentives on projects it was already planning, then funnel the savings into executive bonuses. He says this stimulates the economy through a 'trickle on your heads' theory. Alice corrects the name to 'trickle down', and he replies with a crude quip.
punchline: The Boss's crude quip about poker night turns 'trickle down' into something humiliating, implying that executives treat the rank and file with contempt while pocketing the tax savings.
summary: A manager cheerfully admits that tax breaks will fund executive bonuses while employees get nothing but a crude version of trickle-down economics.

file: 2011/2011-03-22_managers & supervisors_secretaries (office)_work ethic_filling in for boss_workstation vacation_being in charge_pverarted_martini glass_drinking_umbrella in drink_secretary_business.gif
title: Secretary's Workstation Vacation While Boss Away

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'm filling in for your boss this week, and I need twenty copies.

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: That's not how it works. When he's out of the office I take a workstation vacation.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I don't like being in charge.

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: I hear it's overrated.

situation: A woman with big hair, filling in for the absent boss, asks the boss's secretary to make twenty copies. The secretary refuses, explaining she takes a 'workstation vacation' whenever her boss is away. In the last panel she sits at her desk wearing sunglasses and sipping a cocktail with a little umbrella.
punchline: The secretary treats her boss's absence as a vacation at her own desk, and sarcastically dismisses the substitute's complaint about being in charge by calling it overrated.
summary: When the boss is away, his assistant lounges at her desk with a cocktail and sunglasses and won't do any work for the temporary stand-in.

file: 2011/2011-01-24_friendship_secretaries (office)_internet & world wide web_relationships.gif
title: Facebook Rejection Becomes Death Wish

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why did you reject my friend request on Facebook?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm not your friend. I'm a disgruntled wage slave who hopes you die in a freak industrial accident tomorrow at 3 PM.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's disturbingly specific.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hey, look. You have a meeting at the warehouse tomorrow.

situation: The Boss asks Alice why she rejected his Facebook friend request. Alice, seated at her computer, bluntly tells him she is a resentful employee who hopes he dies in a freak industrial accident at a specific time the next day. When he remarks on how specific that is, she cheerfully points out that his calendar has him at the warehouse then.
punchline: Alice's wish for her boss's death is so precise because she has already noticed his meeting at the warehouse, implying she is hoping, or even planning, for the accident to happen there.
summary: A manager wonders why his social media friend request was refused, and his employee answers with a dark, carefully timed wish for his demise.
themes: boundaries between work and personal life

file: 2011/2011-01-10_honesty_meat_question and answer_meat bags_boss and emplyee_realtionship_office.gif
title: Boss Won't Answer, Dilbert Insults

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In this country, it is customary to respond to a question with something called an "answer."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your approach is more like what I would expect to see if clothing were used as bags for meat.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I will ask my question a seventh time. . .

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop saying what you're thinking.

situation: Dilbert stands in front of the Boss's desk and has apparently asked a question several times without getting a real answer. He sarcastically explains what an answer is, then insults the Boss's evasive approach and announces he will ask a seventh time. The Boss responds only by telling him to stop voicing his thoughts.
punchline: The Boss still dodges the question, objecting not to the content of Dilbert's insult but to Dilbert saying out loud what he is thinking, with the 'clothing as bags for meat' line being a roundabout way of calling the Boss a human body in a suit.
summary: After repeatedly failing to get a straight reply, an employee mocks his evasive manager with an elaborate insult, and the manager just complains about the candor.

file: 2011/2011-08-29_courage_electronic mail_thinking_greatest idea ever_email.gif
title: Sending Dumb Idea Anyway

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is the greatest idea ever.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why does it look so dumb when I put it in email?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bad decision 1

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll sort it out later.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Send

situation: Dilbert sits alone at his computer, first convinced he has had the greatest idea ever. After typing it into an email he realizes it looks foolish, but rather than rethink it he decides to deal with the consequences later and clicks send. The final panel is labeled as 'Bad Decision 1'.
punchline: Dilbert recognizes that his idea is dumb once written down, yet sends the email anyway, showing how people knowingly make poor decisions and postpone dealing with the fallout.
summary: An engineer's brilliant brainwave turns embarrassing once typed out, yet he hits send regardless and hopes to fix things afterward.

file: 2011/2011-08-01_actions & defenses_computers & peripherals_internet & world wide web_international data security standards group_security prcedures_bed sores.gif
title: Dogbert's Security Standards Group Goals

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dogbert is chairing the International Data Security Standards Group.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The goal of our organization is to make your security procedures so inconvenient that you give up hope and die from bed sores.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We take pride in being independent from the companies that fund us.

setting: Conference room at a meeting table
situation: The Boss announces that Dogbert is chairing an international data security standards group. Dogbert, seated at the table beside Dilbert, explains that the group's goal is to make security procedures so inconvenient that people give up and die from bed sores. He then adds that the group is proudly independent of the companies that fund it.
punchline: Dogbert admits that security standards are designed to be maddeningly burdensome, then sarcastically claims independence from the very companies paying for them, implying the group's funders are hardly free of influence.
summary: A dog heading a security standards body cheerfully reveals that its mission is to make protective rules unbearably tedious while claiming to be free of its sponsors' influence.

file: 2011/2011-03-24_competition (psychology)_meetings_test script_prodcut.gif
title: Testing the Test Script

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I spent the week writing a test script for our product.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And I wrote a test script to test Dilbert's test script.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Your script was almost perfect. Keep up the good work, buddy.

situation: At a meeting, Dilbert reports that he spent the week writing a test script for the product. Wally then announces that he wrote a script to test Dilbert's script, and finally pats Dilbert on the back, condescendingly praising his work as almost perfect.
punchline: Wally has found a way to look productive and superior by merely critiquing a colleague's work, adding a layer of testing that does nothing for the actual product.
summary: A coworker one-ups a colleague's testing effort by building a script to grade it, then patronizes him about the result.

file: 2011/2011-03-18_laziness_meetings_telephones_returned calls_tragus_phone_research on excuses_useless_big difference.gif
title: Tragus Excuse for Unreturned Calls

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why haven't you returned my calls?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I tried, but when I put the phone to my ear, it pressed my tragus over my ear hole and I couldn't hear a thing.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you do research on your excuses before meetings?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm not lazy, I'm useless. There's a big difference.

situation: A coworker confronts Wally in a meeting about not returning his phone calls. Wally holding his coffee mug offers an absurdly detailed anatomical excuse about his ear's tragus blocking his hearing. When the coworker suggests he researches his excuses, Wally cheerfully insists he is not lazy but useless.
punchline: Wally proudly distinguishes being useless from being lazy, treating total incompetence as a point in his favor over mere laziness.
summary: A man demanding answers about ignored phone calls gets an elaborate ear-anatomy excuse, then an unashamed confession of uselessness.

file: 2011/2011-11-02_conversation_discussion_internet & world wide web_humor consultant_have more fun_internet access to entertainment_funny comment.gif
title: Humor Consultant Versus Internet Filter Consultant

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a humor consultant to teach us how to have more fun at work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does he cancel out the consultant you hired to filter our Internet access to entertainment?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That was a funny comment. How'd you do that without a consultant?

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces he has hired a humor consultant to help employees have more fun at work. Dilbert points out that this conflicts with another consultant the Boss hired to block entertainment on the company's internet. The Boss is impressed by Dilbert's wit and asks how he managed to be funny without a consultant.
punchline: The Boss thinks he needs a consultant to produce humor and fails to notice that Dilbert's sarcastic observation about his contradictory spending was the joke.
summary: Management pays one expert to boost workplace fun and another to block online amusement, then marvels that an employee can be witty unaided.

file: 2011/2011-03-06_honesty_managers & supervisors_proactive_send email_bad time management_creating illuson_sarcasm_crazy boss_business.gif
title: Be Proactive Before I Ask

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: DILBERT by Scott Adams, dilbert.com

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You need to be more proactive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can only appear to be proactive if you stop telling me to do things I've already planned.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How am I supposed to know what you plan to do every minute?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could send you an e-mail every time I have a thought.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't have time for that!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Apparently your bad time management is creating the illusion that I'm not proactive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll take the liberty of signing you up for a time management class.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't do that!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... I should not be proactive?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just do what I want before I know I want it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope the next thing you want is sarcasm.

setting: Boss's office, at a conference table
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to be more proactive, but Dilbert points out that the Boss keeps assigning him things he already planned. The Boss refuses to receive status emails, blames Dilbert's time management, and then signs him up for a class. When Dilbert asks if he should stop being proactive, the Boss demands that he do what the Boss wants before the Boss knows he wants it.
punchline: The Boss's demand for proactivity is impossible, since it requires Dilbert to anticipate wishes the Boss hasn't formed yet, and Dilbert sarcastically hopes the Boss wants sarcasm next.
summary: A manager's contradictory demands leave an employee unable to satisfy him, so the employee answers with deadpan sarcasm.

file: 2011/2011-05-06_annoyance_envy_useful member of society_admiration_respect_peers_talked out of.gif
title: Talked Out Of Being Useful

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm toying with the idea of becoming a useful member of society.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Then I could enjoy the admiration and respect of my peers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The way you respect and admire me?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Great! Now you've talked me out of it!

setting: Office break room or lunch table during lunch
situation: Wally, eating a sandwich at a lunch table with Dilbert and Asok, muses about becoming a useful member of society so he can earn his peers' admiration and respect. Dilbert points out that Wally doesn't actually respect or admire him, even though Dilbert is useful. Wally concludes the effort wouldn't be worth it.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic question reveals that being useful earns no real admiration or respect, so Wally happily abandons the idea and stays lazy.
summary: A slacker coworker considers contributing to society for the praise, but a sarcastic reminder of how he treats a productive colleague kills his motivation.

file: 2011/2011-06-28_annoyance_cruelty_impossible_totally worthless_vacations.gif
title: Dilbert Takes No Vacation Days

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's impossible to get anything done this time of year because everyone who isn't totally worthless is on vacation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: None taken.

setting: Office, next to a window with closed blinds
situation: Alice complains that nothing can get done in summer because every competent person is away on vacation. Dilbert, standing nearby holding a coffee mug, stays silent through the second panel and then dryly says 'None taken,' indicating he hasn't taken any vacation.
punchline: By replying 'None taken' (meaning no vacation days), Dilbert points out that Alice's insult has inadvertently called him totally worthless, since he is still at work.
summary: A coworker's gripe about the summer slowdown accidentally insults the one colleague who stayed behind, and he calmly points it out.

file: 2011/2011-08-12_business ethics_stock market_hedge fund_million dollars_insider trading_algorithm_winning trades_create algorithm_eat fiber_money.gif
title: Hedge Fund Fakes Winning Algorithm

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll pay you a million dollars a year to work at my hedge fund.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll do the insider trading and you pretend you created an algorithm that makes winning trades.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if I actually create the algorithm?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sure. And maybe you can eat fiber and make gold, too.

situation: Dogbert offers Dilbert a million-dollar-a-year job at his hedge fund. He explains that Dogbert will do illegal insider trading while Dilbert pretends an algorithm is responsible for the winning trades. Dilbert asks what if he really creates a working algorithm, and Dogbert scoffs at the idea.
punchline: Dogbert sarcastically implies that building a genuinely profitable trading algorithm is as impossible as turning fiber into gold, so the fund's success must come from cheating.
summary: A scheming dog hires a man as the fake genius front for illegal trades, then mocks the notion that real analysis could ever beat the market.

file: 2011/2011-08-05_conversation_worry_complints_creepy speech_massage therapist_rusty van.gif
title: Boss Tells Employee He's Creepy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Pete, I'm getting complaints that everything you say is creepy.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: You seem tense. I should give you the number of my massage therapist, "Rubbin, Robin."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're doing it again.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: I don't have an address because he works out of a rusty van.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells his employee Pete that coworkers have complained that everything he says is creepy. Pete responds by offering the Boss the number of his massage therapist, 'Rubbin, Robin.' When the Boss points out he's doing it again, Pete makes it worse by explaining the therapist works out of a rusty van.
punchline: Pete is unable to stop being creepy even while being told about it, and each attempt to help only makes his statements more unsettling.
summary: An employee confronted about his unsettling remarks immediately proves the point by recommending a shady, van-based masseur.

file: 2011/2011-07-06_competition (psychology)_ninja_incapable.gif
title: Dilbert's Ninja Tie Attack

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: This can't be done.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You aren't capable of doing it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm not saying I'm incapable! I could do this in my sleep!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because it's easy.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What's happening here?!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ninja.

situation: A coworker says a task cannot be done, and Dilbert calmly suggests the coworker simply isn't capable of it. Provoked, the coworker insists the task is easy enough to do in his sleep, which is exactly what Dilbert wanted him to say. Dilbert then seizes the coworker's necktie and yanks him around, announcing 'Ninja' as if it explains everything.
punchline: Dilbert uses reverse psychology to trick the coworker into admitting the task is easy, then tugs his tie and declares 'Ninja' as the absurd explanation for the sneak attack.
summary: By goading a colleague into boasting that a job is easy, Dilbert wins the argument and then reveals he has been quietly playing ninja.

file: 2011/2011-10-14_debates_discussion_researching every state_engineer_solemn duty_stamp out ignorance_real thing_googled it_engineering.gif
title: Engineer Fact-Checks Coworker With Google

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Please stop researching every statement I make.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As an engineer, it is my solemn duty to stamp out ignorance.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's not a real thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: See for yourself. I just googled it.

setting: Office, with Dilbert and Alice standing in conversation
situation: Alice asks Dilbert to stop looking up everything she says on his phone, but he says he can't because as an engineer he feels obliged to stamp out ignorance. When Alice protests that this duty isn't real, Dilbert holds up his phone as proof that he just googled it.
punchline: Dilbert uses a quick web search to 'prove' that his supposed engineer's duty to fight ignorance exists, which is exactly the compulsive fact-checking habit Alice is complaining about.
summary: A coworker begs a phone-wielding engineer to quit fact-checking her, and he answers by fact-checking the very excuse he gave for doing it.

file: 2011/2011-04-18_embarrassment_ignorance (knowledge)_low hanging fruit.gif
title: Low Hanging Fruit Hits Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Low hanging fruit!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ow!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: See?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wow.

situation: The Boss strolls along with a coffee mug and papers, thinking happily about 'low hanging fruit' as he spots an apple dangling from a tree branch. He walks right into the apple, hitting his nose, and falls over, spilling his coffee and papers. Dilbert and Wally watch from atop a cubicle wall, with Dilbert pointing out that this is why you should be wary of it.
punchline: The Boss's enthusiasm for the business cliché of low hanging fruit literally gets him hit in the face, showing that easy targets can hurt the person who rushes at them.
summary: A cheerful manager spots an easy target dangling from a branch and promptly smacks into it, to the dry amusement of two watching coworkers.

file: 2011/2011-08-16_meetings_questioning_best plan_ignorant nusinace_meeting_business.gif
title: Open for Comments, Nobody Dares

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is the best plan in the world, and anyone who disagrees is an ignorant nuisance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now I'll open it up for comments.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Anyone?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Anyone?

situation: The Boss presents a plan with a flowchart ending in a dollar sign, declaring it the best in the world and calling any critic an ignorant nuisance. He then invites comments, and the exterior-building shot shows only silence as he repeats 'Anyone?'. Wally, seated with Dilbert and Asok, thanks him for making the meeting shorter.
punchline: By insulting anyone who might disagree, the Boss ensures nobody speaks up, and Wally sarcastically thanks him for the shortened meeting that results from intimidated silence.
summary: A manager threatens his audience before asking for feedback and is then thanked for the quick, silent meeting his intimidation produced.

file: 2011/2011-09-09_keep brain out_laziness_long and complicated_technical recommendation_thinking_make decision.gif

transcript.text: No. It's too long and complicated.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do you plan to make a decision without reading it?

transcript.text: It's probably a good idea to keep your brain out of this.

situation: Dilbert asks the Boss whether he read his technical recommendation, and the Boss admits he didn't because it was too long and complicated. Dilbert sarcastically suggests keeping his brain out of it, and the Boss shushes him because his stomach is growling.
punchline: The Boss takes 'going with his gut' literally, treating a growling stomach as decision-making input, which underlines that his decisions involve no real thought.
summary: A manager skips reading a detailed proposal and proudly announces he will decide by instinct, then stops to listen to his rumbling stomach.

file: 2011/2011-03-28_dual core processors_brain_disconcerting_email answer.gif

transcript.text: How bad could it be?

situation: Dilbert, holding a sheet of paper, tells a woman seated across the desk that he will answer her question faster by using both halves of his brain like dual core processors. He warns her it may be disconcerting, and she asks how bad it could be. He then convulses and shrieks, and she hurriedly suggests he e-mail his answer instead.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to run his brain like a dual-core processor produces a painful-looking spasm, so the horrified listener would rather receive the answer by e-mail.
summary: A man's boast about parallel-processing his brain to answer faster ends in a violent fit that makes his questioner back away.

file: 2011/2011-04-20_time travel_elbonia_time_70 years future_great grandson_set thing_won't work out_cave_pool_monster_gun.gif

The call is answered by an Elbonian standing in a muddy cave seventy years in the future, who explains he is the great grandson of the person Dilbert wanted. A green alien with a gun then pops up and warns that the SETI search for extraterrestrial life will not turn out as hoped.
punchline: A routine call to Elbonia about time zones turns into a call to the far future, where an armed alien casually reveals that contacting extraterrestrials ends badly.
summary: A simple long-distance call reaches a descendant decades ahead, and a gun-toting alien ominously spoils humanity's hopes of finding extraterrestrial friends.

file: 2011/2011-06-06_review document_comments_research_postpone_plan a_science.gif
title: Boss Stalls With Fake Research

transcript.text: They know about plan "A."

Dilbert accurately predicts the Boss will read one paragraph and send him off to do pointless research to delay making a decision. In the last panel the Boss, holding a coffee mug, mutters to Catbert that 'they' know about plan 'A', implying Dilbert has seen through his stalling tactic.
punchline: The Boss treats Dilbert's accurate prediction of his procrastination routine as a leak of his secret strategy, as though stalling were a carefully guarded plan.
summary: An employee calls out his manager's habit of dodging decisions by assigning busywork, and the manager reacts as if his covert scheme has been exposed.

file: 2011/2011-05-28_business panics_worry_hackers_firewall_escape pod_firwall.gif

transcript.text: Hackers got through our firewall.
