situation: An employee tells the Boss that hackers breached the company firewall. The Boss panics and orders his escape pod launched, so his chair blasts through the roof, clutching a bag of money. In the last panel he tumbles upside down toward the ground, asking what a firewall is and who designed the pod.
punchline: The clueless Boss reacts to a cyberattack he doesn't understand by fleeing with his cash in a badly designed escape pod, and only afterward asks what a firewall even is.
summary: Upon hearing of a security breach, a clueless executive ejects himself through the ceiling in a flawed rocket chair and plummets earthward while wondering what went wrong.

file: 2011/2011-08-08_announcements_meetings_communicate_other departments_criticize_war on knowledge.gif
title: Communicating Less to Avoid Criticism

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to communicate less with other departments.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The more they know about us, the more they criticize what we do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is this part of your larger war on knowledge?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That was the last thing I'll ever tell you.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that the team should communicate less with other departments because more information leads to more criticism. Dilbert asks if this is part of the Boss's larger war on knowledge. The Boss responds that this was the last thing he will ever tell him.
punchline: The Boss immediately demonstrates his policy of withholding information by cutting off communication with Dilbert, proving Dilbert's point about his war on knowledge.
summary: A manager urges his team to share less with other departments to dodge scrutiny, then instantly practices what he preaches by refusing to tell his own employee anything more.

file: 2011/2011-08-14_business ethics_research facilities_work home_2 days_twice as prodcutive_elaborate science experiment_commute to sit in box_control group_frustration.gif
title: Work-From-Home Request Becomes Frustration Experiment

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I work at home for two days per week?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can be twice as productive, and happier at the same time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I probably shouldn't tell you this...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But you're part of an elaborate science experiment to see how much frustration it takes to kill employees.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why else would the company make you commute for two hours a day just to sit in a tiny box?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't feel bad; no one told me either.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I had to piece it together from the evidence. Now I do my part to keep the experiment moving along.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Other people work from home.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you referring to the control group?

setting: Office and the Boss's desk, with a brief shot of the office building exterior
situation: Dilbert asks the Boss if he can work from home two days a week, claiming he would be more productive and happier. The Boss confides that Dilbert is part of a secret experiment testing how much frustration it takes to kill employees, citing the long commute to a tiny cubicle as evidence. When Dilbert points out that others work from home, the Boss casually calls them the control group.
punchline: The Boss's deadpan explanation that employees who work from home are the 'control group' implies that the company deliberately torments the rest of the staff, and that he is happily helping the experiment along.
summary: A request for remote work is met with a manager's calm revelation that the office routine is a deliberate experiment in grinding workers down.

file: 2011/2011-04-15_big business_children drawing & painting_executives_chalky substance_layers of mangement_new layers_p_avp_director_doplphon_inanimate object.gif
title: Absurd New Management Layers Announced

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm adding a few layers of management below me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The new layers are VP, AVP, Director, Dolphin, Inanimate Object, and Chalky Substance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you have any issues, I encourage you to talk to the Chalky Substance.

setting: Conference room during a presentation with an org chart on a projection screen
situation: The Boss presents a slide showing a new org chart and announces he is adding several layers of management beneath him. The layers start with normal titles but then include a dolphin, an inanimate object and a chalky substance. He then tells the stunned audience, including Dilbert, to take any issues to the chalky substance.
punchline: By filling the new management layers with a dolphin, an object and chalk, the strip suggests that extra management layers add nothing and that the boss is making employees' complaints go nowhere.
summary: A boss unveils a bloated org chart whose lower tiers are absurdly staffed by non-people, then points staff to a powdery substance for their grievances.

file: 2011/2011-10-18_copyright & trademark_inventions_competitor suing_albanian court_design trademark_block manufacturing_shaped like rectangle_design shapes_irregular mole.gif
title: Competitor Trademarks the Rectangle

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: Our competitor is suing us in an Elbonian court for some sort of design trademark violation.

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: They're trying to block us from manufacturing anything shaped like a rectangle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What design shapes are available?

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: Only one, assuming "irregular mole" is a shape.

situation: A bald, bespectacled company lawyer holding a sheet of paper tells the seated Boss that a competitor is suing them in an Elbonian court over a design trademark. The competitor is trying to stop the company from making anything rectangular. The Boss asks which shapes are left, and the lawyer says there is only one.
punchline: With rectangles off limits, the only shape left is an "irregular mole", which is barely a shape at all, mocking absurdly broad design trademark claims.
summary: A lawyer explains that a rival's overreaching design trademark leaves the company almost no legal shapes to manufacture.

file: 2011/2011-03-03_managers & supervisors_mobile (cell) phones_app_awesome_don't fire me_business.gif
title: There's an App for Begging

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, there's an app for you.

transcript.speaker: Phone
transcript.text: Waa-waa! Don't fire me!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How awesome is that?

setting: Office desk, boss and Ted sitting across from each other
situation: The Boss sits across a desk from Ted, a small phone lying between them, and announces that there is an app for him. The phone plays a whiny recording of an employee pleading not to be fired. The Boss is delighted with the app while Ted, who is apparently being laid off, glares angrily.
punchline: The Boss is so pleased with a gadget that mocks begging employees that he is oblivious to how cruel it is to play it to Ted in the middle of firing him.
summary: A manager delights in a phone app that plays a pathetic pleading recording while the employee he is dismissing looks on furious.

file: 2011/2011-10-06_computers & peripherals_gadgets_hardware_robotic arms_hold coffee cups_industry changing products.gif
title: Replacing 99% of Engineers With Robot Arms

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: One percent of engineers create all of the industry-changing products.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I propose replacing the other 99% with robotic arms that hold coffee cups.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: You won't see any of the laggards in the 99% come up with great ideas like this one.

situation: An engineer presents a pie chart showing that only 1% of engineers create all the industry-changing products. He proposes replacing the other 99% with robotic arms that merely hold coffee cups. The Boss listens, and the engineer boasts that none of the 99% would ever come up with such a great idea.
punchline: The engineer's supposedly brilliant idea is absurd, so his boast unintentionally proves he belongs in the unproductive 99% he wants to replace.
summary: A presenter pitches swapping most of his colleagues for coffee-holding machines, unaware that the proposal itself shows why he is no genius.

file: 2011/2011-12-31_celebrations_new year's day_happy new year_oxytocin drug dealer_magical thinking_space time continuum.gif
title: Dilbert Rejects New Year Hug

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Happy New Year!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whoa! Settle down.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't celebrate the magical thinking that says one random point in the space-time continuum is somehow special.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: It's just a hug. You'll enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're like some sort of oxytocin drug dealer.

setting: A New Year's party with a crowd of silhouetted guests in the background
situation: At a New Year's party, a woman reaches out to hug Dilbert while wishing him a happy new year. Dilbert, holding a martini, holds up a hand to fend her off and lectures her on why he refuses to treat an arbitrary moment in time as special. When she insists it is only a hug, he accuses her of being an oxytocin dealer.
punchline: Dilbert's overly rational objection to holiday sentiment ends with him treating a friendly hug as if it were a drug pusher offering a hit of the bonding hormone oxytocin.
summary: A party guest offers a festive embrace, and a pedantic engineer turns down the affection by treating her like a hormone peddler.

file: 2011/2011-06-10_kindness_trick_credibility issue_suscpious_boss compliments_hostile response.gif
title: Boss's Compliment Provokes Alice's Rage

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm just stopping by to say you're doing a great job, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You never do that! It's a trick! Die, monster, die!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I might have a credibility issue.

situation: The Boss visits Alice's cubicle holding a coffee mug and offers her a sincere compliment. Alice, who has never received praise from him, assumes it is a trick and lashes out at him in anger. In the last panel the Boss stands by a desk where Ratbert sits and reflects on what just happened.
punchline: The Boss is so habitually unsupportive that a genuine compliment is treated as a threat, and he drily acknowledges he has damaged his own credibility.
summary: A manager's rare kind word is met with violent suspicion, leaving him to admit his reputation is the problem.

file: 2011/2011-11-20_crimes_gadgets_inventions_world class invenotr_invented prodcuts_key memeber_fired for stealing_stuff to steal_high five_hits boss.gif
title: Hired Inventor Is Really a Thief

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a world-class inventor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Meet Toby. When he worked for our competitor, he invented their coolest product.

transcript.speaker: Toby
transcript.text: I was just a member of the team.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A key member!

transcript.speaker: Toby
transcript.text: Until they fired me for stealing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You came to the right place.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We have tons of stuff to steal and no one ever gets caught!

transcript.speaker: Toby
transcript.text: Give me a high five with a boss head in the middle!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: SLAP!

transcript.speaker: Toby
transcript.text: That's the only thing I ever invented.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Have you seen our storage closet?

situation: The Boss proudly introduces Toby, a new hire billed as a world-class inventor who created a competitor's coolest product. Toby admits he was only a team member who got fired for stealing, and Wally cheerfully welcomes him because the company has plenty to steal. Toby then arranges a high five with the Boss's head in the middle, so they slap his head from both sides.
punchline: The new hire's only real invention is the 'boss head high five', exposing that the supposed genius inventor is just a thief who took credit for others' work, while Wally eagerly points him to the storage closet.
summary: A manager's celebrated new inventor turns out to be a fired thief whose one original creation is a prank at the manager's own expense.

file: 2011/2011-10-13_despair_meetings_six variables_4 imbeciles_brilliant engineer_complexity algorithm_rational deciosn_brilliant career.gif
title: Giving Up on Rational Decisions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, this next decision involves six variables, four imbeciles, and one brilliant engineer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to the Dogbert Complexity Algorithm, it is impossible to make a rational decision in this situation. All in favor of giving up?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I found out I'm a brilliant engineer.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, then an office
situation: Dilbert tells a meeting that the next decision involves six variables, four imbeciles and one brilliant engineer. He then cites the Dogbert Complexity Algorithm to argue that a rational decision is impossible and calls for a vote to give up, and the others raise their hands. In the last panel the Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells a small red creature that he has discovered he is the brilliant engineer.
punchline: Everyone in the meeting assumes the 'brilliant engineer' is someone else, and the Boss's cluelessly confident realisation that it must be him shows the self-flattering blindness of management.
summary: After a meeting votes to abandon a hopelessly muddled decision, the Boss happily announces that he has worked out which attendee is the genius.

file: 2011/2011-10-01_saving & investment_stock market_mba_losing money_money in gold_shiny portfolio_money.gif
title: MBA Loses, Boss Gets Lucky

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I have an MBA and yet I keep losing money in the stock market. How can this be?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I put all of my money in gold because it's shiny. My portfolio doubled last year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm thinking of getting an MBA. How long does it take? A week?

situation: A bald coworker with an MBA complains that he keeps losing money in the stock market. The Boss replies that he put everything in gold simply because it's shiny, and his portfolio doubled. The Boss then casually wonders whether an MBA takes only a week to earn.
punchline: The Boss's success came from a simplistic, lucky choice, which makes him dismiss the value of an MBA while underestimating how long a degree takes.
summary: A degree-holding investor struggles with losses while his clueless boss profits from a decision based purely on gold's shininess.

file: 2011/2011-01-01_new year resolutions_dvr_geeky science shows_snore_asthmatic cow_impose resolutions_habit chnagers_behavior requests.gif
title: Dogbert's New Year's Resolutions For Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I made a list of demands for your new year's resolutions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thou shalt not fill up the DVR with geeky science shows. . . . Thou shalt not snore like an asthmatic cow. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't know other people could impose resolutions on me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's a new thing.

situation: Dogbert stands on the bed beside a sleeping Dilbert and announces he has written a list of demands for Dilbert's New Year's resolutions. He reads out commandments such as no filling up the DVR with geeky science shows and no snoring like an asthmatic cow. Dilbert, now awake and sitting up in bed, says he didn't know other people could impose resolutions on him.
punchline: Dogbert casually claims that having other people dictate your New Year's resolutions is a brand-new custom, a way of getting Dilbert to comply by pretending the rule just changed.
summary: Dogbert wakes his owner with a self-serving list of lifestyle changes he insists Dilbert must adopt for the new year.

file: 2011/2011-02-17_office buildings_work ethic_new cubicles_death eater gray_soul sponge_absorb happiness_fear of the unknown.gif
title: Death Eater Gray Cubicle Fabric

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Office relocation

transcript.speaker: Facilities Manager
transcript.text: Your new cubicles will be a color called "Death Eater Gray."

transcript.speaker: Facilities Manager
transcript.text: The fabric is a soul sponge that will absorb your happiness if you stand near it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How'd the meeting go?

transcript.speaker: Facilities Manager
transcript.text: Well, you know, fear of the unknown.

setting: Conference room and the Boss's office
situation: A black-haired facilities manager presents the office relocation plan to employees, announcing that the new cubicles will be a gloomy color called Death Eater Gray. She warns that the fabric absorbs happiness, while a slide shows a worker slumped against the wall. Afterward she tells the Boss the meeting went badly, blaming the staff's reaction on fear of the unknown.
punchline: She presents openly horrifying news about the cubicles, then blames the employees' dismay on irrational fear of change rather than on the soul-sucking fabric she described.
summary: A relocation presenter describes dreary, happiness-draining cubicle fabric and then dismisses the staff's alarm as mere anxiety about change.

file: 2011/2011-11-13_engineers_inventions_bend light_around obkject_cloak of invisibility_make billions_selling to military_tricked_ploy_sneaky_empty looking chair.gif
title: Invisibility Cloak Excuse to Skip Work

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I discovered a way to bend light around an object to form a cloak of invisibility.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: We'll make billions selling it to the military.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I'll be testing it over the next several months.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: You'll know it's working if you never see me in the office.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: During that time, don't sit in any empty-looking chairs unless you first shout my name and clap.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: What's that over there?!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What? I don't see anything.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: How do you like it so far?

situation: An engineer tells his colleagues in a meeting that he has invented an invisibility cloak and will be testing it for months, so they should not expect to see him in the office. He distracts the Boss by pointing at something, then slips away unnoticed. At the end he is revealed sitting in a chair, asking how they like the invisibility so far.
punchline: The engineer never invented anything; he simply sneaked out to dodge work and then returned to the meeting and boasted about how well his made-up invisibility worked, since nobody noticed he was there.
summary: A coworker spins a tall tale about an invisibility cloak to justify months of absence, then proves it by being overlooked in plain sight.

file: 2011/2011-01-30_laziness_lying_work ethic_wasting time options_two options_truth or lie_pin blame_faster to hear lie_document is perfect_assign balme_later say misinterpreted.gif
title: Dilbert Offers Ruth Two Options

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: Dilbert, your boss asked me to get your input on this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Absolutely, Ruth.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We have two options for wasting our time here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Option one: I could tell you all of the things you should change, and you could ignore me as usual.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Option two: I could lie, and tell you that everything is perfect.

transcript.speaker: Ruth
transcript.text: I prefer the lie. That way I can pin some blame on you if things go bad.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Excellent choice. It's faster, and I can later say I was misinterpreted.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay then, I declare that your document is perfect, under a certain set of assumptions that I won't list.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you help Ruth?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll say yes, but it's sort of a gray area.

setting: Office, in a hallway or cubicle area and then at Dilbert's desk
situation: Ruth asks Dilbert to review her document because the boss told her to get his input. Dilbert offers two options: give honest feedback she will ignore, or lie and say it's perfect. Ruth picks the lie so she can blame him later, and Dilbert happily agrees while adding hedges to protect himself.
punchline: Both Dilbert and Ruth knowingly choose a fake review that lets each of them dodge responsibility, so when the boss asks if Dilbert helped, he can only call it a gray area.
summary: Two coworkers agree to swap a meaningless endorsement for mutual deniability rather than waste time on a real review.

file: 2011/2011-06-27_direction_managers_increase clairty_whining.gif
title: Doubling Managers to Clarify Direction

transcript.speaker: Bald Executive
transcript.text: Employees keep whining that we don't have a clear direction.

transcript.speaker: Bald Executive
transcript.text: So I've doubled the number of managers in each group to increase the clarity.

transcript.speaker: Executive with Horned Hair
transcript.text: I thought we were doubling the direction.

transcript.speaker: Executive with Curly Hair
transcript.text: No, we're doubling the clarity.

situation: At a meeting table, a bald executive explains that because employees complain about unclear direction, he has doubled the number of managers in each group to boost clarity. Two other executives reveal they are confused about what is actually being doubled, direction or clarity.
punchline: Adding more managers does nothing to provide clear direction, and the executives themselves are so confused about the plan that they cannot agree on what is being doubled.
summary: Leadership answers staff complaints about murky goals by piling on extra managers, and the leaders end up just as muddled as everyone else.

file: 2011/2011-03-11_competition (psychology)_competitors_exercise & fitness_jumping jacks_meetings_meetngs_pelt with office supplies.gif
title: Jumping Jacks and Flying Staplers

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your competitors are faster because they have meetings where everyone has to stand up.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll top that by having meetings where everyone does jumping jacks while I pelt them with office supplies.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's working!

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the group that competitors are faster because they hold stand-up meetings. He proposes an even more extreme version: meetings with jumping jacks while he throws office supplies at everyone. In the last panel the attendees are flailing and dodging staplers and tape dispensers while Dogbert declares success.
punchline: Dogbert's absurd escalation of the stand-up meeting trend causes chaos and pain, yet he cheerfully declares that it is working because everyone is moving faster.
summary: A consultant dog tries to outdo rival firms' stand-up meetings by forcing colleagues to exercise while being bombarded with stationery.

file: 2011/2011-01-02_annoyance_eating & drinking_lunchtime_trivial decions_lose faith_humanity_no hope_vending machine_fatasize_competent coworkers.gif
title: Dilbert Skips Lunch, Fantasizes Competence

transcript.speaker: Co-worker
transcript.text: Dilbert, would you like to join us for lunch?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where are you going?

transcript.speaker: Co-worker
transcript.text: We haven't decided.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In that case, no.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't stand watching a small group of people trying to make a trivial decision.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It makes me lose all faith in humanity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Food doesn't taste as good when you have no hope.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll just get something from the vending machine and fantasize that my co-workers are competent.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's see... What goes well with an unrealistic worldview?

setting: Office cubicle and break area; the opening banner shows a presentation with a Dilbert logo slide
situation: A co-worker invites Dilbert to lunch but admits the group hasn't decided where to go. Dilbert refuses, explaining that watching a small group struggle with a trivial decision destroys his faith in humanity. He ends up at the vending machine, choosing a snack to go with his fantasy that his co-workers are competent.
punchline: Dilbert is so disillusioned by his co-workers' indecision that he would rather eat vending machine food alone while pretending they are competent, and he wonders what snack pairs with an unrealistic worldview.
summary: Dilbert turns down a group lunch because their dithering over where to eat convinces him that humanity is hopeless.

file: 2011/2011-05-03_embarrassment_internet & world wide web_website_moradc_nicknames_client satisfactions surveys_group monitors_technology.gif
title: IS Monitors Ted's Browsing History

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Based on that information, we came up with a list of nicknames for you.

situation: Mordac, the head of Information Services, stands over Ted at his computer and tells him that the I.S. group tracks every website he visits. He hands Ted a list of nicknames the group made up from Ted's browsing history. Ted reads it, aghast, as Mordac remarks on how much more enjoyable his job has become.
punchline: Mordac's job became more fun once he no longer had to care about customer satisfaction, so he can freely mock employees using their private browsing data.
summary: A smug IT enforcer gleefully hands an employee a list of insulting nicknames derived from his web history, noting that ignoring customer feedback made the job a pleasure.

file: 2011/2011-07-12_gadgets_mobile (cell) phones_fascinating_twitter_keep boss happy.gif
title: Wally Flatters Boss on Twitter

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You fascinate me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think I speak for all of your followers on Twitter when I say we want more, more, more.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't use Twitter.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I just used it to keep my boss busy.

situation: Wally, holding coffee mugs, lavishes praise on the Boss, claiming to speak for his many Twitter followers and begging for more. Dilbert, standing beside him, points out that Wally doesn't even use Twitter. Wally admits the flattery was just a ploy to keep his boss occupied.
punchline: Wally's fake enthusiasm for the Boss's tweets was a cynical trick to encourage him to spend his time tweeting instead of bothering employees.
summary: A feigned fan of his boss's social media posts turns out to be encouraging the habit purely so the boss stays distracted.

file: 2011/2011-06-23_crimes_internet & world wide web_black hat_websites ranking_search engine_unethical_near certainty_loserish_talking.gif
title: Black Hat SEO Sarcasm Backfires

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to use "black hat" methods to raise our website's ranking on search engines.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What do you like best about that idea — the fact that it's unethical or the near certainty of getting caught?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's sort of a loserish thing to say.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Talking doesn't work for people like me.

setting: The Boss's office, across a desk
situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to use unethical "black hat" tactics to push the company website up the search rankings. Dilbert sarcastically asks whether the boss prefers the unethical part or the near-certain chance of being caught. The Boss dismisses this as a loserish thing to say, and Dilbert resignedly notes that talking never works on people like his boss.
punchline: Dilbert's reasonable objection is brushed off as "loserish," showing that sound arguments are useless against a boss who has already made up his mind.
summary: A manager demands shady search-ranking tricks, and his employee's sharp rebuttal is waved away as weakness, proving that reasoning cannot get through to him.

file: 2011/2011-07-25_fraternization_friendship_laziness_wing man_for laziness_productivity retardant_high priority_relationships.gif

Wally gets up and leaves with his coffee mug. Alice asks if he has a wingman for laziness, and Wally says he thinks of Asok as a productivity retardant.
punchline: Wally has recruited Asok to invent vague, important-sounding excuses that rescue him from work, treating Asok as a tool that slows down productivity.
summary: A coworker's convenient interruption rescues Wally from a task, revealing he has a helper who helps him dodge work.

file: 2011/2011-10-16_choosing_meetings_creative ideas_next prodcut_ignorance on public disply_cost money_increase risk_evaluate each idea_disdain_good idea.gif
title: Boss Demands Ideas, Punishes Everyone

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need creative ideas for our next product.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But not from you. Your ideas are awful.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And don't suggest something that is already being done. That just puts your ignorance on public display.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't want to hear any ideas that cost money or increase risk.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As usual, I'll evaluate each idea by repeating it slowly while I look at you with disdain.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you come up with a good idea, I'll let you take on the project in addition to your existing work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who wants to go first?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How did I hire so many people who have no ideas?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Probably bad luck.

setting: Conference room and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss calls a meeting asking for creative product ideas, then piles on restrictions: no ideas from certain people, nothing already being done, nothing that costs money or adds risk. He adds that he will mock each idea and reward good ones with extra work. When nobody volunteers, he wonders why his staff has no ideas, and Catbert suggests it was bad luck.
punchline: The Boss has made generating ideas so punishing and constrained that no one speaks up, yet he blames bad hiring luck instead of his own behavior.
summary: A manager sabotages his own brainstorming session with insults, impossible rules and extra workload as a reward, then puzzles over the silence.

file: 2011/2011-06-24_computers & peripherals_internet & world wide web_fake links_boost search rank_dung for barins_shut your pie hole.gif
title: Google Punishes Fake Link Scheme

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Google found out that we used fake links to boost our search rank.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now our website only shows up when someone enters the search string "dung for brains."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They won't get away with this!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shut your pie hole.

situation: Dilbert reports to the seated Boss that Google caught the company using fake links to inflate its search ranking. As a penalty, the company website now appears only for the search phrase "dung for brains." The Boss angrily vows that Google won't get away with it, and Dilbert tells him to be quiet.
punchline: The search engine's penalty insults the company in a way that fits its management, and the Boss reacts with indignation at being punished for his own cheating, prompting Dilbert's blunt retort.
summary: After the company gets caught gaming its search ranking, its site is demoted to appearing only for an insulting phrase, and the Boss indignantly protests.

file: 2011/2011-11-03_depression (mental state)_despair_ugly partment_two ugly roomates_ugly bus_ugly building_ugly cubicle_eat lunch.gif
title: Asok's Ugly Life Lunch Confession

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I live in an ugly apartment with two ugly roommates.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Each workday I take an ugly bus to an ugly building and spend the entire day in my ugly cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At least you get to eat lunch with us.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I've said too much.

setting: Office break room or lunch table
situation: Asok, sitting at a lunch table with Dilbert and Wally, laments that his home life, commute and workplace are all ugly. A establishing shot of a drab office building illustrates his gloomy routine. Dilbert tries to cheer him up by pointing out he gets to eat lunch with them, and Asok realizes he has insulted his companions.
punchline: Asok's list of ugly things accidentally includes his lunch companions, since Dilbert's attempt at consolation implies they are just another ugly part of his day, prompting Asok to realize he has said too much.
summary: A young intern gloomily describes his drab daily existence until a coworker's attempt to console him exposes that he considers his lunch mates part of the ugliness.

file: 2011/2011-08-27_fighting_trees_ambassador of trees_crimes against wood_excessive printing_copying_biting_bark is worse.gif
title: Ambassador of Trees Accuses Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Tree
transcript.text: I am the Ambassador of Trees.

transcript.speaker: Tree
transcript.text: You are accused of crimes against wood for your excessive printing and copying.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And then he started biting me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: His bark is worse.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, with a tree beside his desk, then outside an office building
situation: A tree speaking as the Ambassador of Trees confronts Dilbert at his desk and accuses him of crimes against wood for printing and copying too much paper. In the last panel Dilbert, bandaged and bruised, tells Dogbert the tree started biting him.
punchline: Dogbert answers with the pun that the tree's bark is worse than his bite, turning Dilbert's injuries into a dog-and-tree joke.
summary: A self-appointed tree diplomat punishes an office worker for wasting paper, leaving him bandaged and the target of a bark-and-bite pun.

file: 2011/2011-11-18_anxiety_monsters_supernatural beings_beware of bogeyman_bad parenting_one over par_everyhole.gif
title: The Bogeyman Is a Golf Bore

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My mother always told me to beware the bogeyman.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That was bad parenting. There's no such thing as the bogeyman.

transcript.speaker: Golfer
transcript.text: I was one over par on every hole. Let me tell you all about it.

setting: Office break room or lunch table, then Asok's cubicle
situation: At a lunch table, Asok says his mother warned him about the bogeyman, and Dilbert dismisses it as bad parenting since the bogeyman doesn't exist. In the last panel a colleague in golf attire holding a club appears at Asok's desk, announcing he was one over par on every hole and will describe each one. Asok looks horrified.
punchline: The bogeyman is a pun on golf's 'bogey' (one over par): the real bogeyman is the coworker who bores you with a hole-by-hole account of his golf game.
summary: A dismissed childhood monster turns out to be real in the form of a golfing colleague eager to recount his entire round.

file: 2011/2011-12-28_anger_annoyance_online class_improve charisma_stupid fake charisma_weird.gif
title: Charisma Class Versus Ignoring Class

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't let anyone disturb me. I'll be taking an online class to improve my charisma.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: While you're doing that, I'll be taking an online class to learn how to ignore your stupid, fake charisma.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Bring it on!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, this got weird.

situation: The Boss stands by Alice's cubicle holding a coffee mug and tells her not to disturb him while he takes an online class to improve his charisma. Alice retorts that she will take her own online class to learn to ignore his fake charisma. She then shakes her fist and shouts for him to bring it on, leaving the Boss bewildered.
punchline: Alice turns the Boss's self-improvement plan into a petty rivalry by training specifically to resist his charisma, which is so absurd that even the Boss finds it weird.
summary: A boss announces a charisma course and his coworker responds by signing up for a class to tune him out, escalating into a bizarre training duel.

file: 2011/2011-03-16_exercise & fitness_ignorance (knowledge)_managers & supervisors_brain work better_the ighties_debunks science_business.gif
title: Exercise Hasn't Happened Since 1980s

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Scientists say that exercise makes your brain work better.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I haven't exercised since the eighties.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That pretty much debunks science.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It had a good run.

setting: Office hallway near a cubicle wall
situation: Alice, holding a folder, tells the Boss that scientists say exercise improves brain function. The Boss, holding a coffee mug, says he hasn't exercised since the eighties and concludes that this disproves science. Alice dryly replies that science had a good run.
punchline: The Boss treats his own sedentary, poorly functioning brain as proof that science is wrong, and Alice sarcastically writes off science's reputation in response.
summary: A manager takes his own lack of exercise and dull thinking as evidence against a scientific claim, and a coworker mockingly eulogizes science.

file: 2011/2011-06-29_gadgets_mobile (cell) phones_new phone_recommendations_dropped calls_poor battery life_hate the messenger_build phones.gif
title: Pick Your Phone Frustration

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need a new phone. Which one do you recommend?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you want to be angry about your dropped calls or angry about your poor battery life?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Don't hate the messenger.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: People similar to you build phones.

situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, asks Alice which new phone she would recommend. Alice replies that every phone forces a choice between dropped calls and poor battery life. When he reacts, she tells him not to blame her, since people like him build the phones, and she holds up a bent, broken-looking phone.
punchline: All phones are flawed, and Alice sarcastically blames the defects on engineers like Dilbert, who build the phones.
summary: Asked for a phone recommendation, Alice says every option is bad in some way and pins the blame on engineers like her coworker.

file: 2011/2011-09-27_internet & world wide web_office equipment_public speaking_ordinary powerpoint_portal_another dimension_fantasy_reality_trade places_slides.gif
title: Portal to Another Dimension Slide

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This might look like an ordinary PowerPoint slide.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But it is actually a portal to another dimension in which fantasy and reality have traded places.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop playing with my slides.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Beware the horned beast that crosses over.

situation: Dilbert stands beside a projected slide showing an upward-curving revenue chart and dramatically describes it as a portal to another dimension. In the last panel the Boss, whose pointy hair resembles horns, tells him to stop playing with the slides. Dilbert warns of a horned beast that crosses over, apparently referring to the Boss.
punchline: Dilbert's warning about a 'horned beast' is a veiled jab at the Boss, whose pointy hair looks like horns, and the rosy revenue chart is implied to be pure fantasy.
summary: Dilbert hams up a revenue chart as a gateway to a topsy-turvy realm, then cheekily labels his horn-haired boss the monster that emerges from it.

file: 2011/2011-05-13_administrative agencies_project timeline_waste one week_set up meeting_available in a week.gif
title: Timeline Built on Wasted Weeks

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I estimated the project timeline by assuming that everyone involved will waste one week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's a stupid way to do a timeline. Set up a meeting and I'll show you how it's supposed to be done.

transcript.speaker: Administrative Assistant
transcript.text: He's available in a week.

setting: Boss's office and an assistant's desk outside it
situation: Dilbert hands the Boss a project timeline he built by assuming everyone involved will waste a week. The Boss calls this a stupid method and tells Dilbert to set up a meeting so he can demonstrate the proper way. Dilbert goes to the Boss's assistant, who says the Boss is only available in a week.
punchline: The Boss's own scheduling delay wastes exactly one week, proving Dilbert's supposedly stupid estimation method was accurate.
summary: A boss mocks an employee's pessimistic schedule estimate, then immediately causes the very week-long delay it predicted.

file: 2011/2011-10-05_cruelty_employees_employee of month_october 1929_room to grow_past date_past month_business.gif
title: Employee of the Month: October 1929

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Congratulations, Asok. I'm naming you Employee of the Month.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your month is October 1929.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Room to grow.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells Asok at his desk that he is being named Employee of the Month. He then reveals the month assigned to Asok is October 1929, the month of the Wall Street stock market crash. He adds that there is 'room to grow', leaving Asok looking stunned and unhappy.
punchline: The Boss turns the honor into an insult by assigning Asok the month of the 1929 stock market crash, then sarcastically frames the awful market-low as 'room to grow'.
summary: A manager hands out a recognition award tied to the worst possible historical month and spins the disaster as an opportunity.

file: 2011/2011-05-17_test phase_meeting_desk_production phase_being smart_good feeling_confident_business.gif
title: Smart People Lack Confidence

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You scheduled the end of the test phase after the start of the production phase.

transcript.speaker: Blond Coworker
transcript.text: We're feeling confident.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's too bad that being smart doesn't come with some sort of good feeling like that.

setting: Conference room table during a project meeting
situation: Dilbert points out to two coworkers that their project schedule has testing ending after production has already begun. One coworker replies cheerfully that they feel confident. Dilbert responds that intelligence unfortunately doesn't bring the same pleasant feeling.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically observes that the clueless feel confident while the smart, who can see the problems, are left worrying.
summary: A project plan with testing scheduled to finish after launch doesn't dent a colleague's good mood, prompting a wry remark about the happiness of the uninformed.

file: 2011/2011-03-08_center balanced_considered an earring_died getting haircut_jewelry_laziness_normal problems_sleeping in chair.gif
title: Earring Too Risky for Napper

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I considered getting an earring to make myself more fascinating.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But I spend a lot of time sleeping in my chair, so I need my head to be center balanced.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't have normal problems.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I almost died getting my hair cut.

situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, tells Dilbert he thought about getting an earring to seem more interesting. He rejects the idea because he sleeps in his chair at work and needs his head to stay balanced. Dilbert remarks that Wally's problems aren't normal, and Wally replies that a haircut nearly killed him.
punchline: Wally's reasons for avoiding a simple earring are absurd, and he caps it off by claiming that even a routine haircut was a near-death experience, showing how exaggerated his bizarre worldview is.
summary: A habitually dozing coworker explains that jewelry would throw off his napping posture, then claims even a trim nearly finished him off.

file: 2011/2011-01-06_engineers_laziness_managers & supervisors_business.gif
title: Ethical Duty to Do Nothing

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There were eleven ways to interpret the vague assignment you gave me by voicemail.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Given the risks of choosing wrong, and my engineering oath to do no harm, it was my ethical duty to do nothing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You could have asked for clarification.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sounds risky.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: At a meeting, Wally explains to his boss that he did nothing on a vague voicemail assignment because there were eleven possible interpretations. He claims his engineering oath to do no harm made inaction his ethical duty. When the boss suggests asking for clarification, Wally dismisses that as risky too, while Dilbert sits silently beside him.
punchline: Wally dresses up his laziness as professional ethics, and even the simple, obvious fix of asking a question is declared too risky to attempt.
summary: A slacker engineer justifies ignoring an unclear task by citing a noble-sounding oath, then rejects the easy fix of asking questions.

file: 2011/2011-06-13_depression (mental state)_despair_unfulfilled_totally worthless_coffee maker_breakroom_distract.gif
title: Reassurance That Insults Instead

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I am unfulfilled at my job. When does that feeling go away?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Asok, you shouldn't think you're totally worthless.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Um... I didn't say I was worthless.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm trying to take your mind off of the other thing.

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker
situation: Asok, holding a mug, tells Dilbert he feels unfulfilled at his job and asks when the feeling goes away. Dilbert, also holding coffee, responds by telling him not to think he is totally worthless. Asok points out he never said that, and Dilbert explains he is trying to distract him from the 'other thing'.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt at comfort backfires by introducing a new insult, and he admits it is meant as a distraction from the unfulfilled feeling, implying that being worthless is the lesser worry.
summary: A young employee seeks advice about job dissatisfaction and gets a clumsy pep talk that plants an even worse thought in his head.

file: 2011/2011-03-01_business ethics_environmental issues_managers & supervisors_government nagging_rid of waste_motivational paper weight_nice going_avoid licking_business.gif
title: Radioactive Waste Becomes Motivational Paperweights

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The government is nagging us to get rid of our dangerous radioactive waste.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: On a totally different topic, I'm giving each of you a motivational paperweight that says, "Nice going."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try to avoid licking them.

situation: The Boss stands beside a projected image of a glowing pile and tells staff the government wants the company to dispose of its dangerous radioactive waste. He then claims to change the subject and hands out motivational paperweights to the team. Dilbert and Alice sit at the table, wary, as he warns them not to lick the gifts.
punchline: The paperweights are obviously made from the company's radioactive waste, so the Boss is dodging disposal rules by disguising the waste as employee gifts.
summary: A manager sidesteps hazardous waste regulations by secretly repurposing the glowing material as free desk trinkets for his employees.

file: 2011/2011-04-12_computers & peripherals_fraternization_friends with ghots_ghandi_ghost personal page_ghosts_heaven_internet & world wide web_llincoln_satellite pictures_social media_social network_technology.gif
title: Social Network for Ghosts

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our new product will be a social network for people who want to be friends with ghosts.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll post satellite pictures on each ghost's personal page and say the photos were taken from heaven.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Abraham Lincoln posted new pictures.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'm chatting with Gandhi!

setting: Conference room presentation, then a restaurant table
situation: Dogbert stands on a stool pitching a startup idea: a social network for befriending ghosts, faked with satellite photos said to come from heaven. Dilbert and a coworker watch. Later, a couple at a restaurant table ignore each other and stare at their phones, excitedly using the ghost network.
punchline: The scheme is an obvious fake, yet people eagerly buy in, and the couple's absorption in chatting with dead celebrities mocks how social media pulls people away from the real person across the table.
summary: Dogbert pitches a fabricated afterlife social network, and soon a dining couple ignores each other to chat with historical ghosts on their phones.

file: 2011/2011-08-17_mathematics_questioning_second option_feels right_ignore data_intuition_slippery slope_witch craft.gif
title: Intuition Over Data Leads to Witchcraft

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The second option feels right. Let's go with that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should we always ignore what the data says, or is this more of a one-time thing?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's called intuition.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a slippery slope to witchcraft.

setting: The Boss's office, across his desk
situation: The Boss reads from a paper and announces he is choosing the second option because it feels right. Dilbert asks whether ignoring the data is a standing policy or a one-off. The Boss defends his decision as intuition, and Dilbert warns it leads toward witchcraft.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically equates gut-feeling decision making with witchcraft, mocking a boss who disregards evidence.
summary: A manager picks an option on a hunch, and his employee sarcastically questions whether abandoning data is the new normal.

file: 2011/2011-10-03_couples_dating_play games_guess the lie_say 2 things_dating games_obvious things_relationships.gif
title: Two Truths and a Lie, Dilbert Style

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Let's play a game. We each say two things about ourselves and the other has to guess which one is a lie.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I love to play games like that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My second thing is that I eat food.

setting: A social gathering or party where both hold cocktail glasses
situation: At a party, a woman proposes a game where each person states two facts about themselves and the other guesses which is a lie. Dilbert gushes that he loves such games, then offers 'I eat food' as his second statement, revealing his first statement was the lie. The woman looks unimpressed.
punchline: Dilbert's second statement is so blatantly true that it exposes his first claim, loving games like this, as the lie, showing he's too socially awkward to hide it.
summary: A date's icebreaker backfires when a nerdy guy accidentally gives away his fib by pairing it with an absurdly obvious truth.

file: 2011/2011-10-15_cruelty_frustration_surrogate crier_worst meeting_frustrated_streotype.gif
title: Alice's Surrogate Crier Asok

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm so frustrated that I want to cry, but I refuse to fall into the stereotype.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Asok, I'm making you my surrogate crier. This might hurt a little.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Worst meeting ever.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought you did a good job on the high notes.

setting: Conference room, then an office hallway
situation: During a meeting, Alice says she is so frustrated she wants to cry but won't fall into the stereotype of a crying woman. She grabs Asok by the tie and announces he will cry in her place, warning it might hurt. Afterward Asok, disheveled, calls it the worst meeting ever, and Dilbert compliments his high notes.
punchline: Alice physically hurts Asok to make him cry for her, and Dilbert deadpans praise for the pitch of Asok's screaming or crying.
summary: Unwilling to cry in front of colleagues, an angry coworker forces a junior employee to weep on her behalf, and the aftermath is met with a backhanded compliment.

file: 2011/2011-01-14_annoyance_critics_idea tried_failed misarably_skilled at implementing_evaluating_insulting.gif
title: Insulting Himself Through Skilled Critics

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your idea has already been tried by others and it failed miserably.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Were those others as skilled at implementing ideas as you are at evaluating them?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Of course they were!

transcript.speaker: Pointy-haired Boss
transcript.text: Can you tell him to stop insulting himself?

situation: At a meeting, a coworker dismisses Dilbert's idea because others already tried it and failed. Dilbert sarcastically asks whether those others were as skilled at implementing ideas as the coworker is at evaluating them. The coworker proudly answers that of course they were, and a third attendee asks Dilbert to stop insulting himself.
punchline: The coworker misses Dilbert's sarcasm and insists the failed implementers were highly skilled, which unwittingly means his own evaluation skills are poor, so he ends up being the one who is insulted.
summary: A sarcastic jab about skill levels backfires comically when the target takes it as a compliment and agrees emphatically.

file: 2011/2011-11-26_deception_office workers_planning_assignments_entre schedule_next assignment.gif
title: Replanning Never Ends, Work Never Starts

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I spent all of last week planning how to get everything done this week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Add one more thing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Okay, but I'll need to replan my entire schedule.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How long will that take?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Until you give me the next assignment.

setting: Boss's office, with the exterior of the office building in the last panel
situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells the Boss he spent all of last week planning how to finish this week's work. The Boss hands him one more task, and Wally says he must replan his whole schedule. When the Boss asks how long that will take, Wally says it will last until the next assignment arrives.
punchline: Wally has turned planning into a never-ending loop, so every new assignment triggers more replanning and he never has to actually do any work.
summary: A slacking employee uses endless schedule planning as a way to avoid ever starting his actual tasks.

file: 2011/2011-09-11_employees_unemployed_job performance_fire someone_cubicle_fired_wake up call_greatness_business.gif
title: Praise Means Someone Else Gets Fired

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, your job performance is terrific.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaa!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's code for "I'm going to fire someone else and make you do two jobs."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, but it's still better to be you than the guy I'm going to fire.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We don't know that!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This might be the wake-up call that spurs him on to greatness while I work myself to death in this cubicle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's no way to please some people.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, you're fired.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Yes!

setting: The Boss's office and an office cubicle
situation: The Boss compliments Dilbert's job performance, and Dilbert recognizes it as a sign that someone else will be fired and he will have to do two jobs. The Boss says it is still better to be Dilbert, but Dilbert argues the fired person might be better off. The Boss then fires Ted, who cheers.
punchline: Dilbert argues that being fired might be a blessing compared with overwork, and Ted proves him right by celebrating his firing.
summary: A manager's sudden praise warns of impending layoffs, and the employee who gets let go turns out to be delighted.

file: 2011/2011-12-19_big business_inventions_google_develop ideas_60 hours_per week_math_education.gif
title: Google's 20% Time Math

transcript.speaker: Google Employee
transcript.text: At Google, we're encouraged to spend 20% of our time developing our own ideas.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How many hours per week do you work?

transcript.speaker: Google Employee
transcript.text: About sixty.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: It sounds better when you don't do the math.

situation: A Google employee tells Dilbert and another coworker that Google encourages staff to spend 20% of their time on their own ideas. Dilbert asks how many hours a week he works, and the answer is about sixty. The bald coworker observes that the perk only sounds good if you skip the arithmetic.
punchline: Twenty percent of a sixty-hour week is twelve hours, which is barely above a normal week's worth of hours already, so the generous-sounding perk is really just unpaid overtime in disguise.
summary: A tech worker brags about a free-time perk until a quick question about his long hours exposes it as a sham.

file: 2011/2011-03-09_avarice_managers & supervisors_wages_open minded_worst idea_hostory_not give raise_business_money.gif
title: Open-Minded About Not Getting Raise

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need you to be open-minded about this idea.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, really?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's the sort of thing people say before they describe the worst idea in the history of the world.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My idea is to NOT give me a raise.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm hating you a little extra.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss to be open-minded about an idea, and the boss warns that this phrase usually precedes a terrible proposal. Dilbert then reveals his idea is that the boss should not give him a raise. The boss, apparently expecting something else or resenting the absurdity, says he hates Dilbert a little extra.
punchline: Dilbert's 'worst idea in the world' is to deny himself a raise, and the boss, who would presumably benefit financially, responds with irrational annoyance instead of gratitude.
summary: An employee proposes the unthinkable, that he be denied a pay increase, and his manager reacts with extra contempt rather than relief.

file: 2011/2011-12-16_gadgets_phone heard_phone scheduled meeting_schedule a meeting._secretaries (office)_digital world_replaces humans.gif
title: Phone Replaces Assistant, Awkward Silence

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Schedule a meeting with Dilbert and Alice for next Tuesday at ten.

transcript.speaker: Assistant
transcript.text: Done.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Never mind. My phone took care of it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Awkward.

situation: The Boss tells his assistant to schedule a meeting, and the assistant promptly says it's done. The Boss then looks at his phone and says it already handled the scheduling, so the request was unnecessary. He realizes the assistant has just been made redundant and comments on how awkward that is.
punchline: The Boss casually reveals that his phone has made his human assistant obsolete, and then acknowledges the awkwardness of saying so right in front of her.
summary: A manager's smartphone books a meeting before his assistant can, leaving both of them in an uncomfortable moment about who is really needed.

file: 2011/2011-10-17_writing_writing materials_five technology plan_plan for ceo_pie chart.gif
title: Five-Year Plan Is Pure Fantasy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to put together a five-year technology plan for our CEO.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about "Tomorrow will be the same as today, and next year will be all flying cars and whatnot."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Word it up and put a bow on it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll add a pie chart for the sizzle.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to put together a five-year technology plan for the CEO. Dilbert proposes a vague, absurd plan that says nothing will change soon and then everything will be flying cars. The Boss happily approves it and asks for polish, and Dilbert offers to add a pie chart.
punchline: Technology roadmaps are essentially made-up guesses, and the boss only cares that they look polished and impressive with fancy wording and a pie chart, not that they have any substance.
summary: Asked for a long-range technology plan, an employee offers a laughably vague prediction and the manager just wants it dressed up with some presentation flair.

file: 2011/2011-12-03_tv news_financial report_tv show_cable news show_dogbert_gold fillings_remove your own.gif
title: Dogbert's Doomsday Financial Pundit Show

transcript.speaker: TV Host
transcript.text: My next guest on Money-N-Stuff is Dogbert the Doomsday Pundit.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: We're doomed for sure

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Goldman Sachs is forming a hobo army to take over the world. Start hoarding anything with a pointy end.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert: Hobo army coming

transcript.speaker: TV Host
transcript.text: After the break, learn how to remove your own gold fillings.

situation: A financial news anchor introduces Dogbert as a doomsday pundit on her show Money-N-Stuff. Dogbert appears on screen with a falling Dow ticker and warns that Goldman Sachs is forming a hobo army, advising viewers to hoard pointy objects. The host then teases the next segment on removing your own gold fillings.
punchline: Financial news thrives on fear-mongering, and the host cheerfully follows Dogbert's absurd conspiracy panic with a segment encouraging viewers to pull their own gold fillings for cash.
summary: A business news program gives airtime to an outlandish doom-prophesying dog, then promotes a tip that sounds like peak crisis desperation.

file: 2011/2011-02-01_honesty_writing_write_birds walk keyboard_opinion_technical part_blabbing the ethernet.gif
title: Blobbing on the Ethernet

transcript.speaker: Woman with curly hair
transcript.text: Is this how you really write, or did birds walk on your keyboard?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I only need your opinion on the technical part of it.

transcript.speaker: Woman with curly hair
transcript.text: Okay, let's assume that your readers will know what you mean by "blobbing on the Ethernet."

situation: The Boss shows a coworker something he has written and asks for her feedback. She mocks the writing, asking if birds walked on his keyboard. He says he only wants her technical opinion, so she grudgingly reads on and questions his phrase "blobbing on the Ethernet."
punchline: The Boss's writing is so nonsensical that his coworker can only assess the technical part by pretending readers will somehow understand the meaningless phrase "blobbing on the Ethernet."
summary: A manager asks a colleague to proofread the technical side of his writing, but his prose is so garbled she can barely take it seriously.

file: 2011/2011-12-09_anger_annoyance_wrong side of bed_bat like_wrapped around body_funnier in head.gif
title: Bat Joke Falls Flat

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I woke up on the wrong side of the bed this morning.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Were you hanging from the bottom with your wings wrapped around your body?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That was funnier inside my head.

situation: Alice, scowling with her huge hair, announces to the meeting that she woke up on the wrong side of the bed. A bald, bespectacled coworker holding a coffee mug jokes that she must have been hanging upside down like a bat. Alice glares furiously at him, and he admits the joke was funnier in his head.
punchline: The coworker's bat joke insults Alice's wild hair and bad mood, and his deadpan admission that it sounded better in his head comes too late as she glares at him.
summary: A grumpy Alice mentions her bad morning, and a coworker's ill-judged quip about bats earns him a murderous glare and a belated regret.

file: 2011/2011-05-22_ignorance (knowledge)_lawyer_feels wrong_research_harvard law degree_feelingl_greasy food and ignorance_data_harvard degree over cheeseburger_bad mood_science_legal.gif
title: Data Versus The Boss's Gut Feeling

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This doesn't feel right.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It came straight from our lawyer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It just feels wrong. Can you research it a little more?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure. I can do that research in my head.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's see... Our lawyer got his degree at Harvard and has twenty years in this exact field.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whereas you have a "feeling" that is probably the result of an unholy combination of greasy food and ignorance.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The data clearly favors the Harvard law degree over the cheeseburger.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good luck. He's in a bad mood.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: (angry symbols)

setting: Office, the Boss's desk and a hallway
situation: The Boss rejects a document from the company lawyer because it just feels wrong to him, and asks Dilbert to research it further. Dilbert does the research mentally, comparing the lawyer's Harvard degree and twenty years of experience to the Boss's gut feeling, which he attributes to greasy food and ignorance. He delivers the verdict to the Boss's face, then warns a passing coworker that the Boss is in a bad mood.
punchline: Dilbert uses a mock-scientific comparison to tell the Boss his gut feeling is worthless next to the lawyer's expertise, then leaves the consequences to the next person who walks in.
summary: When his manager distrusts a legal opinion based on a hunch, an employee coolly weighs the expert's credentials against the manager's lunch and announces the result.

file: 2011/2011-12-15_industry & manufacturing_manufacturing_more green_ac units_elastic bands_hats covered eyes_don't shoot messenger_elbonian_engineering.gif
title: Green Policy Delays Elbonian Factory

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: We told our Elbonian factory to be more green, so they turned off their AC units.

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: The heat caused the elastic bands in their hats to stretch until their eyes were covered. And that's why we'll miss our ship date.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: They say you shouldn't shoot the messenger, but no one warns you how much you'll want to.

situation: The Pointy-Haired Boss reports to a senior executive that the Elbonian factory, told to be more green, switched off its air conditioning. The resulting heat stretched the elastic bands on workers' hats over their eyes, so the product will ship late. The seated executive, glaring, says he now understands why people want to shoot the messenger.
punchline: The executive's dry remark admits that the proverb about not shooting the messenger fails to mention how strong the temptation is, given the absurd chain of events the boss is reporting.
summary: A manager explains a missed deadline with a ridiculous chain of events starting from an eco-friendly directive, leaving his superior seething.

file: 2011/2011-09-07_business ethics_computers & peripherals_software_install and test_database software_engineering.gif
title: Consultant Recommends His Own Software

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend that you buy the Dogbert database software.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did I just pay a consultant to recommend his own company's software?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm totally objective.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who would install and test it?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe a consultant who knows the product?

situation: Dogbert, acting as a paid consultant, tells the Boss to buy the Dogbert database software. The Boss realizes he is paying someone to recommend his own product, and Dogbert claims to be totally objective. Dogbert then also angles to be hired to install and test the software.
punchline: The consultant's claim of objectivity is absurd because he is selling his own product and is already lining up more paid work to implement it.
summary: A consultant on the payroll pushes his own company's product and then volunteers himself to set it up, cheerfully insisting he has no bias.

file: 2011/2011-09-14_correspondence_electronic mail_genius_unfinished product_writing_hallmark of genius_unexpected use of time.gif
title: Unfinished Project Is Genius

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The hallmark of genius is doing things in a way that other people don't.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You see my project as unfinished. I see it as an unexpected use of time.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Can you see how awesome that is?

setting: Boss's office, at a desk with coffee mugs
situation: Wally sits across the desk from the Boss, who listens silently throughout. Wally explains that doing things differently is a sign of genius, then reframes his unfinished project as an 'unexpected use of time.' He ends by asking the Boss to appreciate how awesome that is, while sipping his coffee.
punchline: Wally spins his failure to complete a project as a mark of genius, using flattering-sounding jargon to excuse his laziness.
summary: Wally tries to pass off his incomplete work as a stroke of unconventional brilliance to his unimpressed boss.

file: 2011/2011-02-27_managers & supervisors_new server_corrupt operating system_bad server_recover data_reinstall_redeploy it_blindingly obvious_alternative is chaos_chaos as good_business.gif
title: Boss's Obvious Server Instructions Versus Chaos

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Build a new server to replace the one with the corrupt operating system.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's what I'm doing right now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Recover the data from the bad server and put it on the new one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's the whole point.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then see if you can reinstall the operating system on the old one and redeploy it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have any instructions that are not blindingly obvious?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is called managing. The alternative is chaos.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How did you just make chaos sound like a good thing?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You should test the new server.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Seriously, can we try the chaos thing?

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, with a title panel showing a presentation screen
situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert and gives him a string of instructions for replacing a server with a corrupt operating system, each one describing exactly what Dilbert is already doing or what is the obvious next step. When Dilbert complains, the Boss defends this as managing and says the alternative is chaos. Dilbert ends up wishing for the chaos instead.
punchline: The Boss's idea of managing is just narrating the obvious, and it is so useless that Dilbert would honestly prefer the chaos he supposedly prevents.
summary: A manager recites painfully obvious steps to his IT worker and insists this guidance is all that stands between the company and disorder.

file: 2011/2011-03-23_business ethics_work ethic_work-life balance_implies life is impirtant_work-life intergration_big thanks_never had a life.gif
title: Work-Life Integration Replaces Work-Life Balance

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We're no longer using the term "work-life balance" because it implies that your life is important.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Now we call it "work-life integration" so it's easier to make you work when you would prefer being with loved ones.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: And I'd like to give a big thanks to those of you who never had a life.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're welcome.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, with an establishing shot of an office building
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, announces at a meeting that the company is replacing the term "work-life balance" with "work-life integration". He explains the change makes it easier to pull employees into work when they would rather be with family. He then thanks the people who never had a life, and Dilbert sarcastically accepts the thanks.
punchline: The new HR buzzword is a cynical excuse to make employees work at all hours, and Dilbert's deadpan "You're welcome" admits that his own lack of a life is what the company is exploiting.
summary: An HR executive rebrands balance as integration so staff can be dragged back to work anytime, then praises the lifeless workers who make it easy.

file: 2011/2011-05-01_boats_business ethics_new boat_engineers_skills_boss's boat_picture_nautical interests.gif
title: Showing Boat Pictures to Strangers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who wants to see a picture of my new boat?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's a very good question.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If we consider the fact that we work much harder than he does...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And we have valuable engineering skills, whereas he can't operate the GPS in his SUV...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And for some reason we don't get paid enough to buy impressive boats.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And we have no nautical interests whatsoever.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think your best bet is people who don't know you.

transcript.speaker: Stranger
transcript.text: And you are?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This only works if we don't get too familiar.

setting: Office hallway, then an elevator lobby
situation: The Boss offers to show off a picture of his new boat, and Dilbert and Alice answer by listing, in a roundabout way, all the reasons they don't want to see it: they work harder, have better skills, earn too little to own a boat, and have no interest in boats. Dilbert suggests he try people who don't know him, so the Boss approaches a stranger by the elevator.
punchline: The Boss's boasting only works on people who haven't yet learned how little they care about him, so he has to show off to strangers, and he admits it only works if they never get to know him.
summary: After his employees politely explain why none of them want to admire his yacht photos, the boss goes off to impress a total stranger instead.

file: 2011/2011-07-01_anger_marriage_fist of work_feel the wrath_totally legal_eye canons_single_higher setting_politically incorrect_relationships.gif
title: Alice's Totally Legal Eye Cannons

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I have been informed that it is politically incorrect to use my Fist of Death at work.

transcript.speaker: Alice
