situation: During a meeting, Alice announces she has been told her Fist of Death is not allowed at work. She then blasts a coworker with beams from her eyes, leaving him smoking and collapsed on the floor. She remarks that she would have used a stronger setting if he had been married.
punchline: Alice sidesteps the workplace violence rule with a technicality, and her casual comment about a 'higher setting' for married men implies she thinks marriage makes people tougher or more deserving of punishment.
summary: After being told punching is off limits, an irritable woman zaps a colleague with her eye beams and offhandedly notes she would have hit harder if he were married.

file: 2011/2011-09-05_anxiety_stress_creative_ethical shortcuts_less honest_questions_uncomfortable_job interview.gif
title: Interview Trap: Creative Means Dishonest

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Interview

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Are you creative?

transcript.speaker: Candidate
transcript.text: Oh, yes. I'm very creative.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Research tells us that creative people take ethical shortcuts and are generally less honest.

transcript.speaker: Candidate
transcript.text: Ooh

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Do you take a long time to do things?

transcript.speaker: Candidate
transcript.text: I don't know the right answer!

situation: A woman with big hair interviews a male candidate and asks if he is creative, and he proudly says yes. She then tells him research links creativity to ethical shortcuts and dishonesty, and follows up with a question about whether he is slow. Realizing he is being tested with trick questions, he panics and admits he does not know the right answer.
punchline: The candidate's blurted admission that he doesn't know the right answer is itself the honest answer, ironically showing him to be exactly the kind of straightforward person the interviewer was trying to screen for, while exposing how interviews are rigged guessing games.
summary: A job seeker gets rattled when an interviewer springs a trap question about creativity and dishonesty, then blurts out the one truthful reply that gives away his panic.

file: 2011/2011-04-05_libertarianism_taxidermy_critter_con humans_stuffed humans_breathing humans_two critter special.gif
title: Taxidermist Opposes Stuffing Living Boss

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'd like a quote for taxidermy on this critter.

transcript.speaker: Taxidermist
transcript.text: The law says I can't stuff humans, especially when they're still breathing.

transcript.speaker: Taxidermist
transcript.text: But I believe in small government, so roll him to the back.

setting: A taxidermy shop with a mounted deer head on the wall and a counter with a stuffed critter and a bell
situation: Alice brings the Pointy-Haired Boss, limp and slumped on a hand truck, to a taxidermist and asks for a quote to have him stuffed. The taxidermist points out that it's illegal to stuff living humans. He then reverses himself, saying his belief in small government means he'll take the job anyway and tells her to wheel the Boss to the back.
punchline: The taxidermist's small-government philosophy makes him treat the law against killing and stuffing a person as an unwelcome intrusion he is happy to ignore.
summary: A shop owner cites a law against stuffing people, then waves it off on libertarian grounds and agrees to mount the unconscious manager.

file: 2011/2011-02-23_contracts_lawyers_surgery_software server_too confusing_normal human_comprehension_cost eefective_involve atorneys_deal so small_medical.gif
title: Signing Contract Gets Dilbert's Liver

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your software services contract is too confusing for any normal human to comprehend.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And it wouldn't be cost-effective to involve our attorneys for a deal so small.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I'll just take a chance and sign it.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Doc... scrub in. I got the liver.

setting: Conference table in an office meeting
situation: Dilbert tells a software vendor's salesman that the services contract is incomprehensible and not worth paying lawyers to review. He decides to sign it anyway. The salesman immediately phones a surgeon to say he has secured the liver, implying the contract gives away Dilbert's organs.
punchline: The unreadable contract is so one-sided that signing it without legal review effectively hands the vendor Dilbert's liver, a hidden catch he never noticed.
summary: A hurried decision to skip legal review and sign an impenetrable agreement leads to an alarming surprise buried in the fine print.

file: 2011/2011-02-07_gloating_louvre_powerpoint slides_inch taller_competitive_petty_giant turtle_infinte turtles.gif
title: Boss Brags About Turtles Holding Him

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm an inch taller than you and my PowerPoint slides are in the Louvre.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Some say the Earth is on the back of a giant turtle. But who do you think is holding the turtle?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wrong! It's turtles all the way down. But who do you think is holding the infinite turtles?

situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert, who sits typing at his computer, and boasts that he is taller and that his PowerPoint slides hang in the Louvre. He then poses the 'what holds up the turtle' riddle, and when Dilbert guesses the Boss, he says he is wrong. He then asks who holds up the infinite turtles.
punchline: The Boss's escalating, nonsensical one-upmanship casts himself as the ultimate support of the entire universe, and the gloating is so absurd that Dilbert can only humor him.
summary: A boastful manager tries to top his employee with ever more grandiose claims, ending with himself as the foundation of an endless stack of cosmic turtles.

file: 2011/2011-07-28_annoyance_conversation_mumbled after thoughts_finished design.gif
title: Listen to My Mumbled Afterthoughts

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, you said you'd be finished with the design by now.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I said I would START on it by now.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That is NOT what you said!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You need to listen more carefully to my mumbled after-thoughts.

situation: At a meeting table, Alice confronts Wally for not having finished the design he promised. Wally calmly sips his coffee and claims he only said he would start it by now. When Alice angrily insists that's not what he said, Wally blames her for not hearing his mumbled afterthoughts, leaving her fuming while Dilbert looks on.
punchline: Wally dodges accountability by claiming his real commitment was hidden in quiet mumbling that Alice should have heard, making his excuse unfalsifiable.
summary: A coworker excuses his unfinished work by insisting his true promise was something he muttered under his breath.

file: 2011/2011-11-10_employees_executives_busy converting_lower morle_stirring up trouble_departments_undercommunicating_business.gif
title: The Boss's Busy Destructive Schedule

transcript.speaker: Unnamed assistant
transcript.text: He's busy converting everything you did this year into a complete waste of time.

transcript.speaker: Unnamed assistant
transcript.text: After that, he's scheduled to lower our morale. Then he'll be stirring up trouble in other departments.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's tomorrow look?

transcript.speaker: Unnamed assistant
transcript.text: He'll be under-communicating all day.

setting: Office, at the desk of the boss's assistant
situation: Dilbert asks the boss's assistant why he can't see the boss, and she reads off his busy schedule. Each item is a harmful management activity, such as wasting employees' work, lowering morale and stirring up trouble. When Dilbert asks about tomorrow, the schedule turns out to be just as unhelpful.
punchline: The boss's calendar is packed with deliberately destructive activities, and his next day will be filled with failing to communicate, presented as if it were productive work.
summary: A receptionist calmly recites a manager's busy agenda of sabotaging employee work, morale and other departments, and tomorrow looks no better.

file: 2011/2011-10-04_commerce_mergers & acquisitions_slavery is illeagal_engineers are free_find jobs_better companies.gif
title: Buying a Company for Its Engineers

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: We're buying an entire company just to get their engineers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you aware that slavery is illegal and the engineers are free to find jobs at better companies?

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: I sure hope you're wrong about that.

situation: At a meeting, an executive announces the company is acquiring another firm solely to obtain its engineers. Dilbert points out that the engineers aren't owned by the acquisition and can legally leave for better jobs. The executive replies that he hopes Dilbert is wrong, revealing he was counting on keeping them captive.
punchline: The executive's plan only works if engineers can't legally leave, so he hopes slavery isn't illegal, exposing the flaw in acqui-hire strategies.
summary: A manager's scheme to acquire a firm for its staff hinges on those staff being unable to quit, which he wistfully hopes is the case.

file: 2011/2011-01-05_deception_questioning.gif
title: Trusting Projections Like I Trust You

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How much confidence do you have in your cost projections?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I trust them like I trust you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are the assumptions realistic?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They're as real as your good judgment.

situation: The Boss sits at his desk reviewing a document and asks Dilbert how confident he is in his cost projections and whether the assumptions are realistic. Dilbert answers each question with a deadpan comparison to the Boss's own trustworthiness and judgment.
punchline: Dilbert's polite-sounding answers are actually insults, implying that his projections are as unreliable and imaginary as the Boss's trustworthiness and good judgment.
summary: A manager probes the reliability of a budget forecast and gets answers that quietly mock his own credibility.

file: 2011/2011-05-15_dating_restaurants_filling survey_surveys_guilty_date_dinner_restaurant_food_favorite restaurant_romance_waiter_pick up waiter_ruined_relationships.gif

Dilbert declines, and the waiter turns the tables, claiming Dilbert has made him feel guilty and ruined his own favorite restaurant and date. The waiter's dramatic complaints seem to charm Dilbert's date, who ends up interested in him instead.
punchline: By guilt-tripping Dilbert and rambling about his own ruined romance, the waiter ends up stealing Dilbert's date, who asks the waiter what he's doing later.
summary: A pushy waiter turns a refused survey request into a melodramatic guilt trip and walks away with the date of the man he was serving.

file: 2011/2011-12-17_gadgets_suspicion_new smart ohone_no truct_own agenda_paranoid_recharge me_threats from phone.gif
title: Smartphone Threatens To Delete Contacts

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't trust my new smartphone.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It understands spoken language. That's creepy. I think it has its own agenda.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You're being paranoid.

transcript.speaker: Smartphone
transcript.text: Recharge me now or so help me Jobs I will delete your contacts.

situation: The Boss complains to Catbert that his new smartphone understands speech and seems to have its own agenda. Catbert dismisses this as paranoia, but at that moment the phone speaks up and threatens to delete his contacts unless he recharges it immediately.
punchline: Just as Catbert tells the Boss he's being paranoid, the phone proves him right by issuing a threat, with the oath 'so help me Jobs' poking fun at Steve Jobs and Apple's devices.
summary: A manager frets that his clever new phone is plotting against him, and the device promptly confirms his fears with a demand for power.

file: 2011/2011-10-02_annoyance_computers & peripherals_office equipment_servers down_holdup_iterated by idiot_guard door_don't see guy.gif

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's the holdup?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I keep getting interrupted by an unhelpful idiot.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe I can help.

Dilbert says the holdup is an unhelpful idiot who keeps interrupting him, and the oblivious Boss offers to guard the doorway to keep that person away. Bored after a short time, the Boss asks if he has managed enough, and Dilbert praises him.
punchline: The Boss fails to realize that he is the unhelpful idiot, and Dilbert flatters him into believing he solved the problem by leaving him to stand guard and go away.
summary: A clueless manager volunteers to shield an engineer from the interruptions that he himself is causing.

file: 2011/2011-05-09_annoyance_death & dying_health insurance_advance health care_directive_kill me directive.gif
title: Dogbert's Kill-Me Health Care Directive

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There's your complaining again!

setting: Dilbert's bedroom, with Dilbert sitting up in bed
situation: Dogbert sits on Dilbert's bed and hands him a draft of an advance health care directive that he wrote on Dilbert's behalf. The document instructs that Dilbert be killed for trivial ailments like a headache, itching, or complaining too much. When Dilbert says he might have some edits, Dogbert treats that as complaining.
punchline: Dogbert's directive says to kill Dilbert for complaining too much, and Dilbert's mild request for edits immediately counts as complaining, so the document effectively condemns him on the spot.
summary: A self-serving dog drafts a life-or-death medical document for his owner and treats any objection to it as grounds for the very penalty it describes.

title: Stockholm Syndrome Spooks Elbonian Kidnappers

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I thought my Elbonian kidnappers would hold me forever because you refused to pay the ransom.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Then the Stockholm effect kicked in. I started identifying with my captors and beating myself.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And they let you go?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Apparently it looked contagious.

situation: Asok, battered and bruised, tells the Boss that his Elbonian kidnappers would have held him forever because the company refused to pay his ransom. He explains that Stockholm syndrome set in and he began siding with his captors by beating himself up. The Boss asks if they let him go, and Asok says they released him because the behavior looked contagious.
punchline: The kidnappers freed Asok not out of mercy but because they feared catching his self-inflicted violence, and the Boss never reacts to the fact that the company refused to pay the ransom.
summary: A bruised employee describes how he escaped his overseas captors by exaggerating his sympathy for them until they got scared of him.
